## II. The Standard Statement of the Measurement Problem

### II.1 The von Neumann measurement scheme

Following von Neumann [vonNeumann1932], a quantum measurement is modeled as a unitary interaction between system S (Hilbert space ℋ\_S) and apparatus A (Hilbert space ℋ\_A). Let {|s\_i⟩}\_i be eigenstates of the system observable Ŝ being measured, and let |A\_0⟩ be the apparatus's initial "ready" state. The von Neumann measurement interaction is the unitary operator U\_meas defined by

  U\_meas |s\_i⟩ ⊗ |A\_0⟩ = |s\_i⟩ ⊗ |A\_i⟩,

where {|A\_i⟩}\_i are orthogonal pointer states of the apparatus correlated with the system's eigenvalues. Linearity of U\_meas extends this to superpositions:

  U\_meas (Σ\_i c\_i |s\_i⟩) ⊗ |A\_0⟩ = Σ\_i c\_i |s\_i⟩ ⊗ |A\_i⟩.

The post-measurement state is therefore an entangled superposition. By (U), this is the correct dynamical evolution. By (R), the apparatus is observed to be in a definite pointer state |A\_k⟩ for some specific k, with probability |c\_k|² (Born rule).

#### II.1.1 Von Neumann's Process 1 / Process 2 distinction and its relation to the McGucken the dx₄/dt = ic Algebraic Channel / the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel duality

The von Neumann measurement scheme above is the formal setting in which von Neumann (1932) [vonNeumann1932, Chapter V.1] introduced the *two-process structure* of quantum mechanics that has organised the orthodox account of quantum dynamics for the last ninety years. Von Neumann distinguished two structurally different forms of state-evolution that he postulated quantum systems undergo:

* **Process 2** (called *Vorgang 2* in the German original; sometimes labelled *Process 2* or *Process II* in the English translation): the *continuous*, *deterministic*, *causal*, *time-symmetric*, *unitary* evolution described by the Schrödinger equation iℏ∂\_t |Ψ⟩ = Ĥ|Ψ⟩. This is the dynamics that holds when no measurement is being performed.

* **Process 1** (*Vorgang 1*, *Process 1* or *Process I*): the *discontinuous*, *stochastic*, *acausal*, *time-asymmetric*, *non-unitary* reduction of the wavefunction $|\Psi\rangle = \Sigma_i c_i |s_i\rangle$ to a single eigenstate $|s_k\rangle$ upon measurement, with probability $|c_k|^2$. This is the dynamics von Neumann postulated to hold *at measurement events* — the formal mathematical content of the orthodox collapse postulate.

Von Neumann's structural claim — and it has been the load-bearing structural claim of the orthodox foundations of quantum mechanics since 1932 — is that the two processes are *both fundamental dynamical laws* and that they are *not derivable from one another*. In particular, Process 1 cannot be derived from Process 2: unitary evolution alone (Process 2) does not produce the wavefunction reduction (Process 1); a separate dynamical principle is required to account for the latter. This is the standard formulation of the measurement problem [Bell1990; Maudlin1995; Wallace2012], with Process 1 corresponding to the (R) law of §II above and Process 2 corresponding to the (U) law.

The structural difficulty is that the two processes are *not merely different* but *mutually inconsistent* in their basic structural features. Process 2 is continuous, deterministic, causal, time-symmetric, and unitary. Process 1 is discontinuous, stochastic, acausal, time-asymmetric, and non-unitary. Every adjective of one process is the negation of the corresponding adjective of the other. Yet von Neumann postulated both as fundamental laws of quantum dynamics, with the boundary between them — *when does Process 2 give way to Process 1?* — left unspecified at the level of physics (the "Heisenberg cut," the "Wigner consciousness threshold," the "von Neumann–London–Bauer abstract observer"). Ninety years of foundational work on the measurement problem is the working-out of the consequences of this unspecified boundary, with each interpretive programme (Copenhagen, Everett, Bohmian, GRW, decoherence, RQM, QBism) supplying a different account of when, where, why, and how Process 2 transitions to Process 1.

**The structural identification with the McGucken the Algebraic Channel / the Geometric Channel duality.** The Process 1 / Process 2 distinction maps onto the Algebraic Channel / the Geometric Channel duality of dx₄/dt = ic (Convention I.5.5; §I.4.4) — but *with a structural correction*. The mapping is:

* **Process 2 (Schrödinger unitary evolution)** ↔ **the Algebraic Channel** (algebraic-symmetry reading of dx₄/dt = ic): the unitary U(t) = exp(−iĤt/ℏ) is the Stone-theorem one-parameter group generated by time-translation invariance of dx₄/dt = ic (Proposition X.2). The Hamiltonian is the generator of x₄-translations. The *i* in *iℏ∂\_t* is the algebraic record of x₄'s perpendicularity to the spatial three, *interior* to the Algebraic Channel's unitary operators (§I.4.4.2). Process 2's continuity, determinism, causality, time-symmetry (in the form-invariance sense), and unitarity are *all* projections of the Algebraic Channel's reading of dx₄/dt = ic.

* **Process 1 (wavefunction collapse / state reduction)** ↔ **the Geometric Channel** in its Euclidean-signature reading via the McGucken–Wick rotation $\tau = x_4/c$: the apparently non-unitary, time-asymmetric, irreversible reduction is the Euclidean-signature reading of the *same* Schrödinger equation whose Lorentzian-signature reading is unitary (Theorem X.B; Corollary X.B.1). The discontinuity, stochasticity, time-asymmetry, and apparent non-unitarity are projections of the Geometric Channel's geometric-propagation reading: the strict +ic monotonic McGucken-Sphere expansion produces the (N+1)-vertex Feynman concentration onto a classical outcome at the apparatus scale (Proposition X.6, with localization rate Γ ∼ Nω\_C).

*The structural correction the McGucken framework makes to von Neumann's diagnosis is that Process 1 and Process 2 are not two distinct dynamical laws but **two parallel readings of one law** — the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic.* Von Neumann was right to recognise that the two structural contents are *both present in quantum dynamics*; he was right to recognise that one (continuous, unitary, time-symmetric) does not derive from the other (discontinuous, irreversible, time-asymmetric); and he was right to insist that both belong to the fundamental description of quantum systems. He was structurally incorrect, however, to posit them as *two separate axiomatic laws* requiring a Heisenberg-cut boundary between them. They are not two laws; they are *two faces of one law*, with the Heisenberg-cut "boundary" being the apparatus-scale crossover from Lorentzian-signature Geometric Channel dominance (microscopic, quantum) to Euclidean-signature Geometric Channel dominance (macroscopic, statistical-mechanical), driven by the (N+1)-vertex Feynman structure of the system-apparatus interaction.

This is the dual-channel resolution of the von Neumann two-process axiom system: Process 1 = the Geometric Channel in Euclidean signature; Process 2 = the Algebraic Channel (and the Geometric Channel in Lorentzian signature). The "Heisenberg cut" is the Lorentzian-to-Euclidean crossover, with localization rate Γ ∼ N ω\_C giving the cut its location in the (N+1)-vertex Feynman expansion (Proposition X.6, §X.11). There is no separate (R) law because Process 1 was always the Euclidean reading of the same equation that Process 2 reads in Lorentzian signature.

**Why von Neumann could not have made this identification.** Von Neumann published *Mathematische Grundlagen* in 1932; the Feynman path integral was not published until 1948 [Feynman1948]; the Feynman–Kac correspondence between Schrödinger amplitudes and Wiener-process expectations was not established until 1949 [Kac1949]; the Wick rotation as a formal device was not introduced until 1954 [Wick1954]; Nelson's stochastic mechanics derivation was not until 1966 [Nelson1966]. Von Neumann therefore lacked the *the Geometric Channel mathematical content* that is the load-bearing recognition of the present subsection — the recognition that the Schrödinger equation has a geometric-propagation reading independent of its Hilbert-space operator reading. He had only Process 2 (the Algebraic Channel) as a mathematical object; Process 1 (the Geometric Channel in Euclidean reading) had no mathematical formulation in 1932. His axiomatic two-process structure was the best diagnosis available given the mathematical tools of 1932; it correctly identified the *structural content* of the two dynamical processes; it could not yet identify the *single physical principle* (dx₄/dt = ic) that forces both as parallel readings.

The McGucken framework's structural correction is therefore not a refutation of von Neumann's diagnosis but its *completion*: von Neumann's two-process axiom system is recognised as the 1932 articulation of the dual-channel content of dx₄/dt = ic, with the structural error being only the axiomatisation of the two contents as *separate* laws when they are *parallel readings* of *one* law. The four sub-problems of §II.2 below — probability, collapse, preferred-basis, irreversibility — are problems that arise *only* under the orthodox two-axiom reading of Process 1 and Process 2 as separate laws. They dissolve under the dual-channel reading: probability is the Geometric Channel SO(3) Haar measure on the McGucken-Sphere cross-section (Proposition III.1); apparent collapse is the Geometric Channel Euclidean signature-reading at apparatus scale (Theorem X.B); the preferred basis is the Geometric Channel Compton-coupled decoherence basis (Proposition VII.1, Proposition X.6); irreversibility is the strict +ic monotonic content of the Geometric Channel (Theorem X.C). The four sub-problems are all Geometric Channel content that the orthodox tradition mistook for *a second dynamical law*. The McGucken framework recognises them as the same equation read in its other signature.

#### II.1.1-bis The founders saw both channels: Einstein 1927, Born 1926, von Neumann 1932, and why quantum mechanics arrived Algebraic-Channel-first

The two-process structure of §II.1.1 was not first seen in 1932, nor is the recognition that quantum probability is bound to nonlocality, nor that unitarity is incompatible with the probabilistic reduction, original to the recent literature (Hsu, Weissman, Finkelstein; §X.8-ter). Each of these recognitions is present at the founding of quantum mechanics, in the words of Einstein, Born, and von Neumann themselves. The founders saw the Geometric Channel content — nonlocality, probability, irreversibility — with precision, and each recorded the tension between that content and the Algebraic Channel algebraic-unitary formalism they were building. What none of them had was the single principle from which both channels descend, so each recorded the tension as an unresolved dualism, an incompleteness, or a pair of incompatible laws. The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ supplies the principle each of them reached for, and it dissolves each tension by the same identification: the two channels are the algebraic-symmetry (the Algebraic Channel) and geometric-propagation (the Geometric Channel) readings of one expanding-Sphere process. This subsection addresses the three founders in turn, then examines why quantum mechanics arrived through the Algebraic Channel with the Geometric Channel entering only as unbidden hints.

**Einstein at the 1927 Solvay Conference: probability over the expanding spherical wavefront requires action-at-a-distance.** At the Fifth Solvay Conference in 1927, Einstein posed a single-particle thought experiment that stated the link between quantum probability and nonlocality in exactly the expanding-spherical-wavefront terms the McGucken framework builds on. A single particle passes through a slit, diffracts into an expanding spherical wavefunction, and reaches a detection screen. Einstein contrasted two conceptions of the wavefunction — Conception I, on which "the de Broglie–Schrödinger waves do not correspond to a single electron, but to a cloud of electrons extended in space; the theory does not give any information about the individual processes, but only about the ensemble of an infinity of elementary processes" (the ensemble/statistical reading), and Conception II, on which "the theory has the pretension to be a complete theory of individual processes" — and observed that the second conception forces a nonlocal collapse [Einstein1927, in the Solvay proceedings; the standard English translation is Bacciagaluppi & Valentini, *Quantum Theory at the Crossroads*, Cambridge University Press, 2009, p. 441]:

> "But the interpretation, according to which |ψ|² expresses the probability that *this* particle is found at a given point, assumes an entirely peculiar mechanism of action at a distance, which prevents the wave continuously distributed in space from producing an action in *two* places on the screen. ... in my opinion, one can remove this objection only in the following way, that one does not describe the process solely by the Schrödinger wave, but that at the same time one localises the particle during the propagation. ... if one works only with the Schrödinger waves, interpretation II of |ψ|² implies to my mind a contradiction with the postulate of relativity."

This is the probability–nonlocality link, stated at a single particle, in 1927 — eight years before the Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen paper and thirty-seven years before Bell. The structure of Einstein's observation is precisely the framework's: the probability |ψ|² is spread over the whole reach of the expanding wavefront — the particle is potentially present, with the wave "continuously distributed in space" — and that spread-out probability requires "an entirely peculiar mechanism of action at a distance" to prevent the wave from "producing an action in two places on the screen." Einstein saw that the probability lives on the extended wavefront and that its collapse to one detection is a nonlocal fact, and that this nonlocal collapse stands, in his view, in "a contradiction with the postulate of relativity." He regarded the peculiar action at a distance as a defect showing quantum mechanics incomplete. Twenty years later, in a letter to Max Born of 3 March 1947, Einstein named the same nonlocal collapse with the phrase that has attached to it since [BornEinstein1971, p. 158]:

> "I cannot seriously believe in it because the theory cannot be reconciled with the idea that physics should represent a reality in time and space, free from spooky actions at a distance [*spukhafte Fernwirkungen*]."

The 1927 "peculiar mechanism of action at a distance" and the 1947 "spooky actions at a distance" are the same recognition: that on the complete-description reading, the collapse of a spatially extended wavefunction to one detection is a nonlocal fact in tension with relativity.

The McGucken framework supplies the mechanism Einstein correctly saw was required and correctly could not name. The expanding spherical wavefront is physical: it is the McGucken Sphere, the wavefront of $x_4$'s spherically symmetric expansion at $c$ (§I.4.1-bis). The probability spread "with almost constant probability over the whole area of the screen" is the isotropic $SO(3)$-Haar measure that the expansion forces, which is $|\psi|^2$ (Proposition III.1) — constant over equal solid angles because no direction on the expanding surface is preferred, since a preferred point would be a preferred direction, which the perpendicularity of $x_4$ to the spatial three forbids (§I.4.1-bis). The "peculiar action-at-a-distance" that prevents detection at two places is the $x_4$-coincidence of the one nonlocal surface: every point on the wavefront shares the emission event's accumulated $x_4$-advance $X_4$ (Theorem XII.A.2; Appendix A (R4)), so the wavefront is one object registered at one first-contact collision (§XI.5-bis), not a spatially extended thing requiring a signal to enforce single detection. What Einstein found "peculiar" — that localization at one point instantly forecloses the others — is the registration of a single $x_4$-coincident object at one event, not a signal propagating across the screen, which needs no signal because the distant parts were never causally separate in $x_4$ (§VIII.6, the Einstein's-Bubble resolution). And the apparent contradiction with relativity that Einstein flagged is dissolved by the no-signaling theorem (Proposition VIII.2): the same isotropic measure that constitutes the nonlocal correlation cloaks it in a flat marginal, so the nonlocality carries no signal and no operational conflict with Lorentz invariance arises. Einstein's 1927 observation is therefore correct in every part — probability over the expanding wavefront, action-at-a-distance at localization, tension with relativity — and each part receives its mechanism from $dx_4/dt = ic$: the physical expanding Sphere, its isotropic Born measure, its $x_4$-coincidence, and its probability-cloaking. Einstein saw the Geometric Channel content (nonlocality and probability on the expanding wavefront) and read it as a defect because he lacked the principle that makes it the geometric content of a physical expansion rather than a peculiarity of an abstract wave.

**Born 1926: the motion follows probability, but the probability propagates causally — the dualism stated at the origin.** In the paper that introduced the probability interpretation of the wavefunction, Born stated the incompatibility of the probabilistic content with the causal-unitary content in a single sentence [Born1926]: "The motion of the particle follows the laws of probability, but the probability itself propagates in accord with causal laws." Pais called this "the essence of wave mechanics" [Pais1982]; the standard reading is that it states "the dualism in quantum mechanics, a strange mixture of indeterminism and determinism, of chance and necessity." Born was precise about which part is which: the *propagation of ψ* is causal and deterministic — it is the Schrödinger evolution, the Algebraic Channel unitary content — while the *outcomes* follow probability laws that the causal propagation does not itself supply. Born himself drew the consequence: "there is no question of any causal description. One gets no answer to the question, 'what is the state after the collision' but only to the question, 'how probable is a specified outcome of the collision.'" The probabilistic content and the causal-unitary content are two different things, and the probability does not come from the causal propagation — which is exactly the statement, in 1926, that unitarity does not carry probability (§X.8-ter).

The McGucken framework identifies Born's two things as the two channels of $dx_4/dt = ic$. The causal propagation of ψ — Born's "probability propagates in accord with causal laws" — is the Algebraic Channel, the algebraic-unitary reading, the deterministic Schrödinger evolution $U(t) = \exp(-i\hat{H}t/\hbar)$ (Proposition II.1.2, the Algebraic Channel produces the complex-unitary content). The probability that the outcomes follow — Born's "motion of the particle follows the laws of probability" — is the Geometric Channel, the geometric reading, the isotropic $SO(3)$-Haar measure on the expanding Sphere realized at the first-contact collision (Proposition III.1, §V.5-bis). Born's dualism, "a strange mixture of indeterminism and determinism," is the modulus boundary of Proposition II.1.2: the deterministic Algebraic Channel propagation carries ψ up to the modulus $|\cdot|^2 : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{R}_+$, and the real probability is Geometric Channel content on the far side of that boundary, which the Algebraic Channel cannot produce (exteriorising the $i$ from the unitary group yields the non-invertible semigroup, no longer Algebraic Channel content). Born's sentence is the 1926 statement of the modulus boundary: the causal propagation is one side, the probability is the other, and they are two readings of one principle rather than one process producing the other. Born recorded the dualism exactly and, lacking $dx_4/dt = ic$, left it as a "strange mixture"; the framework supplies the single expanding-Sphere process of which the causal propagation and the probability are the two signature-readings.

**Von Neumann 1932: two formally incompatible processes, with the probabilistic one tied to thermodynamic irreversibility.** Von Neumann [vonNeumann1932, Chapter V] gave the tension its rigorous form, and — decisively for the framework's Schrödinger-contains-the-Second-Law thesis (§X.8-bis) — he tied the probabilistic process to thermodynamic irreversibility, in 1932. As §II.1.1 records, von Neumann's Process 2 (Schrödinger evolution) is continuous, deterministic, causal, reversible, unitary, and information-preserving, while Process 1 (measurement reduction) is discontinuous, stochastic, acausal, irreversible, and non-unitary; the two are formally incompatible and nothing in the theory specifies when one applies rather than the other. What §II.1.1 did not yet record, and what the historical research makes decisive, is von Neumann's own statement that the difference between the two processes is, specifically, a *thermodynamic* one: Process 1 is thermodynamically irreversible, Process 2 is reversible. Von Neumann analysed the measurement process in Chapter V of the 1932 treatise in explicitly thermodynamic terms — entropy, the Second Law, and irreversibility — and located the irreversibility in Process 1, the probabilistic reduction, not in Process 2, the unitary evolution. He thereby tied, in 1932, the three Geometric Channel contents together: the probabilistic reduction (Process 1), non-unitarity, and thermodynamic irreversibility are one package, set against the unitary, reversible, deterministic Process 2.

This is precisely the framework's dual-channel content, and von Neumann's package is the framework's the Geometric Channel: probability, non-unitarity, and the Second Law are the geometric-propagation reading of $dx_4/dt = ic$, while Process 2's unitary reversibility is the Algebraic Channel (§II.1.1; §X.8-bis, the Schrödinger equation contains the Second Law as its Euclidean signature-reading). Von Neumann's decisive error, as §II.1.1 states, was to axiomatise the two contents as *separate laws* — two fundamental dynamical processes, neither derivable from the other — when they are *parallel readings of one law*. The framework's correction is exact: Process 1 and Process 2 are the Geometric Channel and Algebraic Channel signature-readings of the one expanding-Sphere principle, rather than two laws, related by the McGucken–Wick coordinate identification $\tau = x_4/c$ (§X.8-bis). Von Neumann's "formal incompatibility" — every adjective of one process the negation of the corresponding adjective of the other — is the incompatibility of the Lorentzian and Euclidean signatures of one process, which are one geometric process read in two coordinate-unit conventions on the same expanding axis, rather than two laws in conflict. And von Neumann's tying of Process 1 to thermodynamic irreversibility is, on the framework's reading, correct and prescient: it is the 1932 recognition that the probabilistic-reduction content and the Second-Law content are the same Geometric Channel face of the principle, which is exactly what the Universal McGucken the Geometric Channel Theorem establishes (§X.8-bis; [MG-Destroyer]). Von Neumann saw the package — probability, non-unitarity, irreversibility, thermodynamics — and set it against unitary reversibility as an incompatible second law, lacking the principle that makes the two the two faces of one expansion.

**Why quantum mechanics arrived through the Algebraic Channel, with the Geometric Channel entering only as unbidden hints.** The founders' record shows a consistent pattern: the formalism of quantum mechanics was built through the Algebraic Channel — the algebraic-symmetry content — while the Geometric Channel, the geometric-propagation content that carries nonlocality, probability, and irreversibility, entered only as hints that the founders recorded as anomalies, dualisms, or defects rather than as the co-equal other face of a single principle. The pattern has a historical explanation, and the explanation is itself illuminated by $dx_4/dt = ic$.

Physics arrived at 1925 from a Newtonian and Maxwellian inheritance that was, at its foundation, deterministic and reversible. Newtonian mechanics is deterministic: given initial positions and momenta, the trajectory is fixed for all time, past and future, by time-reversible equations. Maxwell's electrodynamics is deterministic and, in its field equations, time-symmetric. Hamiltonian and Lagrangian mechanics — the very frameworks Schrödinger, Heisenberg, Dirac, and von Neumann carried into quantum theory — are built on deterministic, reversible, symplectic flow. The whole apparatus a physicist brought to the quantum in 1925 was Algebraic Channel apparatus: algebra, symmetry, conservation laws, deterministic evolution operators, reversible flow. When quantum mechanics was formalised, it was formalised in that language, because that was the language available: Heisenberg's matrix mechanics is an algebra of observables; Schrödinger's wave equation is a deterministic, reversible, linear evolution equation; Dirac's transformation theory and von Neumann's Hilbert-space axiomatisation are algebraic-operator frameworks. The unitary evolution operator $U(t) = \exp(-i\hat{H}t/\hbar)$ — the Algebraic Channel in its purest form — is the direct quantum descendant of deterministic Hamiltonian flow, and it is what the tradition was equipped to write down. Quantum mechanics arrived Algebraic-Channel-first because the physics that preceded it was Algebraic Channel physics, and the mathematical language of determinism and reversible symmetry was the only language ready to hand.

Relativity did not change this, and in one respect reinforced it. Special relativity, though it is itself an Algebraic Channel reading of $dx_4/dt = ic$ — the Minkowski metric is the squared rate of the expansion, $(ic)^2 = -c^2$ (Lemma 2.5; §I.4.1-bis), the invariance content of the principle read algebraically — presents as deterministic and reversible. The block-universe reading of Minkowski spacetime, in which past and future "lie spread out before us as in a map" with, in Eddington's words, "no signboard to indicate that it is a one-way street," is manifestly time-symmetric and deterministic: the four-dimensional manifold is given all at once, with no intrinsic arrow. Relativity therefore arrived, like Newtonian mechanics, wearing a deterministic and reversible face — the integrated, static coordinate $x_4 = ict$ rather than the active, oriented rate $dx_4/dt = +ic$ (§I.4.1). The Geometric Channel content of relativity — the $+ic$ orientation that fixes the future light-cone nappe, the arrow of causal order, the retarded-over-advanced selection (§XI.3.11, the two-atom double slit) — was present in the principle but hidden in the integrated coordinate, exactly as the Geometric Channel content of quantum mechanics was present but hidden behind the unitary operator. Both relativity and quantum mechanics were received in their Algebraic Channel dress, deterministic and reversible, because the integrated and algebraic forms are what the deterministic tradition could read; the oriented, dissipative, probabilistic Geometric Channel content of each was left as the residue the tradition could not place. This is why relativity "seemed deterministic" even though it descends from the same oriented expansion that makes the Second Law strict: the coordinate $x_4 = ict$ shows no arrow, and only the rate $dx_4/dt = +ic$ shows the orientation from which the arrow, the probability, and the irreversibility all descend.

Against this Algebraic Channel inheritance, the Geometric Channel content of quantum mechanics could enter only as hints — anomalies the deterministic framework could record but not absorb. Each founder's observation, catalogued above, is such a hint. Born's probability (1926) is Geometric Channel content entering as a "strange mixture" with the causal Algebraic Channel propagation of ψ — the probability that the deterministic wave-propagation could not supply. Einstein's action-at-a-distance (1927) is Geometric Channel nonlocality entering as a "peculiar" defect of the Algebraic Channel Schrödinger wave — the nonlocal collapse the deterministic wave-picture could not accommodate. Von Neumann's Process 1 (1932) is the whole Geometric Channel package — probability, non-unitarity, thermodynamic irreversibility — entering as a second law that had to be postulated separately because the Algebraic Channel Process 2 could not produce it. Schrödinger's entanglement (1935), which he called "the characteristic trait of quantum mechanics, the one that enforces its entire departure from classical lines of thought," is Geometric Channel nonlocality named as the defining novelty. The double-slit interference pattern and the Bell correlation (§X.8-ter) are Geometric Channel content that appears only in the plural, in the ensemble, invisible to the single-event Algebraic Channel reading. In every case the Geometric Channel content arrived as something the deterministic, reversible, algebraic framework registered as foreign — a mixture, a peculiarity, a separate law, a characteristic trait, a statistical residue — precisely because the framework was Algebraic Channel apparatus inherited from a Newtonian and relativistic world that presented as deterministic.

The McGucken framework's reading of this history is that the Geometric Channel content was never foreign; it was the other face of the same principle, entering as hints because the tradition had the Algebraic Channel face and lacked the principle that carries both. Quantum mechanics is not a deterministic theory with anomalous probabilistic and nonlocal residues, and it is not a probabilistic theory with an anomalous deterministic core; it is the theory of the one expanding-Sphere process $dx_4/dt = ic$, whose algebraic-symmetry reading (the Algebraic Channel: Hilbert space, unitary evolution, conservation laws, the deterministic propagation of ψ) is the face the deterministic tradition could read, and whose geometric-propagation reading (the Geometric Channel: the expanding Sphere, the isotropic Born measure, the $x_4$-coincident nonlocal surface, the monotonic $+ic$ irreversibility) is the face that entered as Born's probability, Einstein's action-at-a-distance, von Neumann's irreversible Process 1, and Schrödinger's entanglement. The founders saw both faces; they lacked only the recognition that the faces are one principle. The history of quantum mechanics arriving Algebraic-Channel-first, with Geometric Channel breaking through as ever-more-insistent hints across 1926 (Born), 1927 (Einstein, and de Broglie's pilot wave), 1932 (von Neumann), and 1935 (Schrödinger's entanglement, EPR), is the history of an Algebraic Channel tradition being handed, piece by piece, the Geometric Channel content of a principle it had not yet written down. The principle is $dx_4/dt = ic$, and reading its two channels together is what turns the founders' hints from anomalies into the two faces of one physical expansion.

#### II.1.2 The modulus boundary: where the Algebraic Channel's derivational reach ends

The dual-channel identification of §II.1.1 admits a sharper structural statement, which locates with precision the single point at which probability — and with it irreversibility, the arrow of time, and the existence of definite outcomes — enters quantum mechanics. The statement isolates exactly what the Algebraic Channel can and cannot produce.

**Proposition II.1.2 (The modulus operation as the Algebraic/Geometric Channel boundary).** *Quantum mechanics is derivable through the Algebraic Channel (algebraic-symmetry) reading of dx₄/dt = ic up to, and not including, the modulus operation* |·|²: ℂ → ℝ₊. *Specifically, the Algebraic Channel produces the complex-unitary structure of the theory — the Hilbert space (via the cogeneration cascade of §XIII), the self-adjoint operators (Stone's theorem on the x₄-symmetry generators), the canonical commutator* [q̂, p̂] = iℏ *(Theorem XIII.J), the Schrödinger evolution (Theorem XIII.E), and the uncertainty principle (Robertson–Cauchy–Schwarz on the derived commutator). Each of these objects is complex-valued, Lorentzian-locked, deterministic, and reversible. What the Algebraic Channel cannot produce, structurally, is a real non-negative probability measure: the transformation* ψ ∈ ℂ ↦ |ψ|² ∈ ℝ₊ *requires exteriorising the imaginary unit from the Algebraic Channel operator, and exteriorising the i from the Stone unitary* exp(−iĤt/ℏ) *converts it into the non-invertible semigroup* exp(−τĤ/ℏ)*, which is no longer a unitary representation of the time-translation group and therefore no longer Algebraic Channel content. Every empirical content of quantum mechanics that requires real numbers — Born-rule probabilities, measurement statistics, irreversibility, the existence of definite outcomes — lies on the Geometric Channel side of the modulus boundary, supplied by the McGucken–Wick rotation acting on the Geometric Channel's geometric content.*

**Proof.** The proof has three steps.

*Step 1 (the Algebraic Channel produces the complex-unitary skeleton up to the modulus).* The objects listed — Hilbert space, self-adjoint generators, canonical commutator, Schrödinger equation, uncertainty principle — are each derived in the present paper and its companions through the Algebraic Channel reading, and each is complex-valued and unitary by construction. The Stone-theorem generators are self-adjoint operators on the complex Hilbert space; the evolution U(t) = exp(−iĤt/ℏ) is a one-parameter unitary group; the commutator [q̂, p̂] = iℏ carries the i interior. None of these objects is a real non-negative measure. This is established content (§I.4.4.2, Proposition I.4.4.1).

*Step 2 (The modulus operation is unavailable to the Algebraic Channel).* Consider the map that would take the complex amplitude to a real probability. By the position-of-i diagnosis (Proposition I.4.4.1), the i in dx₄/dt = ic is *interior* to every Algebraic Channel operator: it is the algebraic record of x₄'s perpendicularity, transmitted through Stone's theorem into the operator algebra. To convert a complex amplitude ψ into the real density |ψ|² is to exteriorise this i — to move it from interior-to-the-operator onto the coordinate axis. Applied to the defining Algebraic Channel object, the Stone unitary, this exteriorisation sends exp(−iĤt/ℏ) ↦ exp(−τĤ/ℏ): a one-parameter *semigroup* that is not invertible (it has no inverse for τ > 0 when Ĥ is bounded below) and is therefore not a unitary representation of the time-translation group. The exteriorisation that produces a real measure thus dissolves the Algebraic Channel's defining group structure. the Algebraic Channel cannot perform the modulus operation while remaining the Algebraic Channel. This is the precise content of the Algebraic Channel's Lorentzian-locked status (Proposition I.4.4.1): the i cannot be exteriorised from the Algebraic Channel without dissolving it.

*Step 3 (The real-valued content lies on the Geometric Channel side).* By contrast, the same exteriorisation is available to the Geometric Channel (Proposition I.4.4.1, bi-signature status): removing the i from the Geometric Channel path-weight exp(iS/ℏ) produces the real positive Boltzmann-type weight exp(−S\_E/ℏ), which preserves the iterated-McGucken-Sphere geometric content through the signature change. The real positive Born density |ψ|² emerges on the apparatus three-slice as the Euclidean-signature reading of the Geometric Channel's geometric content (Theorem X.B; Proposition III.1). Every real-valued empirical content of quantum mechanics — probabilities, measurement statistics, irreversibility (Theorem X.C, the strict +ic monotonic content), the arrow of time — is therefore Geometric Channel content beyond the modulus boundary. The four sub-problems of §II.2 are, without exception, demands for real-valued content (a real probability, a definite real outcome, a real irreversible registration, a real preferred basis); each lies on the Geometric Channel side of the modulus boundary. **∎**

**Remark II.1.3 (The measurement problem as the structural footprint of the modulus boundary).** Proposition II.1.2 supplies a one-line diagnosis of the orthodox-tradition measurement problem: the seventy-year debate is the structural footprint of attempting to derive the real-outcome content of quantum mechanics — probabilities, definite outcomes, irreversibility — from the complex-unitary content alone, without recognising that the modulus operation is the channel boundary at which apparatus-registered real content emerges from the Geometric Channel's geometric content under the McGucken–Wick rotation. The orthodox tradition has empirical access to both Process 2 (laboratory unitary evolution between measurements) and Process 1 (laboratory measurement outcomes with Born statistics), but, reading only the Algebraic Channel as "the dynamics," it is forced to introduce the Geometric Channel's real-valued content either as a separate axiom (the Copenhagen Born-rule and projection postulates), as an interpretation question (Everett, Bohmian, QBist), as a hidden physical process (GRW, Penrose–Diósi), or as a statistical-environmental artifact (decoherence-only). None of these supplies a structural source for why Process 1 exists at all, because the Algebraic Channel alone — without the modulus that exteriorises the i — cannot produce a real positive measure. This sharpens, but does not modify, the dual-channel resolution of §II.1.1: the boundary between the two channels is the modulus operation, and that is exactly where the orthodox tradition's two "separate laws" meet.

### II.2 The four sub-problems

The measurement problem decomposes into four sub-problems:

**(P1) The probability problem.** Why is the probability of outcome k given by |c\_k|² rather than some other function of c\_k? The Born rule is taken as a postulate in standard quantum mechanics; its derivation from deeper principles has been the subject of ninety years of foundational work.

**(P2) The collapse problem.** Why does the linear superposition Σ\_i c\_i |s\_i⟩ ⊗ |A\_i⟩ appear to reduce to a single branch |s\_k⟩ ⊗ |A\_k⟩? The reduction is not a consequence of (U); it must either be added as (R) (Copenhagen, GRW) or explained away as observer-relative (Many-Worlds, RQM, QBism) or as ignorance of hidden variables (Bohmian mechanics).

**(P3) The preferred-basis problem.** The reduced density matrix ρ\_S = Tr\_A |Ψ⟩⟨Ψ| of the post-measurement state in the eigenbasis {|s\_i⟩} is diagonal: ρ\_S = Σ\_i |c\_i|² |s\_i⟩⟨s\_i|. But ρ\_S is also diagonal in any other basis obtained by unitary transformation of the eigenbasis. Why is the *eigenbasis of Ŝ* the basis in which we observe definite outcomes, rather than some other basis? The standard answer (decoherence) requires specifying the system-environment coupling — but this just shifts the problem to choosing the coupling.

**(P4) The irreversibility problem.** (R) is irreversible: once the system is in a definite eigenstate, it cannot be returned to the original superposition. (U) is reversible. Where does the asymmetry come from?

To these four standard sub-problems we add a fifth, present in any relativistic treatment:

**(P5) The nonlocality problem.** Bell-type entangled systems exhibit correlations stronger than any local hidden-variable theory permits, with the Tsirelson bound 2√2 setting the maximum quantum violation of CHSH. The standard formalism reports the violation and proves no-signalling, but does not supply a geometric mechanism for the maintained correlations across spacelike separation.

Among the surveyed frameworks, the McGucken framework is distinctive in deriving the Born rule from a single foundational physical principle (Theorem 11 of [MG-QM]; Proposition III.1 below). This is the structural fact that this paper develops in detail.

### II.4 Maudlin's three measurement problems

The contemporary canonical statement of the measurement problem in the philosophy-of-physics literature is the 1995 paper of Tim Maudlin, *Three Measurement Problems* [Maudlin1995]. Maudlin's paper is widely treated as the standard formulation; in F. A. Muller's 2023 survey [Muller2023]: *"in Maudlin (1995) what has since become the standard formulation, the measurement problem is the fact that the conjunction of the following three propositions is a contradiction."* The popular conflation reduces Maudlin's contribution to a single trilemma (Problem 1 below), but Maudlin in fact distinguished *three* structurally distinct problems that any account of quantum measurement must address. Solving Problem 1 alone is insufficient. The McGucken framework addresses all three, and the resolution of each is developed in the present paper; we set them out here for reference, with the resolution chapter (§IX.6) consolidating the three responses.

**Problem 1 — The Problem of Outcomes.** The trilemma of three jointly inconsistent claims [Maudlin1995, p. 7]:

* **(1.A) Completeness.** *"The wave-function of a system is complete, i.e. the wave-function specifies (directly or indirectly) all of the physical properties of a system."*
* **(1.B) Linear dynamics.** *"The wave-function always evolves in accord with a linear dynamical equation (e.g. the Schrödinger equation)."*
* **(1.C) Determinate outcomes.** *"Measurements of, e.g., the spin of an electron always (or at least usually) have determinate outcomes, i.e., at the end of the measurement the measuring device is either in a state which indicates spin up (and not down) or spin down (and not up)."*

The three cannot be jointly true within standard QM. If (1.A) and (1.B) hold, then a z-spin measurement on an electron in an x-spin eigenstate evolves into the superposition $\alpha|\text{up}\rangle|+\rangle + \beta|\text{down}\rangle|-\rangle$, and (1.C) fails: the measuring device is in no determinate pointer state. The three interpretive programmes — collapse (rejecting 1.B), Many-Worlds (rejecting 1.C), hidden variables (rejecting 1.A) — each pay the cost of denying one of the three, and the contemporary debate over the measurement problem is in large part the debate over which of (1.A), (1.B), (1.C) to abandon.

**Problem 2 — The Problem of Statistics.** A second trilemma, involving the Born rule directly [Maudlin1995, §3]:

* **(2.A) Completeness.** Same as (1.A): the wave-function specifies all physical properties.
* **(2.B) Deterministic evolution.** *"The wave-function always evolves in accord with a deterministic dynamical equation (e.g. Schrödinger)."*
* **(2.C) Born statistics.** *"Measurement situations described by identical initial wave-functions sometimes have different outcomes, with probabilities given (at least approximately) by Born's rule."*

The inconsistency: deterministic evolution of identical initial states (2.B) yields identical final states; completeness (2.A) then implies the systems are identical in all physical respects; but Born statistics (2.C) require that measurement outcomes can differ. Two systems with identical complete descriptions cannot have different empirical results if the dynamics is deterministic and the description is complete. Maudlin emphasizes that this is a *separate* problem from Problem 1 — solving Problem 1 by rejecting (1.A), (1.B), or (1.C) does not automatically resolve Problem 2 (which requires that the same letter be rejected consistently, or that some alternative structural distinction be drawn between deterministic 4D evolution and probabilistic 3D outcome readings).

**Problem 3 — The Problem of Effect.** The third problem concerns repeated measurements and the dynamics of possessed properties between them [Maudlin1995, §4]. The claim that a measurement reveals a possessed determinate property of the measured system — the central commitment of modal interpretations — must be reconcilable with the fact that this measurement *has no effect* on subsequent property ascriptions if the property is to remain stably possessed between successive measurements. As Muller's 2023 analysis notes [Muller2023]: *"Maudlin does not deduce a contradiction from explicit claims, and therefore Problem 3 is not in the same logical category as his other two problems."* Problem 3 targets modal interpretations specifically, demanding a coherent dynamics for possessed properties between measurements that is not supplied by the modal-interpretive bare claim of possessed determinate properties. Resolution requires a concrete mechanism for how the system's post-measurement state determines the dynamics of subsequent measurements.

Maudlin's structural conclusion in 1995 was that *"only collapse theories and hidden variables theories have a chance of succeeding [against all three problems], and, of the latter, the modal interpretations fail. Any real solution demands new physics"* [Maudlin1995, abstract]. The McGucken framework supplies the new physics Maudlin called for: dx₄/dt = ic. The resolution of all three problems is consolidated in §IX.6 below.
