## III. The Born Rule as Geometric Theorem

### III.1 Proposition III.1 (Born rule as squared-amplitude geometry of x₄-wavefront cross-sections)

**Proposition III.1 (The Born rule is a theorem of dx₄/dt = ic).** *The probability density of finding a quantum particle at spatial position x at time t, given wavefunction ψ(x, t), is*

  P(x, t) = |ψ(x, t)|²,

*as a forced geometric consequence of three structural facts about x₄'s spherically symmetric expansion: (i) the complex character of ψ is the perpendicularity marker of x₄ relative to the spatial three; (ii) the squared exponent is the unique simple polynomial order producing a positive-definite probability density that respects superposition and gives correct interference patterns; (iii) the SO(3) Haar measure on the McGucken-wavefront cross-section forces the squared-amplitude form on the angular distribution. The full three-piece derivation is imported from [MG-Bohmian, §VII] and [MG-QM, Theorem 11]; we reproduce it here in self-contained form.*

**Proof.** The proof proceeds in three pieces, each of which independently rules out alternatives to |ψ|² and which jointly force the Born rule.

#### Piece 1: Why ψ is complex

By Convention I.5.2, x₄ = ict, with the i the perpendicularity marker of x₄ relative to the spatial three. From [MG-QM, Theorem 5] (the rest-mass phase factor) and [MG-Wick, §V.5] (the twelve-i catalog), every appearance of i in quantum theory is the algebraic marker of perpendicularity to the three spatial dimensions, inherited from x₄ = ict. The wavefunction ψ(x, t) is, by [MG-QM, Theorem 6] (wave-particle duality as dual-channel reading), the 3D cross-section of the four-dimensional McGucken-wavefront associated with the particle. The four-dimensional object has both a spatial-three projection (real-valued) and an x₄ projection (imaginary-valued), and the complex amplitude

  ψ(x, t) = Re ψ(x, t) + i · Im ψ(x, t)

records both projections simultaneously. The complex structure of ψ is, on this reading, the algebraic expression of the four-dimensional structure of the McGucken-wavefront, with i tracking the x₄-component, rather than an independent postulate. Real-valued wavefunctions exist as standing waves but cannot account for the probability current j = (ℏ/m) Im(ψ\* ∇ψ) or coherent time-evolution; the i is required because x₄ is required.

#### Piece 2: Why the exponent is 2 (not 1 or 3)

A probability density derived from ψ must satisfy four conditions:

**(C1) Positivity.** P(x, t) ≥ 0 everywhere.

**(C2) Normalization.** ∫ P(x, t) d³x = 1 over all space.

**(C3) Superposition-respecting.** If ψ = αφ + βχ with α, β ∈ ℂ, P(x, t) must be computable from φ and χ in a way that gives correct interference patterns observed in double-slit, Mach-Zehnder, neutron interferometry, and matter-wave experiments [Davisson-Germer1927; Tonomura1989; Arndt1999; Fein2019].

**(C4) Lorentz-covariance.** Under a Lorentz transformation, P(x, t) transforms as the time-component of a four-current (with appropriate normalization).

Consider the candidates for the form of P(x, t) as a function of ψ:

* P = |ψ|¹ = |ψ|: violates (C3). For ψ = αφ + βχ, |ψ| = |αφ + βχ| does not produce the cross-term cos(θ) interference observed experimentally; it produces |α||φ| + |β||χ| in the worst case (no interference) or some non-quadratic combination that does not match observation.

* P = |ψ|³: violates (C3) in the same way as |ψ|¹ — the cross-term in |αφ + βχ|³ has the wrong functional form to produce experimentally correct interference patterns — and lacks the conserved-current structure (C4) that the bilinear form ψ\*ψ supplies; it does not arise as the time-component of any conserved four-current.

* P = Re(ψ) alone: violates (C1) — ψ may be purely imaginary, in which case Re(ψ) = 0 globally even for nonzero ψ.

* P = Im(ψ) alone: violates (C1) — symmetric problem.

* P = Re(ψ)² + Im(ψ)² = |ψ|²: satisfies all four conditions. (C1) is automatic; (C2) is the requirement that ψ be normalized in L²; (C3) is satisfied because

  |αφ + βχ|² = |α|²|φ|² + |β|²|χ|² + 2 Re(α\*β φ\*χ),

  and the cross-term 2 Re(α\*β φ\*χ) is exactly the interference term observed experimentally; (C4) is satisfied because ψ\*ψ is the time-component of the conserved Klein-Gordon current j^μ = (iℏ/2m)(ψ\*∂^μψ − ψ∂^μψ\*) divided by appropriate factors.

* P = |ψ|^{2n} for n > 1: candidates such as |ψ|⁴, |ψ|⁶ violate normalization (C2) without ad hoc rescalings, and produce wrong interference patterns in Piece-2 (C3) tests: the cross-term in |αφ + βχ|^{2n} has higher-order correlations not observed experimentally.

The squared exponent is therefore *forced* by the four conditions (C1)–(C4) and the requirement that the probability density match observed interference patterns. No exponent other than 2 satisfies all conditions.

#### Piece 3: Why the spherical-symmetric SO(3) Haar measure forces the squared form

By Convention I.5.3, the McGucken Sphere is a 2-sphere expanding at speed c from each spacetime event. Spherical symmetry of x₄'s expansion (Convention I.5.2) forces SO(3) invariance of the angular distribution of the McGucken-wavefront cross-section. The unique SO(3)-invariant measure on the 2-sphere is the SO(3) Haar measure, which in standard spherical coordinates (θ, φ) takes the form sin θ dθ dφ.

The probability density of finding the particle in solid angle dΩ at angle (θ, φ) is therefore proportional to the projected amplitude of ψ at that angle, weighted by the SO(3) Haar measure. Explicitly, for a wavefunction with angular structure ψ(r, θ, φ) = R(r) Y(θ, φ),

  P(θ, φ) dΩ ∝ |Y(θ, φ)|² sin θ dθ dφ.

The squared form |Y|² is *forced* by the SO(3) invariance: any other functional form (e.g. |Y|, |Y|³, Re(Y)²) breaks SO(3)-equivariance under change of polar axis, since complex amplitudes Y(θ, φ) acquire phases under SO(3) rotation but |Y|² is phase-invariant. This is the standard fact that |Y\_lm|² is the SO(3)-invariant angular distribution; here it is recovered as a forced consequence of the spherical symmetry of x₄'s expansion.

#### Conclusion

The three pieces *jointly* force P = |ψ|² as the unique probability density on the McGucken-Sphere wavefront cross-section consistent with the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic:

* The complex character of ψ (Piece 1) is forced by the perpendicularity marker i of x₄.
* The squared exponent (Piece 2) is forced by positivity, normalization, superposition, and Lorentz-covariance.
* The squared form on angular distributions (Piece 3) is forced by the SO(3) symmetry of x₄'s spherical expansion.

The Born rule is therefore not a postulate — it is the unique probability density consistent with all three structural facts about x₄'s expansion. **∎**

### III.1-bis The wavefront reading: why the oscillatory structure the Born rule rests on is in the premise

Piece 1 established that ψ is complex because the i marks x₄-perpendicularity. A further reading of the same principle grounds the oscillatory and action content that the Born statistics depend on, and it bears directly on the reply to Kinney in §XIV-bis: the value ℏ and the Compton frequency ω_C = mc²/ℏ enter the Born-rule apparatus, and their status — derived or posited — is settled by reading the advance as a wavefront.

The clause of the principle that x₄ expands "in a spherically symmetric manner at velocity c from every event" is, read precisely, the statement that x₄ expands as a wavefront. A wavefront is an oscillatory object: the surface of constant phase of an oscillation. To call the x₄-advance a wavefront is therefore to commit to its carrying a wavelength λ (the spatial period), a frequency ω (the temporal period, with the rate c relating the two), a phase (the wavefront being the surface of constant phase, so the advance carries exp(iθ) with θ accumulating along it), and an action — a phase accumulated per oscillatory cycle, the quantity exp(iS/ℏ) records, with an action-per-cycle that is the quantum of action of the advance. A surface with no wavelength and no frequency is not a wavefront but a bare moving locus; the wavefront reading of dx₄/dt = ic thus entails the oscillatory action structure at the level of the founding statement.

On this reading c and ℏ are twin properties of the one advance: c is the rate of the wavefront, ℏ is the action accumulated per oscillatory cycle. They are not two independent inputs — a rate measured in relativity and an action measured in quantum mechanics — but two properties of a single oscillatory expansion. The existence of an action-per-cycle is not a separate commitment adjoined to a bare rate; it is entailed by the advance being a wavefront, because a wavefront oscillates and an oscillation that carries phase carries action. The oscillatory structure from which the Compton frequency, the de Broglie relation, and the phase content of ψ descend was in the premise the moment the advance was read as a wavefront.

The rigorous boundary is between existence and value. The wavefront reading entails that there is a wavelength, that there is a frequency, and that there is an action-per-cycle; it does not by itself fix their numerical values. That the action-per-cycle takes the value ℏ is the empirical anchor (the measured value of Planck's constant); that the frequency of a massive particle's wavefront is the Compton frequency ω_C = mc²/ℏ specifically is fixed by the mass-shell normalization relating rest energy to oscillation frequency. The wavefront reading therefore converts the existence of the oscillatory action structure from a separate postulate into an entailment of dx₄/dt = ic read as wavefront expansion, while the value of ℏ remains an empirical anchor and the Compton value of the frequency routes through the mass-shell. This is the precise sense in which the dynamics are in the premise: the oscillatory structure is entailed, and only the scale-setting numbers are external — which is the reduction-in-posits that the reply to Kinney (§XIV-bis) makes central.

### III.1-ter The physical origin of the conjugate factor: two McGucken Spheres, and PT-symmetry through the source event

Proposition III.1 derives the Born density $P = \psi^*\psi = |\psi|^2$ as the isotropic $SO(3)$-Haar measure on the McGucken-Sphere cross-section, with the bilinear $\psi^*\psi$ structure forced by the rank-2 character of the Minkowski metric (Lemma 7.1 of [MG-Minkowski-Hilbert], inherited from $(ict)^2 = -c^2$). That derivation fixes that the density is bilinear in $\psi$ and its conjugate $\psi^*$, and that the exponent is 2. It leaves a distinct question, which this subsection answers: what is the conjugate factor $\psi^*$, physically? In orthodox quantum mechanics $\psi^*$ is a formal algebraic operation on $\psi$ with no physical referent. The McGucken framework supplies $\psi^*$ a physical meaning, and it does so in two complementary readings — one for the detection event, one for free propagation — both imported here from the flagship derivation [MG-Minkowski-Hilbert, §7.10; Theorems 7.7 and 7.11]. The two readings, together with the cascade-level reading of Theorem 7.4, are the three jointly consistent physical accounts of the one squaring operation $\psi \mapsto \psi^*\psi$.

**The detection-event reading: two McGucken Spheres meeting head-on (Theorem 7.7).** At a measurement, two wavefronts of one excitation are present: the emitter's McGucken Sphere and the absorber's McGucken Sphere, both expanding forward at $+ic$ from their respective source events. The Born product $\psi^*\psi$ is the algebraic record of these two Spheres meeting head-on in $x_4$ at the detection event. The physical content of the conjugate factor is this: because the two Spheres emanate from different spacetime events, the absorber's outgoing $+ic$-expansion, viewed in the emitter's frame, appears antiparallel to the emitter's along the shared normal at the point where the two Sphere surfaces meet. The geometry is sharp: where two expanding Spheres intersect, their surfaces are tangent at the meeting point, sharing one tangent plane and one normal line through it; by the Huygens structure (every point of a McGucken Sphere is itself the origin of a secondary Sphere expanding along the normal to the wavefront), each surface is locally generated at the meeting point by its secondary Sphere expanding along that common normal — and the two secondary expansions run along the same normal line but in opposite directions, the source's outward from the source side and the absorber's outward from the absorber side, meeting head-on. This antiparallel appearance is the frame-relational content of complex conjugation: $\psi$ is the emitter's forward expansion, $\psi^*$ is the absorber's equally-forward expansion read in the emitter's frame, where the reversed radial orientation along the connecting axis reverses the phase, $e^{i\varphi} \mapsto e^{-i\varphi}$, which is exactly conjugation. The conjugate factor is therefore not a wave propagating backward in time — every Sphere expands forward at $+ic$ — but the forward expansion of the absorber's Sphere seen from the emitter's frame (the discriminator against Cramer's advanced wave, §XI.3.9). At the head-on meeting the two $x_4$-momenta cancel, and the cancelled $x_4$-momenergy is redeposited as 3-spatial momenergy by four-momentum conservation, localizing both participating systems at the collision event (§XI.5-bis). The Born product $\psi^*\psi$ is thus the physical meeting of two forward-expanding Spheres of one excitation from two different origins, and the modulus $|\cdot|^2 : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{R}_+$ (Proposition II.1.2) is realized at that meeting. Two Spheres from a single origin would be one Sphere with no relative sign; the conjugation is present precisely because the emitter and absorber are at different events, so that a preferred antiparallel axis — the line joining the two source events — exists to carry the relative phase reversal.

The cancellation that produces a real probability is then explicit. The emitter Sphere's advance carries the wavefunction $\psi$ with its $+i$ perpendicular phase; the absorber Sphere's advance carries the conjugate $\psi^*$ with its $-i$ perpendicular phase; their head-on meeting at the shared point is the product $\psi\,\psi^* = |\psi|^2$, a real non-negative number, because in polar form $\psi = r\,e^{i\varphi}$ and $\psi^* = r\,e^{-i\varphi}$, so $\psi\,\psi^* = r^2$. The $+i$ phase of the one advance and the $-i$ phase of the other cancel exactly in the product: the phase — the perpendicular $x_4$-content — is what the meeting annihilates, and the amplitude-squared is what survives. The Born density is therefore the physical overlap of two forward $x_4$-advances of one excitation, one read as $+i$ and the other as $-i$ along the shared normal, their perpendicular phases cancelling into the real measure $r^2 = |\psi|^2$. The realness and non-negativity of the Born density, which orthodox quantum mechanics secures by the formal act of multiplying by a complex conjugate, is here the geometric fact that two oppositely-oriented perpendicular advances meeting head-on annihilate their phase and leave their squared amplitude.

**The free-propagation reading: PT-symmetry through the source event (Theorem 7.11).** The detection-event reading supplies $\psi^*$ from an external absorber. A free particle propagating before it interacts with any detector has a well-defined $\psi$ and a well-defined $|\psi|^2$ with probability content, yet no absorber Sphere is present. For this regime the conjugate factor is supplied by the McGucken Sphere's own intrinsic symmetry through its source event, rather than by an external absorber. The McGucken Principle states that $x_4$ advances as a spherically symmetric wavefront expanding at $c$ from every event $E$; the natural symmetry of such a wavefront is reflection through $E$, which in four-dimensional spacetime is the combined parity-and-time-reversal operation $PT_E$ sending $(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_E,\, t - t_E) \mapsto -(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_E,\, t - t_E)$. This 4D $PT_E$-reflection is an exact symmetry of the McGucken-Sphere expansion, and under it the McGucken-derived wavefunction satisfies the identity $\psi(PT_E \cdot \text{event}) = \psi^*(\text{event})$ exactly, established by Fourier decomposition over plane-wave components with their explicit $PT_E$ transformation [MG-Minkowski-Hilbert, Theorem 7.11]. Complex conjugation in quantum mechanics is therefore the McGucken-Sphere $PT$-symmetry through the source event: the Born density at any event is the multiplication of $\psi(\mathbf{P}, t)$ with $\psi(2\mathbf{x}_E - \mathbf{P},\, 2t_E - t)$, the value of the wavefunction at the $PT_E$-reflected event.

An earlier framing of this reading, on which the symmetry was the antipodal map $\mathbf{P} \mapsto 2\mathbf{x}_E - \mathbf{P}$ on the 2-sphere at fixed parameter time $t$, is geometrically suggestive but mathematically incomplete, and the distinction is stated here rather than passed over. For a plane-wave component $\psi_k(\mathbf{P}, t) = \exp(i\mathbf{k}\cdot(\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{x}_E) - i\omega(k)(t - t_E))$, the antipodal-at-fixed-$t$ map reverses the spatial phase $\mathbf{k}\cdot(\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{x}_E) \mapsto -\mathbf{k}\cdot(\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{x}_E)$ but leaves the temporal phase $\omega(k)(t - t_E)$ unchanged, so it yields complex conjugation only up to a residual temporal-phase factor $\exp(-2i\omega_k(t - t_E))$ that vanishes only for energy eigenstates, where $\omega$ is single-valued and the temporal phase is global. For general non-stationary wavefunctions the residual factor does not vanish. The exact statement is therefore the full 4D $PT_E$ symmetry, which reverses the temporal phase along with the spatial phase; the spatial-slice antipodal map appears as its restriction at fixed $t$ — exact for stationary states with definite parity, approximate up to a residual temporal phase for general states.

**The two readings together.** The detection-event reading (Theorem 7.7) and the free-propagation reading (Theorem 7.11) place the conjugate factor on the same geometric foundation as the complex character of $\psi$ itself: the complex structure comes from $i$ as the perpendicularity marker of $x_4$ (Proposition III.1, Piece 1; Theorem 3.1 of [MG-Minkowski-Hilbert]), and the conjugation comes from the reversal of $x_4$-orientation — the absorber's Sphere seen antiparallel in the detection-event reading, the $PT_E$-reflection through the source event in the free-propagation reading. Both are the reversal of the forward $+ic$-advance relative to a reference: relative to the emitter's frame in the first case, relative to the source event $E$ in the second. Neither invokes a backward-in-time wave. The bilinearity $\psi^*\psi$ that Lemma 7.1 forces from the rank-2 metric is thereby given its physical content: the two factors are the forward $x_4$-expansion and its orientation-reversed reading, meeting at the event where the Born density is evaluated, and the squaring operation $\psi \mapsto \psi^*\psi$ that produces real probability from complex amplitude is the meeting of a forward McGucken-Sphere expansion with its orientation-reversed counterpart.

**What derives the conjugation, and what interprets it.** A precise accounting separates the physical picture from the derivation, because the flagship grades the two differently [MG-Minkowski-Hilbert, Lemma 7.7.5]. The physical picture — the two Spheres meeting head-on, the absorber's forward expansion seen antiparallel along the common normal, the $+i$ and $-i$ perpendicular advances overlapping — is the physical *interpretation* of the conjugation; it exhibits where in the world the two factors of $\psi^*\psi$ live and why their meeting is real. The *derivation* of the conjugation is separate and is what carries the rigor: the coincidence pairing of two amplitudes has the product form $\psi_A\,\psi_B$ (rather than a sum, maximum, or mean) by the action-additivity of independent paths combined with the exponential phase content $\exp(iS/\hbar)$ of each wavefront (Lemma 7.7.5, Step 1), and the conjugation of one factor — converting the forward-times-forward product $\psi_A\,\psi_B$ to the sesquilinear $\psi_A\,\psi_B^*$ — is forced by the complexification of the symmetric rank-2 metric $\eta_{\mu\nu}$ (Lemma 7.1, symmetric since $\eta_{\mu\nu} = \eta_{\nu\mu}$) together with the requirement that the Born density be real on the diagonal (requirement R1 of Proposition III.1): the bilinear complex extension of a symmetric form has a generally non-zero imaginary part on the diagonal, while the sesquilinear extension uniquely gives a real diagonal, so R1 excludes the bilinear extension and forces the sesquilinear one, which is exactly the extension carrying conjugation (Lemma 7.7.5, Step 2). The conjugation is therefore the structural conjugation of the sesquilinear inner product — a theorem of the rank-2 metric plus R1, both McGucken-internal — and neither a Lorentz-boost frame change (the action $S$ is a Lorentz scalar) nor the Stueckelberg–Feynman time-reversal postulate. The head-on-collision antiparallelism is the physical realization of this structural conjugation, not its source: the geometry shows the conjugation happening in the world, and the rank-2 metric with R1 proves it must. On the flagship's own grading this upgrades the conjugation from a residual postulate to a derived result [MG-Minkowski-Hilbert, Lemma 7.7.5(d)].

The two-Sphere origin of $\psi\psi^*$ can be set directly against the one prior programme that reached for the same structure — Cramer's Transactional Interpretation, which also identified the Born density as the product of a forward amplitude and its conjugate (§XI.3.9). The comparison is feature by feature.

| Feature | McGucken $dx_4/dt = ic$ | Transactional Interpretation (Cramer 1986) |
|---|---|---|
| Status | Physical derivation from a principle | Interpretation of standard QM |
| Origin of $\psi\psi^* = |\psi|^2$ | Two Spheres meeting at a tangent point, $+i$ against $-i$ | Offer wave $\times$ advanced confirmation wave |
| The conjugate $\psi^*$ | Derived: the other Sphere's forward advance, oppositely directed along the shared normal | Postulated: a real wave travelling backward in time |
| Backward-in-time waves | None | Required (advanced solutions, real) |
| Perfect-absorber universe | Not required | Required (Wheeler–Feynman) |
| Causal paradoxes | None | Avoided only by declaring the transaction atemporal |
| Scope | GR, QM, thermodynamics as theorem chains | Reinterprets non-relativistic QM only |

Both accounts recognize that the Born density is the product of a forward amplitude and a conjugate, and that this product is what makes $|\psi|^2$ real and non-negative; the Transactional Interpretation reached for this physical reality of $\psi\psi^*$ honourably and first. The difference is that the conjugate factor the Transactional Interpretation had to postulate as a real backward-in-time wave — at the cost of the perfect-absorber universe and the atemporal handshake — is here the absorber Sphere's ordinary forward $+ic$-advance, oppositely directed along the shared normal, so that no backward-in-time propagation, no perfect-absorber requirement, and no causal paradox is incurred. The fuller treatment of the Transactional Interpretation as an interpretation-versus-derivation is given at §XI.3.9.

### III.2 Comparison with prior derivations

The Born rule has been the subject of multiple derivations from auxiliary axioms over ninety years. We compare each to the McGucken derivation.

**Gleason's theorem (1957).** Gleason proved that the only probability measure on the closed subspaces of a separable Hilbert space of dimension ≥ 3 satisfying noncontextuality (the probability of a subspace depends only on the subspace, not on the basis containing it) and σ-additivity is the Born rule [Gleason1957]. The theorem is mathematically rigorous but takes the Hilbert-space structure and the noncontextuality assumption as starting points. The McGucken framework derives both — the Hilbert space follows from the linear superposition of McGucken-wavefronts (Convention I.5.3), and noncontextuality follows from SO(3) invariance of the cross-section (Piece 3 above).

**Decision-theoretic derivation (Deutsch 1999; Wallace 2012).** Within Many-Worlds, the Born rule is derived from rationality axioms governing how an agent should bet on outcomes. The derivation requires accepting (i) the equivalence of all branches as "real" outcomes, (ii) specific rationality axioms (independence, transitivity, dominance), and (iii) the Many-Worlds ontology. Multiple critics [Albert2010; Saunders2010] have argued that the rationality axioms themselves require justification not present in the framework. The McGucken derivation requires no decision theory and no specific ontology: it follows from the geometric structure of x₄'s expansion.

**Envariance (Zurek 2005).** Zurek derives the Born rule from "environment-assisted invariance" — symmetry properties of system-environment entangled states. The derivation requires treating environmental degrees of freedom as part of the framework, and assumes a specific form of environment-system coupling. The McGucken derivation requires no environmental coupling: the Born rule is forced by the geometry of x₄'s expansion alone, with environmental coupling appearing only later in the preferred-basis selection (Proposition VII.1 below).

**Bohmian equilibrium hypothesis.** Bohmian mechanics derives the Born rule from the assumption that particles are initially distributed according to |ψ|² [Dürr-Goldstein-Zanghì1992]. Valentini [Valentini, 1991] showed that quantum non-equilibrium states (with distributions other than |ψ|²) are stable under Bohmian dynamics, so the equilibrium hypothesis is a separate postulate not derivable from the Bohmian dynamics itself. The McGucken framework requires no equilibrium hypothesis: the Born rule is forced by the geometry of x₄'s expansion at all times, not just initially.

**Frequentist / many-trial limit (Hartle 1968; Farhi-Goldstone-Gutmann 1989).** The Born rule is derived as the limit of relative frequencies in an infinite ensemble of measurements. The derivation requires accepting specific operational definitions of probability and infinite-trial limits, and has been criticized for circularity (the derivation uses |ψ|² in defining the limit). The McGucken derivation makes no reference to ensembles or trial limits.

**Structural diagnosis.** Each prior derivation requires auxiliary assumptions: the Hilbert-space structure (Gleason), Many-Worlds ontology plus rationality axioms (decision theory), specific environmental couplings (envariance), the equilibrium hypothesis (Bohmian), or ensemble limits (frequentist). The McGucken derivation requires only the McGucken Principle plus the standard conditions (positivity, normalization, superposition, Lorentz-covariance, SO(3) symmetry) shared with all reasonable physical theories. The structural reduction is substantial: where seven other frameworks each make the Born rule depend on auxiliary postulates, the McGucken framework makes it depend only on the geometry of x₄'s expansion.

### III.3 What this gains structurally

Proposition III.1 closes a foundational question that has stood since Born's 1926 paper. The Born rule is no longer a postulate in need of interpretation; it is a theorem of one geometric principle. Five structural consequences follow.

**First**, Q3 of the Dirac–von Neumann postulate system (Born rule) is removed from the foundational base of quantum mechanics. The McGucken framework does not require Born as a postulate; it derives Born from dx₄/dt = ic.

**Second**, the structural simplification is quantitative. By [MG-LagrangianOptimality, §3.1], the McGucken Principle has Kolmogorov complexity K(McG) ∼ 10² bits; the Dirac–von Neumann axiomatic system has K(Q1–Q6) ∼ 10⁴ bits. Removing Q3 from the postulate list and recovering it as a theorem is one of six such reductions performed by the McGucken framework, which together account for the two-orders-of-magnitude compression.

**Third**, the squared-amplitude structure now has a geometric source: the spherical-symmetric expansion of x₄. Without the McGucken Principle, |ψ|² is a fact in need of interpretation; with the principle, |ψ|² is the algebraic expression of SO(3)-invariant angular distributions on the McGucken-wavefront cross-section.

**Fourth**, the i in ψ is now traceable to x₄ = ict. The complex structure is not an algebraic peculiarity but the perpendicularity marker of the fourth dimension. This connects the Born rule to the complex structures of [MG-Wick, §V.5] (the twelve i's by hand): the Schrödinger i, the canonical commutation [q̂, p̂] = iℏ, the path integral weight e^(iS/ℏ), the Dirac iγ^μ, the +iε prescription, the Fourier kernel, the Heisenberg evolution, the Wick rotation, and the complex wave function itself are all geometric consequences of the same dx₄/dt = ic.

**Fifth**, the Lorentz-covariance of the Born rule (condition C4 in Piece 2) is automatic in the McGucken framework, since dx₄/dt = ic is Lorentz-covariant by construction (the Minkowski metric is recovered from x₄ = ict; see [MG-QM, §1.5.2; MG-Proof]). In other frameworks, Lorentz-covariance of the probability density requires separate argument [Streater-Wightman1964].

### III.4 The Stern–Gerlach experiment: spin-1/2, the two-outcome splitting, and the 50/50 distribution as theorems of dx₄/dt = ic

The Stern–Gerlach experiment (Gerlach and Stern 1922 [SternGerlach1922]) is the canonical empirical test of quantum angular-momentum quantization and the cleanest single setting in which to exhibit the McGucken account of probability at work. A beam of spin-1/2 atoms (the original used silver, each atom carrying one unpaired electron spin) passes through an inhomogeneous magnetic field with gradient along a chosen axis, conventionally z. The beam splits into exactly two components; an initial state with spin oriented perpendicular to z (along x, say) yields a 50/50 split between the two outcomes; and an initial state at polar angle θ to z yields outcome frequencies cos²(θ/2) and sin²(θ/2).

This subsection establishes three facts as consequences of the McGucken framework, each at the level of rigor the underlying corpus results support, and each with its load-bearing assumption stated explicitly rather than concealed: (i) the spin-1/2 structure — the two-valuedness itself — descends from the SU(2) double cover of the McGucken-Sphere SO(3) symmetry; (ii) the two-outcome splitting is the antipodal structure of the measurement axis intersecting the Bloch sphere; (iii) the 50/50 distribution, and the general cos²(θ/2) law, follow from the Born rule of Proposition III.1 once the spin state space is in hand. A concluding remark identifies precisely the one premise on which the probability content rests, and records a structural fact about the orthodox tradition's most celebrated Born-rule derivation — Gleason's theorem — that bears directly on this experiment.

#### III.4.1 Spin-1/2 from the SU(2) double cover of the McGucken-Sphere SO(3)

We first establish that the spin-1/2 structure — the existence of a two-dimensional complex state space carrying a faithful action of the rotation group's double cover — is forced by the McGucken framework. The argument is imported from [MG-SMGauge, Part I], whose relevant content we state precisely, marking what is forced by dx₄/dt = ic and what is consumed from standard mathematics.

**Lemma III.4.1 (SO(3) symmetry of the McGucken Sphere).** *The McGucken Sphere Σ\_M(p₀, t) = { x ∈ ℝ³ : |x − x₀| = c(t − t₀) } generated by dx₄/dt = ic from a source event p₀ carries SO(3) as its maximal connected compact symmetry group, and this SO(3) is the algebraic content of the rotational invariance of the rate constant c on the right-hand side of the principle.*

*Proof.* For R ∈ SO(3) acting on ℝ³ about x₀, one has |R(x − x₀)| = |x − x₀| = c(t − t₀), so R preserves Σ\_M; applying the same to R⁻¹ gives equality, so SO(3) is a symmetry group. Maximality is the classical fact that the isometry group of the round 2-sphere is O(3), with SO(3) its connected orientation-preserving subgroup [Petersen2016, Ch. II]. The structural origin within the framework: dx₄/dt = ic asserts that the rate constant c is a scalar under spatial rotations — independent of the direction along which the wavefront's spatial intersection is measured. Were c direction-dependent, the level set |x − x₀| = c(t − t₀) would be a metric ellipsoid with symmetry broken to a proper subgroup of SO(3). The rotational invariance of c forces the level set to be a metric sphere with full SO(3) symmetry. **∎**

*Scope note.* What is forced by dx₄/dt = ic is the SO(3) symmetry of the wavefront, via the rotational invariance of c. The classification of the isometry group of S² is standard differential geometry, consumed by citation, not re-derived.

**Lemma III.4.2 (The spin lift and the two-dimensional complex representation).** *Let Cl(1,3) be the Clifford algebra of the McGucken-derived Minkowski space, selected by the four-dimensional structure of ℳ\_G per [MG-SMGauge, Lemma on Clifford structure]. Its even subalgebra satisfies Cl(1,3)⁺ ⊗\_ℝ ℂ ≅ M₂(ℂ) ⊕ M₂(ℂ), whose two simple summands carry exactly two inequivalent irreducible complex representations S⁺, S⁻, each of complex dimension 2. The SO(3) symmetry of Lemma III.4.1 lifts to its double cover Spin(3) ≅ SU(2), acting on each S^± as the spin-1/2 representation, and this action lies in SU(S^±) ≅ SU(2).*

*Proof.* The Clifford and representation-theoretic facts are standard [LawsonMichelsohn, Thm I.5.7] and are stated here, not reproved. The SO(3) action of Lemma III.4.1 extends to the Clifford algebra Cl(3,0) ↪ Cl(1,3)⁺ and is implemented on spinors by the Spin group via Clifford multiplication; the lift Spin(3) → GL(S^±) exists and is unique up to the double-cover ambiguity [LawsonMichelsohn, Ch. I]. The image lies in SU(S^±): Clifford multiplication preserves the Cl(1,3)-invariant Hermitian pairing, so the image is unitary; and since Spin(3) ≅ SU(2) is connected and simply connected with trivial abelianization, any homomorphism to U(1) is constant, forcing the determinant to be unity, hence the image lies in SU(S^±). The dimension being exactly 2 — and the gauge/representation group being SU(2) rather than SU(N), N ≠ 2 — is forced by the complex dimension of the Cl(1,3)⁺ irreducible representation, which is fixed by the four-dimensionality of ℳ\_G. **∎**

*Scope note.* The framework forces (a) which Clifford algebra applies — Cl(1,3), selected by the 4D structure of ℳ\_G — and hence (b) the representation dimension 2, hence (c) the appearance of SU(2) specifically. The double-cover relation SU(2) → SO(3), the Clifford classification, and the representation theory are standard mathematics consumed by citation. In the precise sense of [MG-SMGauge], dx₄/dt = ic *selects* the structure that fixes spin-1/2; it does not re-derive the group theory of Spin groups, which holds independently.

**Corollary III.4.3 (Spin-1/2 two-valuedness).** *The state space of the McGucken spin degree of freedom is the two-dimensional complex representation S^+ ≅ ℂ², acted on by SU(2) as the spin-1/2 representation. The half-integer character — that a 2π spatial rotation returns the state to its negative, requiring 4π for the identity — is the defining signature of the SU(2) double cover, and is therefore present by Lemma III.4.2.*

This establishes the arena of the Stern–Gerlach experiment — a qubit, ℂ² with its SU(2) action — as a consequence of the SO(3) symmetry of x₄'s expansion together with the standard spin representation theory the framework consumes.

*McGucken Principle anchor.* The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic predicts that matter carries an x₄-orientation: the rest field accumulates the phase exp(−Bω_C t) of the spherically symmetric wavefront at the Compton frequency ω_C = mc²/ħ, on the right-hand side of the field (Definition 7.1 of [MG-DiracSpinors]). #### III.4.2 The two-outcome splitting

**Proposition III.4.4 (Two outcomes from the antipodal structure of the measurement axis).** *A Stern–Gerlach apparatus with field gradient along the unit axis n̂ measures the spin projection operator n̂ · σ, where σ = (σ₁, σ₂, σ₃) are the generators of the SU(2) action on S^+ ≅ ℂ². This operator has exactly two eigenvalues, ±1, corresponding to the two antipodal points ±n̂ on the Bloch sphere. The beam therefore splits into exactly two components.*

*Proof.* On the two-dimensional representation S^+ ≅ ℂ², the spin operators are represented by the Pauli matrices σ₁, σ₂, σ₃ (the standard generators of SU(2) in the spin-1/2 representation [Hall2015, Ch. 4]). For any unit vector n̂ ∈ S², the operator n̂ · σ is Hermitian and satisfies (n̂ · σ)² = |n̂|² · (identity) = (identity), since |n̂| = 1, so its eigenvalues satisfy λ² = 1, giving λ ∈ {+1, −1}. Each eigenvalue is non-degenerate on ℂ² (the two eigenspaces are one-dimensional), and the two eigenvectors are the spin states aligned and anti-aligned with n̂ — the points n̂ and −n̂ on the Bloch sphere. The number of distinct measurement outcomes equals the number of distinct eigenvalues, which is exactly two. **∎**

The two-outcome structure is therefore the statement that a measurement axis n̂ intersects the Bloch sphere — the geometric realization of the spin-1/2 state space — in exactly two antipodal points. The two-valuedness traces to the dimension-2 representation of Corollary III.4.3, which traces to the Clifford structure selected by the 4D McGucken manifold.

#### III.4.3 The 50/50 distribution and the general cos²(θ/2) law

With the spin-1/2 arena (Corollary III.4.3) and the two-outcome structure (Proposition III.4.4) in hand, the outcome frequencies follow from the Born rule of Proposition III.1.

**Proposition III.4.5 (Outcome probabilities).** *Let the apparatus measure along ẑ, with eigenstates |+z⟩, |−z⟩ ∈ ℂ². Let the incoming spin state be the Bloch-sphere unit vector at polar angle θ to ẑ, which up to global phase is*

  |ψ(θ)⟩ = cos(θ/2) |+z⟩ + sin(θ/2) |−z⟩.

*Then the Born rule of Proposition III.1 assigns outcome probabilities*

  P(+z) = |⟨+z | ψ(θ)⟩|² = cos²(θ/2),  P(−z) = |⟨−z | ψ(θ)⟩|² = sin²(θ/2),

*with P(+z) + P(−z) = 1. In particular, for an initial state perpendicular to the apparatus axis (θ = π/2, e.g. spin along x), P(+z) = cos²(π/4) = 1/2 and P(−z) = sin²(π/4) = 1/2 — the exact 50/50 splitting of the canonical setup.*

*Proof.* The amplitudes are read directly from the expansion of |ψ(θ)⟩ in the {|+z⟩, |−z⟩} basis: ⟨+z|ψ(θ)⟩ = cos(θ/2) and ⟨−z|ψ(θ)⟩ = sin(θ/2). Proposition III.1 gives the probability as the squared modulus of the amplitude. Hence P(+z) = cos²(θ/2) and P(−z) = sin²(θ/2). Normalization is the trigonometric identity cos²(θ/2) + sin²(θ/2) = 1. The θ = π/2 case gives cos²(π/4) = sin²(π/4) = 1/2. **∎**

This recovers the full empirical content of the Stern–Gerlach experiment: the two-outcome splitting, the exact 50/50 for a perpendicular initial state, and the cos²(θ/2)/sin²(θ/2) law for general orientation, all confirmed across more than a century of measurement.

#### III.4.4 The spatial separation: the deflection formula and the two-spot pattern

The preceding subsections establish the spin-1/2 arena, the two outcomes, and their probabilities. It remains to exhibit the experiment's directly observed quantity — the spatial separation of the two beams on the detector — as a quantitative consequence, and to state honestly how the framework's two channels relate in producing it. The deflection physics here is standard and is verified against the textbook treatments [Townsend2000; McIntyre2012; CT2019]; the McGucken content is the geometric reading laid over it, which we are careful not to overstate.

**Theorem III.4.6 (Stern–Gerlach spatial separation).** *A silver atom traverses a region of length giving traversal time T in an inhomogeneous field B = B\_z(z) ẑ with gradient ∂\_z B\_z. Writing the atomic magnetic moment as μ̂ = γ Ŝ with gyromagnetic ratio γ = g\_s μ\_B/ℏ (g\_s ≈ 2 the electron spin g-factor, μ\_B the Bohr magneton), the atom in the eigenstate S\_z = +ℏ/2 is deflected by*

  $z_+ = +\tfrac{1}{4}\,\gamma\hbar\,(\partial_z B_z)\,T^2 / m,$

*and the atom in S\_z = −ℏ/2 by z₋ = −(1/4) γ ℏ (∂\_z B\_z) T² / m, where m is the atomic mass. The total separation at the detector is*

  $\Delta z = z_+ - z_- = \gamma\hbar\,(\partial_z B_z)\,T^2 / (2m),$

*with the two spots appearing at ±Δz/2 from the undeflected axis and no intermediate accumulation.*

*Proof.* The interaction Hamiltonian of a magnetic moment in the field is Ĥ\_int = −μ̂ · B = −γ B\_z(z) Ŝ\_z, to leading order in the gradient with B along ẑ. The force on the atomic centre of mass follows from Ehrenfest's theorem, ⟨F̂\_z⟩ = −⟨∂\_z Ĥ\_int⟩ = γ ⟨Ŝ\_z⟩ (∂\_z B\_z), giving acceleration a\_z = γ ⟨Ŝ\_z⟩ (∂\_z B\_z)/m. For an atom in the S\_z = +ℏ/2 eigenstate, ⟨Ŝ\_z⟩ = +ℏ/2 is constant (Ŝ\_z commutes with Ĥ\_int when the field is parallel to the spin-measurement axis), so the kinematic displacement over traversal time T is z₊ = (1/2) a\_z T² = (1/4) γ ℏ (∂\_z B\_z) T²/m. The S\_z = −ℏ/2 case is identical with sign reversed, giving Δz = γ ℏ (∂\_z B\_z) T²/(2m). The restriction to exactly two values of the deflection is the two-element spectrum σ(Ŝ\_z) = {+ℏ/2, −ℏ/2} of the spin-1/2 silver atom (one unpaired 5s electron), established in §III.4.1–III.4.2: the eigenvalues ±1 of n̂·σ (Proposition III.4.4) scaled by ℏ/2. There is no third eigenvalue, hence no third spot. **∎**

*External verification.* The force law F\_z = μ\_z(∂\_z B\_z) with μ\_z = −g\_s(e/2m\_e)S\_z, the quadratic-in-time deflection, and the two-valued S\_z = ±ℏ/2 spectrum of the silver atom (whose moment derives from the single 5s electron spin) are the standard textbook content of the experiment [Townsend2000, §1.1; McIntyre2012, §1.1; CT2019]. The formula above is the textbook deflection formula; the present theorem reproduces it, and the framework adds no modification to this standard kinematics.

**Remark III.4.7 (How the two channels relate here — stated without overclaim).** It is tempting to present the spatial separation as the output of two independent derivations — the dx₄/dt = ic Algebraic Channel derivation via the Pauli Hamiltonian and Ehrenfest's theorem, and the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel derivation via the McGucken Sphere splitting into two oppositely-oriented sub-spheres that couple differentially to the field gradient. What is and is not independent is as follows. The *kinematic* result Δz is produced once, by the Algebraic Channel derivation above; the spin spectrum {±ℏ/2} that fixes the two-spot count traces to the SU(2) representation structure of §III.4.1 (which the framework does ground in the McGucken-Sphere SO(3) symmetry). The geometric "sub-sphere" reading is a *redescription* of the same dynamics in the framework's language: the impulse it assigns to each sub-sphere, ±γ(ℏ/2)(∂\_z B\_z)T, is the Algebraic Channel Pauli-coupling result restated, not an independently derived quantity. The geometric reading therefore does not constitute a second, logically disjoint derivation of the deflection magnitude; it is the same physics read on the McGucken-Sphere wavefront. What the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework contributes is upstream: the two-valuedness itself (§III.4.1, the SU(2) double cover forced by the sphere's SO(3) symmetry; §III.4.1-bis, the spinor as the homogeneous coordinate on the McGucken Sphere's direction space, Theorem 8.1 of [MG-DiracSpinors]) and the probability law (§III.4.3, via the Born rule). The deflection magnitude is shared, standard physics. We state this explicitly because the convergence of two readings is evidential only when the readings are genuinely independent; here the genuine independence is at the level of the spin structure and the probability rule, not at the level of the deflection formula.

#### III.4.5 The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic Reading of the Forward–Conjugate Identification: the Quadratic Born Density from Conservation Under x₄'s Expansion, the Overlap Theorem, the Two-Sphere Collision, and PT-Symmetry Through the Source Event

*McGucken Principle anchor.* The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic predicts that the McGucken Sphere carries a weight conserved as x₄ advances, and that the propagation of the Sphere's wavefront — the Klein–Gordon equation, second order because the interval (ict)² = −c²t² is quadratic — conserves the quadratic function of the modulus |ψ| and no other function of it (Lemma 7.1 of [MG-BornCentury]). It predicts that the conjugate factor ψ\* is a physical wavefront: at a detection event, the absorber's own forward +ic Sphere read in the emitter's frame (Theorem 7.7 of [MG-BornCentury]); for a freely propagating particle, the reflection of the emitter's Sphere through its source event, ψ(PT_E · event) = ψ\*(event) (Theorem 7.11 of [MG-BornCentury]).

Proposition III.1 and [MG-Hilbert-Born, Theorem 7.2] establish P = |ψ|² from four requirements on a probability density built from ψ: reality, non-negativity, phase invariance, and bilinearity in (ψ, ψ\*). Given all four, the squared-modulus form is forced by elementary algebra — the general bilinear form a ψ² + (b + c) ψ\*ψ + d (ψ\*)² has its ψ² and (ψ\*)² terms eliminated by phase invariance, its surviving coefficient pinned real and non-negative by reality and non-negativity, and fixed to unity by normalization. The candidates |ψ| (degree 1, not bilinear), |ψ|⁴ (degree 4, requiring a rank-4 pairing), and Re(ψ) or Im(ψ) alone (not phase-invariant) are each excluded.

Bilinearity is itself a theorem of dx₄/dt = ic. [MG-BornCentury] §7.3 states the four requirements with (R4) as locality and conservation of the total ∫P d³x under x₄'s expansion, and states: "No bilinearity in (ψ, ψ^\*) is required; Lemma 7.1 derives it." Lemma 7.1 of [MG-BornCentury] proves, under the regularity conditions on F stated there, that if ∫F(|ψ(x, t)|) d³x is independent of t for every wavefront ψ(t) = W(t)f propagated by W(t) = exp(−itΩ), Ω = c(−∇² + μ²)^(1/2), μ = mc/ħ, then F(s) = κs². Theorem 7.2 of [MG-BornCentury] then gives P(x) = |ψ(x)|²/∫|ψ|² d³x as the unique density satisfying (R1)–(R4). In the formulation of [MG-Hilbert-Born, Theorem 7.2] stated in the preceding paragraph, the fourth requirement is bilinearity; §§7.9–7.10 of [MG-BornCentury], reproduced below, use the label "R4" in that sense, for the bilinearity that Lemma 7.1 derives.

The identification of the Born density with the forward–conjugate overlap is Theorem 7.4 of [MG-BornCentury]: "The Born density P = ψ\* ψ at an event B is the geometric overlap, at B, of the forward x₄-expansion (carrying phase from x₄ = ict) and the conjugate x₄\*-expansion (carrying phase from x₄\* = −ict)." The conjugate factor is supplied physically by Theorem 7.7 of [MG-BornCentury], the head-on x₄-collision of the emitter's and absorber's Spheres at the detection event, and by Theorem 7.11 of [MG-BornCentury], the PT-symmetry of the Sphere through its source event — the two readings set out in §III.1-ter.

The exponent 2 is fixed by five routes, which [MG-BornCentury] Part IX.2 lists: the Conservation Route (Lemma 7.1), the Haar Route (Lemma 7.1.5), the Norm Route (Lemma 7.6), the Collision Route (Theorem 7.7, Lemma 7.7.5, Corollary 7.7.6), and the PT-Symmetry Route (Theorem 7.11). The five share only the Principle and the Sphere: "A challenge to any one route leaves the other four standing" ([MG-BornCentury] Part IX.2).

The spinor construction reaches the same quadratic norm from the complex structure of the matter field. For S = ℂ² with one complex structure i and the reconstructed four-vector V^μ = ⟨ψ|σ^μ|ψ⟩, the timelike component is V⁰ = ⟨ψ|ψ⟩, the Born norm, and the lone timelike direction written as a sum of four squares is x₄ = ict, whose i is the i of S (Theorem 6.1(ii)–(iii) of [MG-DiracSpinors]).

Each prior derivation of the Born rule enters with a supplementary input that the derivation does not itself supply. Born (1926) fixed |ψ|² empirically, by matching scattering data; Gleason (1957) [Gleason1957] derived the squared form from non-contextuality of a probability measure on the closed subspaces of a Hilbert space of dimension at least 3; the decision-theoretic programme (Deutsch, Wallace) from rationality axioms on agents in a branching state space; the operational reconstructions (Hardy, Masanes–Galley–Müller) from associativity or tomographic axioms. [MG-BornCentury] §7.1 surveys sixteen such programmes, 1926–2025, and §7.7 records the supplementary axiom each imports. Of Gleason, [MG-BornCentury] Part IX.2 states that his theorem "has one route, and that route presupposes the lattice of closed subspaces of a complex Hilbert space."

The texts below are reproduced verbatim and in full from [MG-BornCentury] §§7.3–7.5, §§7.8–7.10 and Part IX.2, and from Theorem 6.1 of [MG-DiracSpinors]. Bracketed numerals and theorem, lemma and section numbers inside the reproduced text refer to the numbering and bibliography of the source paper.

##### [MG-BornCentury] 7.3 The four requirements for the Born density forced by dx₄/dt = ic: reality, non-negativity, phase invariance under global x₄-shift, and locality with conservation under x₄’s expansion

The McGucken Principle asserts that the fourth dimension x₄ is expanding at the velocity of light: dx₄/dt = ic, with x₄ = ict, as a spherically symmetric McGucken Sphere whose wavelength sets the action h and whose volume defines a nonlocality.

The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic predicts that a probability density P on ℝ³ derived from the McGucken wavefunction ψ of Definition 2.6 satisfies four requirements, each supplied by a property of the Sphere, and that these four fix P = |ψ|² with the quadratic form as the conclusion rather than an input.

- **(R1) Reality.** P is real-valued. (A probability density counts detection events; it is real by physical interpretation.)

- **(R2) Non-negativity.** P ≥ 0. (Detection counts are non-negative; the Sphere collision of Theorem 7.7 at the detection event has a non-negative rate.)

- **(R3) Phase invariance under global x₄-shift.** P(e\^(iα)ψ) = P(ψ) for all real α. (A global phase is a shift of the x₄-origin, and the expansion is the same from every event by the universality clause of Theorem 2.4(iv).)

- **(R4) Locality and conservation under x₄’s expansion.** (a) The density at an event B is a function of the wavefront at B; with (R3) this means P(x) = F(|ψ(x)|). This is Theorem 7.4: the density at B is the overlap at B of the forward and conjugate x₄-expansions. (b) The total ∫ P d³x is the same at every time. The expansion of x₄ carries the wavefront forward by the propagation W(t) = exp(-itΩ), where Ω = c(-∇² + μ²)\^(1/2) with μ = mc/ħ is the positive-energy square root of the Klein–Gordon operator — the Klein–Gordon equation (□ - m²c²/ħ²)ψ = 0 being the differential expression of the McGucken-Sphere wavefront, Theorem 9.0 of [1] and the textbook’s theorem QM T8 ([25] Chapter 8) — and the Sphere’s weight — in standard terms the total probability it carries — is conserved along its expansion ([25] Lemma 6.6C step 2), so a detection is certain at every time. In the non-relativistic regime W(t) reduces to the Schrödinger evolution of Theorem 9.2.

Requirement (R4)(b) is the Sphere’s conservation law, Lemma 6.6C of the textbook, applied to the wavefront: the weight the source deposits on its Sphere is neither created nor destroyed as x₄ advances. No bilinearity in (ψ, ψ\^\*) is required; Lemma 7.1 derives it.

##### [MG-BornCentury] 7.4 Lemma 7.1: the conserved density is quadratic — conservation under x₄’s expansion forces F(s) = κs²

**Lemma 7.1 (Quadratic form from conservation under x₄’s expansion).** *Let F be continuous on [0, ∞) and twice continuously differentiable on (0, ∞), with F(0) = 0, F′ bounded on bounded sets, and F(s) and sF′(s) both of order s\^δ as s → 0 for some δ > 0. If ∫ F(|ψ(x, t)|) d³x is independent of t for every wavefront ψ(t) = W(t)f with f a Schwartz function, then F(s) = κ s² for a constant κ.*

*Notation for the proof.* R̂ is the operator that multiplies the Fourier transform by r(k) = ω_C + c|k|²/2μ - ω(k), where ω(k) = c(|k|² + μ²)\^(1/2) and ω_C = cμ is the Compton frequency of Proposition 2.2. For x ≥ 0, 0 ≤ 1 + x/2 - (1 + x)\^(1/2) ≤ x²/8, which gives 0 ≤ r(k) ≤ c|k|⁴/(8μ³).

*Proof.* Take a profile f = g e\^(iθ) with g > 0 a Gaussian and θ a real smooth function with bounded derivatives, and its dilations f_λ(x) = f(x/λ), λ ≥ 1.

*Step 1, the derivative.* Since ∂ψ/∂ t = -iΩψ and |f| > 0, the derivative of |ψ| at t = 0 is Im(e\^(-iθ)Ω f), and the difference quotients of F(|ψ|) are dominated by an integrable function, because F′ is bounded on the range of |ψ| and ψ, Ωψ are Schwartz functions uniformly for t in a bounded interval. Hence

d/dt∫ F(|ψ|) d³x = ∫ F′(g) Im(e\^(-iθ)Ω f) d³x, t = 0.

*Step 2, splitting Ω.* By the bound just stated, Ω = ω_C + (c/2μ)(-∇²) - R̂, where R̂ multiplies the Fourier transform by r(k) with 0 ≤ r(k) ≤ c|k|⁴/(8μ³). The term ω_C contributes Im(e\^(-iθ)ω_C f) = 0.

*Step 3, the main term.* Im(e\^(-iθ)(-∇² f)) = -(1/g) ∇·(g²∇θ). Integrating by parts twice, with H(s) = sF′(s) - 2F(s), so that H’(s) = sF″(s) - F′(s), and with no boundary terms because H(g) and gF′(g) are of order g\^δ and g is a Gaussian,

∫ (F′(g))/g(-∇·(g²∇θ)) d³x = ∫ ∇(H(g))·∇θ d³x = -∫ H(g) ∇²θ d³x.

*Step 4, scaling.* For f_λ the main term equals -(c/2μ) λ∫ H(g)∇²θ d³x, since the volume element contributes λ³ and the Laplacian λ⁻². The remainder is bounded by sup|F′(g)|·‖(1 + |x|²/λ²)⁻¹‖₂·‖(1 + |x|²/λ²)R̂f_λ‖₂ ≤ Cλ\^(3/2)·λ\^(3/2 - 4) = Cλ⁻¹, because λ⁴ r(k/λ) and its first two derivatives are bounded by polynomials in |k| uniformly in λ ≥ 1.

*Step 5, conclusion.* Conservation makes the derivative vanish for every λ. Dividing by λ and letting λ → ∞ gives ∫ H(g)∇²θ d³x = 0 for every admissible θ, in particular for every smooth θ of compact support. So H(g(x)) is a continuous weakly harmonic function on ℝ³ that tends to H(0) = 0 at infinity, and it vanishes identically by the maximum principle. A Gaussian of height a takes every value in (0, a], so H(s) = 0 for all s > 0. Then sF′(s) = 2F(s), whose solutions are F(s) = κ s². ∎

For the Schrödinger propagation of Theorem 9.2, Ω is replaced by -(ħ/2m)∇² up to the rest-energy constant, Steps 2 and 4 are void, and Step 3 alone gives ∫ H(g)∇²θ d³x = 0.

*McGucken Principle anchor.* The exponent 2 is the exponent that x₄’s expansion conserves. The rank-2 character of the interval (ict)² = -c²t² enters through the Klein–Gordon equation, which is second order because the interval is quadratic, and the lemma shows that its propagation conserves the quadratic density and no other function of the modulus. The conservation itself is the Sphere’s: Lemma 6.6C of the textbook, the weight of the Sphere conserved along its advance.

**Lemma 7.1.5 (Uniqueness of the SO(3)-invariant probability measure on the McGucken Sphere).** *The McGucken Sphere Σ₊(p) at parameter time t is a round 2-sphere S² of radius ct, carrying the transitive action of the rotation group SO(3) fixed by the isotropy of the x₄-expansion from p (clause 3 of §2.4). Then there exists a unique SO(3)-invariant Borel probability measure on the Sphere, namely the normalized round measure dμ(θ,φ) = sinθ dθ dφ/(4π), and every SO(3)-invariant probability density on the Sphere is this dμ. This is the measure that supplies the Born-rule probability over detection directions.*

*Proof.* The Sphere is a homogeneous space for SO(3): the isotropy of the expansion makes the action transitive, and the stabilizer of any direction is the subgroup SO(2) of rotations about that axis, so Σ₊(p) ≅ SO(3)/SO(2) = S². SO(3) is compact; by Haar’s theorem (1933) every compact group carries a unique normalized invariant measure, which pushes forward to a unique invariant probability measure on any homogeneous space. Existence: dμ = sinθ dθ dφ/(4π) is invariant because rotations are isometries of the round metric and sinθ dθ dφ is its area element. Uniqueness: if ν is any SO(3)-invariant probability measure, then for continuous f, invariance plus transitivity give ∫ f dν = ∫ f dμ (both equal the round average f̄); since this holds for all continuous f, ν = μ by the Riesz representation theorem. The corresponding result [19] Theorem 22.6 develops the same uniqueness in the correlation setting; the self-contained statement is the one given here. ∎

*Remark 7.1.5a (Why this is the measure the Born rule needs).* A probability rule over outcomes requires a measure on the outcome space, and a measure is physically forced only if a symmetry singles it out uniquely. Minkowski’s four-velocity norm u\^μ u_μ = -c² carries no group action and hence no distinguished measure; the McGucken Sphere carries the transitive SO(3) action, and Lemma 7.1.5 shows this action forces exactly one probability measure. The Born-rule weight over detection directions is that measure. This is the route to P = |ψ|² that proceeds from the Sphere’s *symmetry group*, independently of the route that proceeds from conservation under the Sphere’s expansion (Lemma 7.1).

**Lemma 7.6 (Parallelogram identity from the sesquilinear inner product of the McGucken Hilbert space).** *Let ⟨·, ·⟩ : 𝓥 × 𝓥 → ℂ be the sesquilinear inner product ⟨φ, ψ⟩ = ∫ φ\^\*ψ d³x on the McGucken pre-Hilbert space 𝓥 of Theorem 6.1, whose quadratic diagonal ⟨ψ, ψ⟩ = ∫|ψ|² d³x is the conserved total of Lemma 7.1. Let ‖ψ‖ := √(⟨ψ, ψ⟩) be the associated norm. Then for all x, y ∈ 𝓥, the parallelogram identity*

‖x + y‖² + ‖x - y‖² = 2(‖x‖² + ‖y‖²)

*holds as a direct two-line algebraic consequence of sesquilinearity, without invocation of the Jordan–von Neumann theorem or any external functional-analytic input.*

*Proof.* By sesquilinearity (conjugate-linear in the first slot, linear in the second), direct expansion gives

‖x + y‖² = ⟨ x + y, x + y⟩ = ⟨ x, x⟩ + ⟨ x, y⟩ + ⟨ y, x⟩ + ⟨ y, y⟩ = ‖x‖² + 2Re⟨ x, y⟩ + ‖y‖²,

‖x - y‖² = ⟨ x - y, x - y⟩ = ⟨ x, x⟩ - ⟨ x, y⟩ - ⟨ y, x⟩ + ⟨ y, y⟩ = ‖x‖² - 2Re⟨ x, y⟩ + ‖y‖²,

using ⟨ y, x⟩ = ⟨ x, y⟩\^\* (conjugate symmetry of the McGucken inner product, established in §6.4 from the complex conjugation under the integral sign) so that ⟨ x, y⟩ + ⟨ y, x⟩ = 2Re⟨ x, y⟩. Adding the two expansions, the cross-terms ± 2Re⟨ x, y⟩ cancel:

‖x + y‖² + ‖x - y‖² = 2‖x‖² + 2‖y‖² = 2(‖x‖² + ‖y‖²). □

The Jordan–von Neumann theorem (1935) [26] gives the converse direction — that any norm satisfying the parallelogram identity arises from an inner product. In the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework the inner product is supplied by Theorem 6.1 and its quadratic diagonal is forced by Lemma 7.1, so the parallelogram identity is a downstream consequence and Jordan–von Neumann a consistency check rather than an upstream selection principle.

##### [MG-BornCentury] 7.5 Theorem 7.2 (Born rule from dx₄/dt = ic): the unique density on ℝ³ satisfying (R1)–(R4) is P(x) = |ψ(x)|²

**Theorem 7.2 (Born rule from dx₄/dt = ic).** *Let ψ: ℝ³ → ℂ be the McGucken wavefunction of Definition 2.6. The unique density P: ℝ³ → ℝ_(≥ 0) satisfying (R1), (R2), (R3), (R4) is*

P(x) = (|ψ(x)|²)/(∫|ψ|² d³x).

*Proof.* By (R3) and (R4)(a), P = F(|ψ|). By (R4)(b) and Lemma 7.1, F(s) = κ s². (R1) and (R2) hold for κ > 0, and normalization fixes κ. ∎

*Status note (form of the Born rule derived).* Theorem 7.2 derives the *projective* form of the Born rule P = |ψ|² on the McGucken-derived Hilbert space 𝓗 — the form Born stated in 1926, the form in every textbook, and the form that the Dirac–von Neumann measurement axiom (Corollary 11.3) instantiates. The POVM generalization (Davies–Lewis 1970; Neumaier 2025; see §7.1.16) extends the projective form to real quantum measurements with finite efficiency, losses, dark counts, and simultaneous position–momentum readings. The POVM rule is recoverable in the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework via Naimark dilation: any POVM on 𝓗 lifts to a projection-valued measure on 𝓗 ⊗ 𝒦 for an ancilla space 𝒦, and Theorem 7.2 applies on the dilated space, reproducing the POVM rule on 𝓗.

*Extended status note (the exponent 2 reinforced through the Hilbert-space route).* The exponent 2 is derived in Lemma 7.1 from conservation of the density under x₄’s expansion, with the rank-2 character of (ic)² = -c² entering through the second-order Klein–Gordon equation (Theorem 9.0) whose positive-energy propagation W(t) the lemma uses. A second route to the same exponent descends from the Hilbert space itself, derived from dx₄/dt = ic in Theorem 6.1: the parallelogram identity of Lemma 7.6 and the L²-norm conservation under the McGucken-derived unitary evolution of Theorem 9.2. For p ≠ 2 the Lᵖ norm of a normalized solution of the Schrödinger equation is in general not preserved: for a normalized three-dimensional Gaussian wavepacket with spatial width σ(t) ∼ ħ t/(2mσ₀) at large t, ‖ψₜ‖ₚ ∼ σ(t)\^(3(2-p)/(2p)), which decays for p > 2 (at p = 4 as t\^(-3/4)) and grows for p < 2; only p = 2 makes the exponent vanish. Lesovik [27] gives the derivation of the exponent 2 from this unitarity argument on a given Hilbert space; in the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework it applies on the *derived* Hilbert space of Theorem 6.1 with the evolution derived in Theorem 9.2, and Lemma 7.1 is its general form, for an arbitrary function F of the modulus rather than the power laws |ψ|ᵖ alone.

The exponent 2 is therefore overdetermined by two McGucken-internal routes that share no intermediate machinery between the Principle and the conclusion. *Conservation Route:* dx₄/dt = ic → Klein–Gordon equation on the Sphere wavefront (Theorem 9.0) → positive-energy propagation W(t) → conservation of the Sphere’s weight (Lemma 6.6C of [25]) → F(s) = κ s² (Lemma 7.1) → P = |ψ|² (Theorem 7.2). *Norm Route:* dx₄/dt = ic → Hilbert space as completion of x₄-projections (Theorem 6.1) → sesquilinear inner product → parallelogram identity (Lemma 7.6) → L² structure, reinforced by the unitarity of Theorem 9.2. Gleason (1957) derived the form of the Born rule on a *given* Hilbert space; Jordan–von Neumann (1935) characterized the parallelogram identity on *given* Lᵖ spaces; Lesovik (2014) derived the exponent from unitarity on a *given* Hilbert space. The McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework operates one level upstream of all three: the Hilbert space is derived (Theorem 6.1), the conservation that forces the exponent is the Sphere’s (Lemma 6.6C), and the inside-Hilbert-space arguments reinforce the exponent with their inputs themselves traced to dx₄/dt = ic.

##### [MG-BornCentury] 7.8 Theorem 7.4: the geometric meaning of ψ\*ψ — the Born density at event B is the geometric overlap at B of the forward x₄-expansion (carrying phase from x₄ = ict) and the conjugate x₄\*-expansion (carrying phase from x₄\* = -ict)

The uniqueness theorem establishes *that* P = |ψ|². The geometric meaning of why follows from the construction.

**Definition 7.3 (Conjugate expansion).** *The* conjugate *of the McGucken expansion x₄ = ict is the expansion obtained by complex-conjugating both sides: (x₄)\* = (ict)\* = −ict. We denote this conjugate x₄-coordinate by x₄\* = −ict.* Geometrically, complex conjugation reverses the orientation of the perpendicular x₄-axis: where the forward expansion advances at +ic, the conjugate expansion has the opposite orientation. The conjugate is the same expansion read in opposite orientation; it has no independent physical existence. The conjugate wavefunction ψ\*(B) = ∑\_γ exp(−iS[γ]/ℏ) is the path-integral expression of this conjugate-orientation reading: same paths, opposite phase.

**Theorem 7.4 (Geometric meaning of the Born rule).** *The Born density P = ψ\* ψ at an event B is the geometric overlap, at B, of the forward x₄-expansion (carrying phase from x₄ = ict) and the conjugate x₄\*-expansion (carrying phase from x₄\* = −ict). The overlap decomposes into diagonal terms (probability contributions from individual paths) and off-diagonal terms (interference between distinct paths), with the off-diagonal interference being the geometry of quantum coherence.*

*Proof.* By Theorem 3.1, the McGucken wavefunction (equivalently, the path-integral propagator) from event A to event B is

K(B, A) = ∑\_γ: A → B exp ((i S[γ])/(ℏ)),

where γ ranges over paths from A to B with B ∈ 𝓜_A(t) on the null wavefront of the x₄-expansion from A, and S[γ] is the action along γ. By Definition 7.3, the conjugate kernel obtained by reversing the orientation of x₄ (equivalently, complex-conjugating each factor in the path-sum) is

K\^\*(B, A) = ∑\_γ : A → B exp (-(i S[γ])/(ℏ)).

The Born density at B is the product ψ\^\*(B) ψ(B) = K\^\*(B, A) K(B, A) (relative to a source event A; the absolute-position case takes A as the preparation event of the system). Expanding the product:

P(A → B) = K\^\*(B, A) K(B, A) = (∑\_γ′ e⁻i S[γ′]/ℏ) (∑\_γ eⁱ S[γ]/ℏ) = ∑\_γ, γ′ eⁱ (S[γ] - S[γ′])/ℏ.

This double sum has two derivationally distinct contributions:

*Diagonal terms (γ = γ′).* When the two indices coincide, S[γ] - S[γ′] = 0 and e\^i · 0 = 1. The diagonal contribution is

∑\_γ 1 = Nₚaths(A → B),

the count of distinct paths from A to B with B on the null wavefront 𝓜_A(t) (regularized by the path-integral measure; for the continuum, replaced by the appropriate path-integral norm). These are the *probability* contributions from each path treated independently — classical-particle-like terms.

*Off-diagonal terms (γ ≠ γ′).* When the indices differ, S[γ] - S[γ′] ≠ 0 in general, and e\^i(S[γ] - S[γ′])/ℏ is a nontrivial phase. These are *interference* contributions, with phase determined by the action difference between the two paths. Summing over γ ≠ γ′ produces the constructive and destructive interference patterns characteristic of quantum mechanics (the double-slit pattern, the Aharonov–Bohm phase, the interference fringes in any quantum experiment).

The total density P(A → B) is therefore the geometric overlap of the forward x₄-expansion with the conjugate x₄-expansion at B, with the diagonal terms supplying the classical-probability-like content and the off-diagonal terms supplying the quantum-coherent interference content. The two together are the “two expansions meeting at B” — a geometric picture in which the macroscopic apparatus, localized at a definite x₄-coordinate by prior decoherence, is the location at which the forward expansion (carrying phase from x₄ = ict) and the conjugate expansion (carrying phase from x₄\^\* = -ict) overlap. The probability of detection is the overlap density ψ\^\* ψ. The “collapse” is the geometric incidence of the two expansions on a localized absorber. ∎

**Remark 7.4b (dx₄/dt = ic anchoring of Theorem 7.4 — the geometric meaning of |ψ|²).** *Theorem 7.4 supplies the geometric mechanism for the Born rule: |ψ|² at event B is the geometric overlap of the forward x₄-expansion (phase from x₄ = ict) and the conjugate x₄\^\*-expansion (phase from x₄\^\* = -ict) at B. The dx₄/dt = ic content operative: (C2) perpendicularity marker i supplies the complex phase exp(iS[γ]/ħ) in both forward and conjugate kernels; (C5) Sphere generation supplies the McGucken Sphere 𝓜_A(t) on which the wavefunction propagates from source event A; (C6) Huygens-Fresnel-Kirchhoff Sphere self-replication supplies the propagation mechanism; (C3) action quantum ħ supplies the action-quantization scale in exp(iS[γ]/ħ); Definition 7.3 supplies the conjugate expansion as the orientation-reversed reading of dx₄/dt = ic (i.e., -ic rather than +ic). The identification of the conjugate expansion with the absorber’s forward expansion viewed from the emitter’s frame (Theorem 7.7) supplies the physical interpretation: the conjugate is the same expansion read from the antipodal frame. The diagonal+off-diagonal decomposition |c_γ|² + 2Re(c_γ\^\* c_(γ′)) supplies the classical-probability + quantum-interference content. The dx₄/dt = ic machinery in Theorem 7.4 is: (C2), (C3), (C5), (C6); the cascade-upstream dependence is Theorem 3.1 (complex amplitudes) → Definition 2.6 (wavefunction) → Theorem 7.2 (Born rule uniqueness) → Theorem 7.4 (geometric reading). See §17.6.7 for the comprehensive audit position.*

**Proposition 7.5 (Malus correspondence).** *The Born rule is to x₄-projection what Malus’s law is to spatial projection: the squared cosine of the angle between the polarization direction (the x₄-direction along which the state advances) and the projection axis (the spatial slicing of the measurement) gives the transmitted intensity.*

This is the geometry of the squaring. Classical optics has used the squared-projection move since Malus in 1809. The Born rule is the same move in a different setting: project a unit four-velocity component along x₄ onto the spatial slicing of a measurement, the projection density is the squared modulus.

**Remark 7.5b (dx₄/dt = ic anchoring of Proposition 7.5).** *The Malus correspondence makes the dx₄/dt = ic content of the Born rule explicit. In Malus’s 1809 setup, a polarized light beam with polarization direction p̂ encountering a polarizer with transmission axis â has transmitted intensity Iₜ = I₀ cos²θ where θ = ∠(p̂, â) — the squared cosine of the angle between polarization direction and transmission axis. In the McGucken dx₄/dt = ic framework reading: the polarization direction is the x₄-direction along which the McGucken-Sphere wavefront advances at +ic (the universal feature of dx₄/dt = ic at every event); the transmission axis is the spatial-slice direction of the measurement (the projection of the McGucken Sphere onto the spatial slice at parameter time t); the squared cosine |cosθ|² of the angle between x₄-direction and projection axis gives the projection probability density at the measurement event. The Born rule P(x) = |ψ(x)|² is precisely Malus’s law applied to the x₄-projection: θ is the angle between the wavefunction’s x₄-perpendicular direction and the spatial-slice projection axis at the measurement event; |cosθ|² = |ψ(x)|² is the projection density at that event. The dx₄/dt = ic machinery operative in Proposition 7.5 is: (C2) the perpendicularity of x₄ to the spatial slice (the wavefunction’s complex character marks this perpendicularity via Theorem 3.1); (C4) per-event universality of the x₄-perpendicular direction at every event of 𝕄_G; (C5) the McGucken Sphere supplying the geometric structure that the projection operates on at every event. The Malus correspondence makes the Born rule’s content visible as a per-event projection-squared operation, with dx₄/dt = ic supplying the x₄-perpendicular direction that is being projected. See §17.6.7 for the comprehensive audit position.*

##### [MG-BornCentury] 7.9 The physical mechanism: Born rule as head-on x₄-collision of two McGucken spheres

Theorem 7.4 established that the Born density ψ\^\*ψ at a detection event B is the geometric overlap of the forward x₄-expansion (carrying phase from x₄ = ict) and the conjugate x₄-expansion (carrying phase from x₄\^\* = -ict) at B. The reading is geometrically complete but leaves one physical question open: what is the physical referent of the conjugate sphere? On the geometric-overlap reading alone, the conjugate is the orientation-reversed image of the forward expansion — an algebraic partner of ψ with no independent physical existence required. This subsection identifies the conjugate sphere physically: it is the absorber’s own forward x₄-expansion, viewed from the emitter’s frame, where it appears antiparallel in x₄. The Born rule’s bilinearity then has an explicit two-particle physical mechanism — the head-on x₄-collision of the two McGucken spheres at the detection event — and the rotation-out-of-x₄ that Theorem 12.2 will identify as the universal measurement mechanism is here exhibited as the result of x₄-momentum cancellation at the collision.

**Theorem 7.7 (Born rule as head-on x₄-collision of two McGucken spheres).** *Let particle A at event E_A and particle B at event E_B each propagate, by the canonical ontology (clause 3, §2.4) and Definition 2.6, a McGucken sphere outward at dx₄/dt = +ic in its respective rest frame. Let P ∈ 𝓜_{E_A}(t) ∩ 𝓜_{E_B}(t) be a spacetime event where both McGucken spheres arrive on the spatial slice at parameter time t. Then:*

*(i) (Frame-relational antiparallelism in x₄.) In A’s rest frame at P, A’s outgoing x₄-component carries the signature dx₄/dt|\_A = +ic. B’s outgoing x₄-component along the shared spatial geodesic from E_B to P, as expressed in A’s frame at P, carries the opposite sign: dx₄/dt|\_B (as seen in A’s frame at P) = -ic. By the A↔︎B symmetry of the construction, the converse holds in B’s rest frame.*

*(ii) (Algebra of the antiparallelism.) The antiparallel signs in (i) realize, frame-relationally, the algebraic conjugation z ↔︎ z\^\* on the imaginary unit: i ↔︎ -i. The conjugate kernel ψ\^\* of Definition 7.3 is therefore the absorber’s forward x₄-expansion viewed in the emitter’s frame; equivalently, ψ is the emitter’s forward x₄-expansion viewed in the absorber’s frame. Complex conjugation in the Born rule is the dx₄/dt = ic framework’s expression of the frame-relational relationship between the two physical participants in the head-on collision.*

*(iii) (x₄-momenergy cancellation forces 3-localization.) Each McGucken sphere carries x₄-component of four-momentum p_4 = i m c in its own rest frame (the four-momentum form of dx₄/dt = ic; cf. §9.2 step 1 and the four-velocity budget u\^μ u_μ = -c² of §2.3). At the head-on meeting P, the two x₄-momenta, expressed in a common frame, are antiparallel: p_4\^A = +imc and p_4\^B = -imc in A’s frame at P (for identical-mass particles; the relative x₄-momentum vanishes more generally in the center-of-momentum frame along the head-on axis). The sum of x₄-components vanishes at P. By four-momentum conservation (translation invariance of the Lorentzian metric, Lemma 2.5), the momenergy that cancelled in x₄ must reappear in x₁x₂x₃ at P. Both particles are thereby rotated out of pure x₄-expansion and localized at P — the geometric reorientation that Theorem 12.2 will name “rotation out of x₄.”*

*(iv) (Bilinear collision rate.) The local rate of the head-on collision event at P is the sesquilinear product ψ_A(P) · ψ_B\^\*(P) up to a positive normalization constant. The product structure ψ_A(P) · ψ_B(P) of the two amplitudes is derived rigorously in Lemma 7.7.5 Step 1 below from action-additivity of independent paths, ruling out sum, max, min, arithmetic/geometric/harmonic means as candidate functional forms. The conjugation ψ_B ⇝ ψ_B\^\* that converts the forward × forward product to the Born sesquilinear ψ · ψ\^\* is derived in Lemma 7.7.5 Step 2 from the complexification of the symmetric rank-2 metric (Lemma 2.5) combined with R1 (real Born density on diagonal) — the bilinear complex extension fails R1, only the sesquilinear extension gives a real diagonal for symmetric forms. The conjugation is therefore the CONJUGATION of the sesquilinear inner product, NOT a Lorentz-boost frame change (the action S is a Lorentz scalar) and NOT the Stueckelberg–Feynman time-reversal postulate (which is one PHYSICAL INTERPRETATION but not the source of the conjugation). Higher-rank pairings (cubic, quartic, etc.) are excluded by the same rank-counting that excluded them in Theorem 7.2.*

*(v) (Reduction to single-particle ψ\^\*ψ.) For single-particle QM with a macroscopic absorber localized at P by prior decoherence (the standard idealization of a detector), the absorber is well-modeled as a localized point at P whose McGucken sphere’s forward x₄-expansion is, in the emitter’s frame, the conjugate kernel ψ\^\* by (ii). The collision rate at P reduces to ψ\^\*(P) ψ(P) = |ψ(P)|², recovering the Born rule of Theorem 7.2 as the rate of head-on x₄-collisions between the emitter’s outgoing sphere and the absorber’s outgoing sphere viewed conjugately.*

**Proof.**

*(i)* By canonical clause 3 (§2.4), the McGucken sphere expansion from any event proceeds isotropically at rate c with respect to that event’s rest frame. The spatial-slice projection of A’s expansion at P points from E_A toward P along the spacelike geodesic E_A P; in A’s rest frame, A’s x₄-component advances at dx₄/dt = +ic along this expansion. The spatial-slice projection of B’s expansion at P points from E_B toward P along E_B P; in B’s rest frame, B’s x₄-component advances at dx₄/dt = +ic. The two spheres meet at P traveling toward each other in spacelike orientation. Express B’s outgoing x₄-component in A’s frame at P: along the line E_A P E_B at P, A’s outgoing x₄-direction is the +ic direction (by A’s frame definition), and B’s outgoing x₄-direction at P points back toward E_B along the same spacelike line, which is the opposite spatial orientation — and by the same construction of “outgoing x₄-direction at P relative to the source,” in A’s frame this is the -ic direction. The antiparallelism follows. The A↔︎B symmetry of the entire construction yields the converse in B’s frame.

*(ii)* Complex conjugation in ℂ is the orientation reversal of the imaginary axis: i ↔︎ -i. The i-marker for x₄-perpendicularity (Theorem 3.1, §4.3) thereby reverses sign under conjugation, exactly as in (i). The conjugate kernel ψ\^\*(B) = ∑\_γ exp(-iS[γ]/ℏ) of Definition 7.3 is the path-integral expression of orientation-reversed expansion; by (i), this orientation reversal is the absorber’s forward x₄-expansion (which is +ic in its own frame) as seen from the emitter’s frame (-ic). The conjugate is therefore the absorber-frame partner of the emitter’s forward expansion — the dx₄/dt = ic framework’s frame-relational reading of complex conjugation.

*(iii)* By the four-velocity budget (§2.3, §9.2 step 1), each particle’s four-momentum in its rest frame has x₄-component p_4 = i m c, with full magnitude m c² the rest-energy content (mass-energy equivalence descending from the same dx₄/dt = ic — cf. companion paper [2] for the corpus derivation). At the head-on collision at P, the two x₄-momentum components in a common frame are antiparallel by (i); for identical-mass particles their sum vanishes, and for non-identical masses the sum vanishes in the center-of-momentum frame along the head-on axis. Four-momentum is conserved at P (translation invariance of the Lorentzian metric, Lemma 2.5). What cancels in the x₄-component must therefore reappear in the x₁x₂x₃-components for total four-momentum to be conserved at P. The cancelled x₄-momenergy is deposited as 3-spatial momenergy at P, rotating both particles’ free four-velocity budget from x₄-dominated to spatial-dominated — both particles localized at P.

*(iv)* The probability per unit time per unit spatial volume at P of the head-on collision event is the sesquilinear product ψ_A(P) · ψ_B\^\*(P) of the two amplitudes (with the conjugation of ψ_B\^\* prescribed by the postulated frame-relational antiparallelism of (i)-(ii) — see Step 2 of Lemma 7.7.5 below for the honest accounting of this conjugation as a postulate, not a frame consequence). The product structure ψ_A · ψ_B — rather than sum, max, geometric mean, or any other symmetric function of the two amplitudes — is derived rigorously in Lemma 7.7.5 Step 1 below from action-additivity of independent paths combined with the exponential phase of each McGucken-Sphere wavefront. The conjugation ψ_B ⇝ ψ_B\^\* that converts the forward × forward product to the Born sesquilinear is the input doing the work and is currently a postulate, with three plausible derivation routes identified in Remark 7.7.7.
