### V.2 The (R) postulate in standard quantum mechanics

The reduction postulate (R) asserts that upon measurement, the state vector |ψ⟩ collapses to one of the eigenstates |a\_i⟩ of the measured observable Â, with probability P(a\_i) = |⟨a\_i|ψ⟩|². The collapse is stochastic, nonlinear, and time-irreversible. Standard quantum mechanics treats (R) as a separate dynamical law alongside (U), and most interpretive programmes either accept (R) as primitive (Copenhagen, RQM, QBism), modify (U) to incorporate (R) (GRW), or explain (R) away as appearance (Many-Worlds, Bohmian, decoherence).

The McGucken framework does neither. Instead, it derives the apparent (R) phenomenon as the 3D spatial cross-section reading of an x₄-extended state evolving unitarily, with no separate (R) postulate required.

### V.3 Proposition V.1 (Collapse as 3D cross-section reading)

**Proposition V.1 (The apparent reduction R is the 3D cross-section reading of unitary x₄-evolution).** *Let |Ψ(t)⟩ ∈ ℋ\_S ⊗ ℋ\_A ⊗ ℋ\_E be the unitary-evolved state of system + apparatus + environment at time t after a measurement interaction. Let π\_{x\_obs} be the projection onto the spatial three-slice Σ\_{t} containing the observer at time t. Then the apparent collapse |Ψ(t)⟩ → |s\_k⟩ ⊗ |A\_k⟩ ⊗ |E\_k⟩ observed by the observer is the algebraic content of π\_{x\_obs} |Ψ(t)⟩, with no separate (R) postulate required. The "outcome" of the measurement is the configuration of the four-dimensional state |Ψ(t)⟩ that lies in the observer's accessible region of the spatial slice Σ\_{t} as x₄ advances.*

**Proof.** The proof proceeds through three steps.

**Step 1: The four-dimensional state.** From [MG-QM, Theorem 6] (wave-particle duality as dual-channel reading), every quantum state has a four-dimensional structure: it is simultaneously a McGucken Sphere (the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel reading: spherically expanding x₄-wavefront cross-section) and a localizable particle (the dx₄/dt = ic Algebraic Channel reading: eigenvalue event of position observable at each spacetime point of detection). The unitary-evolved state |Ψ(t)⟩ at time t describes the four-dimensional structure across the entire spacetime region accessible from the measurement interaction's past null cone.

**Step 2: The 3D cross-section.** A specific observer at spatial location x\_obs at time t accesses the state through the 3D spatial cross-section Σ\_t, the spacelike hypersurface t = const at the observer's instantaneous time. The projection π\_{x\_obs} : ℋ\_S ⊗ ℋ\_A ⊗ ℋ\_E → ℋ\_{Σ\_t}^{loc} extracts the locally accessible content of the four-dimensional state at the observer's location. By (U), the global state evolves unitarily; the locally accessible content at the observer is the 3D restriction of this unitary evolution.

**Step 3: The apparent collapse.** The observer, accessing the state through the records correlated with their own branch on the spatial cross-section Σ\_t, registers a *single* configuration: the branch |s\_k⟩ ⊗ |A\_k⟩ ⊗ |E\_k⟩ with which the observer's own degrees of freedom have become correlated through the measurement interaction. In the Schmidt decomposition of |Ψ(t)⟩ into system–apparatus–environment components, the branches |s\_j⟩ ⊗ |A\_j⟩ ⊗ |E\_j⟩ for j ≠ k are all present in the four-dimensional |Ψ(t)⟩, distinguished from one another by their *apparatus and environmental configurations* — the pointer reading, the record state, the correlated environmental degrees of freedom — not in general by the observer's spatial coordinate. (For a position measurement these configurations are realised at different spatial detection points, as in the double-slit case of §V.5; for a spin or energy measurement they are realised as different apparatus pointer-states at the same location. In every case the distinguishing label is the full apparatus–environment configuration, of which spatial position is the special case for position measurements.) The observer's records are correlated with exactly one branch; that branch is the observer's unique registered outcome.

The probability that the observer's local cross-section intersects branch k rather than branch j is governed by the Born rule (Proposition III.1): P(k) = |c\_k|², the squared amplitude of branch k in the four-dimensional state. The squared amplitude is the SO(3)-Haar-weighted geometric measure of the branch's "size" in the spherically symmetric expansion of x₄ from the measurement interaction event. Branches with larger amplitude occupy larger fractions of the McGucken Sphere; the observer's local cross-section is more likely to intersect a larger branch.

The apparent collapse R is therefore not a separate dynamical law: it is the algebraic content of the observer's correlation with one branch of π\_{x\_obs} |Ψ(t)⟩. The observer registers one branch because the observer's own records have become correlated with one branch through the measurement interaction; a different run of the experiment correlates the observer with a different branch, with frequencies given by the Born weights below. All branches exist in the four-dimensional |Ψ(t)⟩; the observer's restricted access — correlation with a single branch on their own cross-section — is what creates the *appearance* of collapse.

The structure differs from Many-Worlds in that the branches are not separate "worlds" but separate spatial configurations within the same four-dimensional state. It differs from Bohmian mechanics in that there are no hidden variables — the four-dimensional state is the complete state, not a guidance function for hidden particles. It differs from Copenhagen in that there is no operational cut and no observer-relative information — the four-dimensional state is observer-independent. It differs from GRW in that there is no modification of (U) — the unitary evolution is exact. It differs from decoherence-plus-environmental-selection in that the preferred basis is selected by the spatial-three-slice structure of the 3D cross-section, not by the system-environment coupling alone. **∎**

### V.4 Comparison with Many-Worlds, Copenhagen, and Bohmian readings

The McGucken account of apparent collapse shares features with Many-Worlds (the unitary evolution is exact and all branches are present in the full state) and with Bohmian mechanics (the observer's outcome is determined by the observer's spatial configuration), but differs from both in three structural respects.

**Difference from Many-Worlds.** Many-Worlds treats branches as separate "worlds" — independent realities each containing an observer who sees a different outcome. The McGucken framework treats branches as separate spatial configurations within the same four-dimensional state. There is one reality (the four-dimensional |Ψ(t)⟩); observers at different spatial locations access different parts of it. The "branching" is a feature of the projection π\_{x\_obs}, not a feature of the dynamics. This avoids the standard objection to Many-Worlds — the proliferation of worlds and the question of why probabilities apply to branches at all — by replacing branching with spatial-slice projection.

**Difference from Bohmian mechanics.** Bohmian mechanics adds hidden variables (definite particle positions guided by ψ via the guidance equation). The McGucken framework adds *no* hidden variables. The wavefunction ψ is not a guidance function for hidden particles; it is the 3D projection of the four-dimensional state. The "definite outcome" the observer sees is the configuration of the four-dimensional state at the observer's spatial location, not a hidden particle position revealed by measurement.

**Difference from Copenhagen.** Copenhagen treats the wavefunction as the experimenter's knowledge and (R) as a Bayesian update. The McGucken framework treats the wavefunction as a 3D projection of an objective four-dimensional state, with the apparent collapse a structural feature of the projection (not an epistemic update). There is no observer-relative information; there is one objective four-dimensional reality, with multiple observers accessing different parts of it.

### V.5 In plain language

A photon traveling through a double-slit apparatus emerges as a McGucken Sphere — a four-dimensional object whose 3D cross-section is the Huygens wavefront we describe with ψ. The wavefront passes through both slits simultaneously, producing the interference pattern on the screen. When the photon "is detected" at a specific pixel, what has happened is that the four-dimensional McGucken Sphere has intersected the detector's spatial slice at that specific pixel. The other pixels of the screen — where the photon is not detected — are spatial locations where *this particular* McGucken Sphere does not intersect the slice. The wavefunction did not collapse; the four-dimensional object simply happened to land at one specific pixel as x₄ advanced. From the perspective of an observer at a different pixel (had the photon arrived there instead), it would have looked like the wavefunction collapsed at *that* pixel. There is no privileged collapse event; there is only the geometric fact that a four-dimensional McGucken Sphere intersects each spatial slice at a specific configuration determined by the SO(3)-invariant probability distribution.

The Born rule probabilities |c\_k|² govern *which* configuration the McGucken Sphere lands at, and they do so because the squared amplitude is the SO(3)-Haar-weighted geometric measure of the branch's contribution to the spherical expansion. Bigger branches (larger |c\_k|²) occupy more of the McGucken Sphere and are more likely to intersect a given observer's spatial slice. There is nothing stochastic about the four-dimensional dynamics — (U) is exact and deterministic. The apparent stochasticity arises from the observer's restricted access to the 3D cross-section. The structural deeper reason this account is forced — and not merely consistent — is the space-operator co-generation theorem of §XIII.10: because $\mathcal{M}_G$ and $D_M$ are co-generated by $dx_4/dt = ic$, there is no categorical room in the framework for a separate dynamical $(R)$ mechanism, and the apparent collapse must be a structural feature of the spatial-slice projection. Proposition XIII.6 establishes this categorical impossibility formally.

### V.5-bis Worked example: a photon at the centre of a closed detector sphere

The simplest case that exhibits where probability comes from, and that shows the cross-section reading of Proposition V.1 and the first-contact collision of §XI.5-bis to be one event, is a single photon emitted from the centre of a sphere of detector screens. Take the detectors to be silicon photodiodes and the photons short-wavelength (blue), so that detection efficiency approaches unity: the depleted silicon absorbs a blue photon at shallow depth when the photon's momenergy meets an electron's, and essentially every emitted photon is registered somewhere on the sphere. The whole $4\pi$ solid angle is instrumented, so detection *somewhere* is certain.

*Propagation (the Algebraic Channel readable, the Geometric Channel real).* On emission the photon advances as a spherically symmetric wavefront — the McGucken Sphere from the emission event — surfing the outbound expansion of $x_4$ at $c$. Every point on that wavefront is $x_4$-coincident with the emission event (Theorem XII.A.2): the wavefront is one point in $x_4$, spread across the $3$-spatial sphere. This is the outbound First Law of Nonlocality (§VIII.6): the local emission event is carried outward into an extended nonlocal surface by the expansion. The wavefront reaches all the spherically arranged detectors on one $x_4$-coincident surface — in that precise sense, "at the same time." Before any detection, the photon's evolution is Algebraic Channel readable: complex, reversible, and indistinguishable in a single trial from a photon on a definite unitary trajectory (a photon between two mirrors would present the same single straight-line record). The wavefront is Geometric Channel geometric content — the expanding $x_4$-sphere — but it *appears* unitary until the modulus is applied.

*Detection (the modulus, physically applied).* Detection occurs when one detector electron's momenergy collides head-on with the photon's momenergy: the first-contact collision of §XI.5-bis, at which the antiparallel $x_4$-momentum components cancel and four-momentum conservation deposits the outcome in the spatial sector, absorbing the photon. This absorption is a physical Wick rotation (Theorem X.D): the silicon photoelectron exteriorises the imaginary unit from the photon's phase $\exp(iS/\hbar)$ onto the real $\tau = x_4/c$ axis, and the outcome registers as real Geometric Channel content. The photon's spatial momenergy is rotated into the electron's $x_4$-advance — the photon, which had $v_{x_4} = 0$ and rode the spatial surface of the expansion, is absorbed as its momenergy enters the electron's localised, $x_4$-advancing state. The modulus operation $|\cdot|^2:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{R}_+$ of Proposition II.1.2 is here physically instantiated as this collision --- the concrete event at which the complex Algebraic Channel amplitude becomes a real registered outcome.

*The three parts of the Born rule, each forced by a physical fact of the closed sphere.* The Born rule states three things — that the probabilities are normalized, that they follow $|\psi|^2$, and that one outcome occurs — and in the closed detector sphere each is forced by a physical fact, with no probability postulate laid on top. First, the photon cannot pass every detector: the sphere is closed, the detectors cover the whole surface the wavefront must cross, and at unit efficiency there is no gap to escape through, so detection somewhere is certain. This forces normalization — total probability unity — as a geometric fact: $\int |\psi|^2 = 1$ holds because the photon must land, not because normalization is imposed. Second, by the isotropy of the expansion no detector is privileged: $x_4$ is perpendicular to all three spatial dimensions equally, so no ray from the source is preferred, since a preferred detector would be a preferred direction the Principle forbids (§I.4.1-bis). Every detector stands on equal geometric footing, which forces the measure to be the unique $SO(3)$-invariant (Haar) measure over the sphere — equal solid angles carry equal probability — and that measure is $|\psi|^2$ (Proposition III.1). Third, the photon is one quantum: one wavefront, one $x_4$-coincident object, registered at a single head-on momenergy-cancellation event (§XI.5-bis), so exactly one detector fires. This forces single-outcome definiteness. The photon must land (normalization from closure), it may land anywhere with equal geometric right ($|\psi|^2$ from isotropy), and it lands at exactly one place (definiteness from one quantum): the three parts of the Born rule are the three physical facts of the closed sphere, and standard quantum mechanics postulates as one rule what the geometry here forces in three.

*Where the probability comes from.* Two facts fix the distribution. First, the expansion is isotropic — spherically symmetric, no preferred direction — so no detector is privileged. Second, the closed $4\pi$ sphere makes detection somewhere certain: the photon cannot avoid every detector, because the detectors cover the whole surface the wavefront must cross. Isotropy plus closure force the outcome to be distributed by the unique $SO(3)$-invariant (Haar) measure over the sphere, which is exactly $|\psi|^2$ (Proposition III.1): the probability of detector $k$ is the Haar measure of its solid angle. The probability is therefore not a separate postulate laid over the propagation; it is the isotropic measure of the single nonlocal $x_4$-surface, made observable by the certainty that the first-contact collision lands somewhere on it. Probability is wed to the nonlocality of the $x_4$-expansion: the photon has equal chance of first contact at any patch of equal solid angle, because every patch carries the one accumulated $x_4$-advance $X_4$ of the emission event, carried outward isotropically (Appendix A (R4)).

*Why one trial cannot show it, and many trials must.* A single photon yields one record — emitted, detected at $k$, apparently a straight line — and this record is compatible with an Algebraic Channel unitary story; the Geometric Channel sphere is invisible in one trial, because one point does not distinguish an isotropic wavefront from a definite trajectory. Only the statistics over many photons expose the $|\psi|^2$ distribution over the detector sphere, and that distribution is the direct imprint of the expanding wavefront's $SO(3)$ symmetry. This is the observable content of the modulus boundary (Proposition II.1.2): the Algebraic Channel carries the account up to the single complex amplitude, and it is the accumulation of real registered outcomes — Geometric Channel content beyond the modulus — that reveals the geometry was a sphere. The probabilistic distribution is the signature of the Geometric Channel; the ensemble makes the expanding $x_4$-sphere manifest.

*The two collapse-accounts are one event here.* In this closed single-photon case there is no branch-proliferation to self-locate among: one photon, one wavefront, one collision. The Proposition V.1 cross-section reading — the observer's spatial slice intersecting the configuration consistent with the outcome — and the §XI.5-bis first-contact collision are the same event: the observer's slice intersects the wavefront exactly at the detector where the collision registered, because that collision *is* the physical event that applies the modulus and produces the real outcome. No self-location weight over pre-existing copies is required, because there are no copies; there is one collision, and the cross-section update is the formalism recording that it occurred. The example therefore identifies, in the simplest concrete setting, the physical event (collision, §XI.5-bis), its description-level shadow (cross-section update, Proposition V.1), and its signature-reading (Euclidean Wick rotation at the apparatus, Theorem X.B/X.D) as one and the same measurement.

*Foundational probability is derived, not postulated.* The primary result of this example must be stated as the positive fact it is: the *existence* of probability, and its specific form, are forced by $dx_4/dt = ic$. That nature is probabilistic at all — that a definite emission yields a distribution of detection outcomes rather than a single determined one — is a consequence of the photon being a spherically symmetric wavefront co-present across the closed surface, not an added indeterminacy. That the distribution is uniform over equal solid angles is a consequence of the isotropy of the expansion. That its measure is $|\psi|^2$ is a consequence of the $SO(3)$-Haar structure (Proposition III.1). The empirical prediction — that ten million blue photons register uniformly over the detector sphere — is therefore a theorem of the principle, and it is confirmed by experiment, on which physics rests. Foundational probability is thus a derived law here: its necessity, its uniformity, and its $|\psi|^2$ form all descend from spherically symmetric expansion at $c$. This is the sense in which the framework does derive probability, and it is the substantive result; the "equal chance at any patch" is the derived content of isotropy, not an independent assumption.

*The one element left open, and its proper scope.* Distinct from the derived law of probability is the realization of a single trial: which detector fires on trial number $n$ — which electron achieves head-on momenergy cancellation first as the wavefront arrives. The derived distribution fixes the weights with which outcomes occur across the ensemble; whether the individual draw is fixed by the detector's microstate (a hidden-variable completion the secondary-source structure could support) or is irreducibly chancy is the determinism-versus-chance fork common to every interpretation (§XI.5-bis). This is a separate and smaller question than the origin of probability: the origin is derived (above), and only the metaphysical status of the single seed is open — a question no experiment can adjudicate, since any one outcome is compatible with both readings, and physics rests on the ensemble statistics the framework does derive. The framework supplies the physical locus of the seed (the head-on momenergy race among the sphere's electrons) and the derived distribution it is drawn from; it does not, and no framework can from single-trial data, settle the seed's determinism status.

*The residual, located precisely.* The example derives the certainty of detection (closed geometry), the form of the distribution ($SO(3)$-Haar $=|\psi|^2$), the definiteness of each outcome (pointlike first-contact), and the identity of the three collapse-accounts (one photon, no branches). What it does not fix is which detector fires on a given trial — which electron achieves head-on momenergy cancellation first as the wavefront arrives. Whether that seed is fixed by the detector's microstate (a hidden-variable completion the secondary-source structure could support) or is irreducibly chancy is the determinism-versus-chance fork common to all interpretations (§XI.5-bis), and the framework does not claim to close it. What the framework does supply is the physical locus of the open question — the head-on momenergy race among the sphere's electrons — and the derived distribution the seed is drawn from.

*Three experiments, three faces of one expansion.* The detector-sphere example is one of three experimental manifestations of $dx_4/dt = ic$, each exhibiting a different consequence of the one spherically symmetric expansion at $c$. The closed detector sphere exhibits *foundational probability*: ten million photons distribute uniformly over the sphere by the isotropic $SO(3)$-Haar measure, the derived form of $|\psi|^2$. The double-slit experiment exhibits *nonlocality*: the photon's wavefront passes through both slits at once, because it is one $x_4$-coincident object spanning both openings rather than a particle selecting one (the geometric double-slit reading; Proposition IV.1). Entanglement experiments exhibit *shared locality*: two photons travelling in opposite directions from a common creation event remain $x_4$-coincident as the expansion carries them outward, so their measured correlation is the persistence of the shared origin (Proposition VIII.1; the First Law of Nonlocality). The isotropic measure, the single wavefront through both slits, and the shared origin of the entangled pair are three experimentally confirmed faces of the same outbound expansion — probability, nonlocality, and entanglement each forced by $dx_4/dt = ic$ and each demonstrated in the laboratory.

*Connection to the arrow of time.* The same expansion that distributes the probability is the outbound $+ic$ advance that grounds irreversibility (Proposition VI.1). A photon idealised as bouncing between two mirrors does not persist indefinitely: nothing escapes the expansion of $x_4$, so the confined mode disperses, and the same $x_4$-monotonicity that makes the detection statistics accumulate in one time direction is the second law of thermodynamics. The probabilistic distribution over the detector sphere and the arrow of time are the same Geometric Channel outbound expansion, not two separate facts.

### V.5-ter What is caused, and what "collapse" is: the detector, the localization event, and the nonlocal wavefront that was one locality

The photon-detector-sphere example (§V.5-bis) makes precise a question that the word "collapse" usually leaves blurred: when a detector is placed close to a photon source and the photon is measured there, what exactly is caused, and what exactly collapses? The framework's answer separates two claims that the ordinary phrase "the measurement caused the wavefunction to collapse" runs together, and it supplies a physical mechanism for what is otherwise named without one.

**What the detector causes: the localization event.** Placing a detector near the source, with electrons available for the head-on momenergy collision (§III.1-ter, §XI.5-bis), is what makes the first-contact collision occur at that location and time. Move the detector and the collision occurs elsewhere; remove it and no collision occurs there at all. This dependence — intervene on the setup, and the outcome-event changes — is contentful, local causation of exactly the kind every experiment relies on (the interventionist content of §XI.3.8-bis): the detector's placement and its physical interaction with the arriving wavefront cause the localization event. The causation here is real, local, and $+ic$-oriented; it is the collision of the two McGucken Spheres at a definite spacetime event, produced by the detector being where it is. When one places a detector close to a photon source and the photon is measured, one does cause the photon's localization at that detector — this much of the ordinary sentence is exactly right.

**What is not caused: a signal that collapses the distant wavefront.** The tempting further picture is that the detection at the detector dispatches something — a collapse — that propagates out across the rest of the wavefront and forecloses detection at the far locations. That picture the framework denies (§VIII.6, the Einstein's-Bubble resolution). The far detectors do not fire, for that photon, not because a message reached them from the collision but because the entire wavefront was one $x_4$-coincident object from the start: every point on the expanding McGucken Sphere shares the emission event's accumulated $x_4$-advance $X_4$ (Theorem XII.A.2; Appendix A (R4)). When the one object is registered at one first-contact event, there is nothing remaining at the far locations to register — the distant parts were never causally separate things that a signal would have to update. What appears as an instantaneous collapse sweeping the wavefront is the single registration of one four-dimensional object, read as a spatial cross-section at each slice (Proposition V.1). There is no superluminal causal act; there is one local causal event (the collision) and one object of which it is the registration.

**The physical mechanism for what is called collapse.** Orthodox language speaks of collapse as a physical process — a very fast, or strictly instantaneous, change of something real, the sudden gathering of a spread-out wave into a point. The framework supplies a physical mechanism, and under it the character of "collapse" changes. What was spread out before detection was not a physical substance awaiting compression but the nonlocal wavefront of $x_4$'s expansion — one expanding surface that represented a single locality, the emission event, carried outward (the outbound First Law of Nonlocality, §VIII.6). The wavefunction $\\psi$ is the cross-section reading of that surface (Proposition V.1), and $|\\psi|^2$ is the probabilistic distribution of where the first-contact collision may occur on it (Proposition III.1, §V.5-bis). When the collision localizes the particle, that probabilistic distribution is simply no longer the relevant description: the particle has been registered at one point, and the distribution of where it might have been registered has no further referent. This is the probabilistic bookkeeping wavefunction ceasing to describe anything once the particle is localized, rather than the fast compression of a physical wave. "Collapse" names the fact that after the registration the observer's cross-section intersects the branch consistent with the outcome, so the pre-detection distribution is no longer what is read (Proposition IX.1: no separate dynamical collapse law). The framework thus gives the physical content behind the word: there was a nonlocal wavefront representing a single locality; the collision registered that one locality at one event; and the spread-out probabilistic description, having served to distribute the possible registration points, is afterward simply absent — no physical substance was compressed, and no instantaneous physical process propagated.

**A consequence worth stating: the nonlocality may persist beyond the measured particle.** The mechanism invites a reading of what was measured that the orthodox collapse picture forecloses. If what spread out was the nonlocal wavefront of $x_4$'s expansion — a property of the fourth dimension's isotropic advance, not a substance belonging to the particle alone — then it is coherent that the $x_4$-expansion continues after the particle is detected, and that the measurement observed the nonlocal properties of $x_4$ only through the interaction between the expansion and the particle. On this reading the particle rides the expanding surface (§III.1-bis, the photon as tracer of $x_4$); the detection is the collision that localizes the particle out of the expansion (§XI.5-bis); and the expansion of $x_4$ itself — the nonlocal surface — is not a thing that the particle's localization annihilates, but the ongoing advance of the fourth dimension, which the particle made observable during the interaction and which continues once the particle has been registered. This is offered as a reading the mechanism supports rather than as a separately established theorem: what the framework establishes is that the wavefront is the $x_4$-expansion (§III.1-bis) and that measurement is the localizing collision (§XI.5-bis); that the $x_4$-expansion persists independently of any one particle's registration is the natural consequence, and it reframes "collapse" as the end of one particle's participation in the nonlocal expansion rather than the destruction of the expansion itself.

**Why there was a distribution to collapse at all: the isotropy of the expansion.** The probabilistic distribution whose disappearance is called collapse exists for one reason, and it returns the account to the foundation. When $x_4$ expands, there is no preferred direction — nothing in $dx_4/dt = ic$ selects one spatial direction over another, since $x_4$ is perpendicular to all three spatial dimensions equally (§I.4.1-bis). An advance with no preferred direction is isotropic, and an isotropic advance from a point is a sphere: a local point must become a sphere of expanding locality. That forced isotropy is what makes the probability a distribution rather than a certainty — the particle is equivalently locatable anywhere on the expanding surface, with no point preferred because no direction is preferred, so the registration point is drawn from the isotropic $SO(3)$-Haar measure that is $|\\psi|^2$ (Proposition III.1). The distribution that "collapses" is therefore the isotropic measure of the one nonlocal surface, and it exists because the expansion of $x_4$ has no preferred direction; the collapse is the registration of one point of that surface, and the measure that described the possibilities is afterward absent because the possibility it distributed has been resolved into the one actual registration. Probability, nonlocality, and the localization at measurement are, once more, the three readings of the one isotropic expansion $dx_4/dt = ic$.

### V.6 What this means for Schrödinger's cat and Wigner's friend

Two thought experiments dominate the canonical statement of the measurement problem: Schrödinger's cat (1935) and Wigner's friend (1961). Both were proposed as *reductio ad absurdum* arguments — Schrödinger to show that quantum mechanics applied consistently produces "ridiculous cases" of macroscopic superposition, and Wigner to show that quantum mechanics cannot consistently formulate a universal observer-independent description. Each remains a touchstone for any candidate resolution of the measurement problem. The present subsection addresses both directly: what the McGucken framework's cross-section reading of $R$ (Proposition V.1) means concretely for each thought experiment.

#### V.6.1 Schrödinger's cat

The standard reading of Schrödinger's cat treats the cat as in a superposition of "alive" and "dead" until the box is opened, with the wavefunction $\psi_{\text{cat}} = \alpha|\text{alive}\rangle + \beta|\text{dead}\rangle$ collapsing at observation. Schrödinger himself, in *Die gegenwärtige Situation in der Quantenmechanik* [Schrödinger1935a, quoted in §XIII.13.11.3], proposed this as an absurdity — he did not believe a cat could really be in such a superposition, and the absurdity was the structural point of the thought experiment.

The McGucken framework dissolves the apparent paradox concretely through two complementary mechanisms.

**First**, the Compton-frequency decoherence threshold (Proposition VII.1) sets a structural cut between configurations that can sustain superposition long enough to be experimentally relevant and configurations that decohere on timescales below detection thresholds. The Compton frequency of a system of mass $m$ is $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$. For a cat of mass $\sim 5$ kg, $\omega_C \sim 4 \times 10^{51}$ Hz. The cat's rest-mass coupling to $x_4$-flow produces decoherence on timescales orders of magnitude below any conceivable physical detection threshold (cf. §VII.2 for the explicit cross-species ratio $T_{\text{dec},A}/T_{\text{dec},B} = (m_B/m_A)^2$). The cat's pointer states — alive, dead — are einselected by Compton-frequency coupling, *not* by an arbitrary system-environment Hamiltonian as in standard decoherence accounts, but by the cat's own rest mass coupling to the $x_4$-flow that the framework derives as foundational. The cat is in a definite state long before the box is opened. The "superposition" exists only at the level of the *atom* (microscopic, low Compton frequency, decoherence timescale long enough to matter for the radioactive-decay branching).

**Second**, even setting decoherence aside, the four-dimensional state of the system is well-defined throughout (Proposition V.1). The "alive" and "dead" outcomes are not two ontologically simultaneous states of one cat — they are two cross-sections of the same $x_4$-extended wavefront emanating from the radioactive-decay event $p_0$. The atom's $x_4$-wavefront has spherical SO(3)-Haar measure (Proposition III.1), and the observer's spatial slice $\Sigma_t$ at the moment of opening intersects this wavefront in *one* configuration. The probability of intersecting the "decayed" branch versus the "undecayed" branch is given by the spherical measure on the atom's $x_4$-wavefront — exactly the Born-distributed outcomes of the radioactive decay, propagated through the Geiger-counter—hammer—poison chain to the cat's macroscopic state.

Schrödinger's apparent paradox dissolves because the categorical separation it requires — between microscopic quantum and macroscopic classical — is replaced by a *continuous* Compton-frequency mechanism. There is no Heisenberg cut to be drawn arbitrarily between system and apparatus, between atom and cat, between cat and observer. The cut is set by the rest mass, and the rest mass varies continuously across the chain. The relevant microscopic degree of freedom — the radioactive nucleus's decay channel — sustains a coherent superposition of decayed and undecayed branches because what governs that branch's decoherence is the small energy splitting of the decay process and its weak coupling to the environment, not the nucleus's full rest-mass Compton frequency; the decay superposition persists over the decay's characteristic timescale (the half-life regime), which is long enough to matter. The cat (Compton frequency $\sim 10^{51}$ Hz, decoherence timescale astronomically below any detection threshold) is, by contrast, *not* in a superposition of alive and dead in any operationally meaningful sense — it is in one definite state, with Born-distributed probability of being alive or dead determined by the nucleus's branching at the moment the chain was triggered.

Schrödinger's reductio is therefore vindicated rather than refuted: he was right that a cat cannot be in a superposition of alive and dead. The McGucken framework explains *why* — not by adding a stochastic localization term (GRW), not by branching universes (Many-Worlds), not by a guidance equation (Bohmian), and not by an arbitrary system-environment coupling (decoherence), but by deriving the Compton-frequency cut from the same primitive law that derives the Born rule itself.

#### V.6.2 Wigner's friend

Wigner's thought experiment, presented in *Remarks on the Mind-Body Question* [Wigner1961, quoted in §XIII.13.11.4], goes further. A physicist (Wigner) and a friend both have access to the same quantum system. The friend performs a measurement and obtains a definite result. Wigner, who has not yet asked the friend, describes the joint friend-plus-system state as a superposition. *How can the same physical situation be in superposition for Wigner and definite for the friend?*

In the standard categorical structure of quantum mechanics, this produces an apparent contradiction. If both descriptions are correct, then the state is observer-relative — different observers report different states for the *same* physical situation. If only one description is correct, then standard quantum mechanics has a privileged-observer structure that is foreign to the rest of physics. Wigner himself, in 1961, took this as a reductio of the standard formalism, suggesting that consciousness must play a role in collapse. He later disavowed the consciousness-causes-collapse mechanism, but the structural difficulty he identified remained unresolved.

The McGucken framework dissolves the friend paradox through four structural features.

**First**, there is one underlying $x_4$-extended state $|\Psi(t)\rangle \in \mathcal{H}$ that includes the full system: the measured object, the friend, the apparatus, and Wigner. Both Wigner and the friend are configurations in $\mathcal{M}_G$ (Theorem XIII.I, the space-operator co-generation theorem); both are subject to $D_M$'s flow; neither has privileged status. There is no observer-relative state — there is a single four-dimensional state, viewed by two observers.

**Second**, what each observer *sees* is the cross-section of this single state at their respective spatial slice. The friend's spatial slice $\Sigma_{t,\text{friend}}$ intersects the wavefront when the friend looks at the apparatus; Wigner's spatial slice $\Sigma_{t,\text{Wigner}}$ intersects it later, when Wigner asks the friend (Proposition V.1). Both readings are correct cross-sections of the same underlying state. The friend's "definite description" and Wigner's "superposition description" are not two competing descriptions of the same 3D-now reality — they are *projections* of one $x_4$-extended state onto different spatial slices.

**Third**, the apparent paradox arises only when one assumes a single privileged 3D-now ontology — the assumption that there is one categorically true state of the universe at each moment, which Wigner and the friend should be reporting on consistently. The McGucken framework explicitly rejects this assumption. The four-dimensional state is the foundational object; 3D cross-sections are projections of it; different observers project onto different slices and therefore report different cross-sections, *without contradiction*. A 3D object's shadow on a wall and its shadow on a floor can look very different without the object being inconsistent. The friend's "definite outcome" is the shadow on $\Sigma_{t,\text{friend}}$; Wigner's "superposition" is the shadow on $\Sigma_{t,\text{Wigner}}$ before he asks; once Wigner asks, his shadow updates to a definite outcome too. The four-dimensional object never moved.

**Fourth**, the consistency of the two readings is structurally guaranteed by $x_4$-coincidence (Proposition VIII.1; First Law of Nonlocality). When Wigner asks the friend, the friend's outcome is communicated to Wigner not via "collapse propagation" along the U-curve of cosmological time, but via $x_4$-coincidence: Wigner's detection event and the friend's measurement event are points on the same expanding McGucken Sphere from the original quantum measurement source. The two readings agree because they are readings of the same wavefront, with $x_4$-coincidence supplying the structural connection between them. There is no observer-relative inconsistency; there is one wavefront, two cross-sections, one shared $x_4$-coincidence.

The deeper structural point is that Wigner's paradox depends on the standard categorical structure where "definite outcome" and "superposition" are mutually exclusive ontological states of *the same single 3D reality*. In the McGucken framework, both are projections of one $x_4$-extended state onto different spatial slices. Projections from different slices need not agree pointwise; what is required is that they agree on the common $x_4$-coincidences — and Proposition VIII.1 establishes that they do, by construction. Wigner's reductio dissolves because the categorical structure that makes it a reductio does not exist in the McGucken framework's category structure (Proposition XIII.6).

#### V.6.3 What both thought experiments share, and what each isolates

Schrödinger's cat and Wigner's friend isolate different aspects of the standard measurement problem. The cat isolates the *quantum-classical cut*: where, and on what physical basis, does macroscopic definiteness emerge from microscopic superposition? The friend isolates the *observer-independence*: how can a definite outcome be a definite outcome regardless of which observer sees it? Standard quantum mechanics struggles with both because (U) and Born are independent inputs whose connection at measurement is not supplied by either of them; the cat exposes the lack of a structural cut, and the friend exposes the lack of observer-independent reality.

The McGucken framework supplies both structural pieces from the same source. The cut is supplied by Compton-frequency decoherence, derived from rest-mass coupling to $x_4$-flow (Proposition VII.1). Observer-independence is supplied by the four-dimensional state with cross-section projections (Proposition V.1) and $x_4$-coincidence between observer-events (Proposition VIII.1). Both pieces follow as theorems of $dx_4/dt = ic$ via the source-pair $(\mathcal{M}_G, D_M)$, with no additional postulates. The cat is in a definite state because its Compton frequency is enormous; the friend's outcome is observer-independent because the four-dimensional state is observer-independent and the cross-section reading at any spatial slice is unique.

Schrödinger's "subject and object are only one" [Schrödinger1958, quoted in §XIII.13.11.3] and Wigner's "the dividing line cannot be eliminated" [Wigner1961, quoted in §XIII.13.11.4] are, in the McGucken framework, two readings of the same structural fact: the source-pair $(\mathcal{M}_G, D_M)$ co-generated by $dx_4/dt = ic$, with subject and object as configurations in the same source-space, and the dividing line between them as the spatial-slice projection rather than a categorical division. Both founders of the canonical thought experiments were correct in what they identified; what they lacked was the formal mathematics to make their identifications theorems. The McGucken framework supplies that mathematics.

#### V.6.4 Brukner's no-go theorem for observer-independent facts

The observer-independence claimed in §V.6.2–§V.6.3 must be tested against Brukner's no-go theorem [Brukner2018], which is the sharpest formal constraint on any framework asserting observer-independent measurement facts. Brukner proves that four assumptions are jointly incompatible: (1) universal validity of quantum theory (it applies at every scale, including an observer and her laboratory); (2) locality (one observer's setting choice does not influence a distant observer's outcome); (3) freedom of choice (settings are statistically independent of the rest of the experiment); and (4) observer-independent facts (the outcomes of Wigner and of his friend can be assigned joint truth values in a single Boolean algebra). The proof is a CHSH test on a nested Wigner-friend arrangement — super-observers Alice and Bob measure sealed laboratories containing observers Charlie and Debbie — reaching $S = 2\sqrt{2}$, above the bound of 2 that assumption (4) requires. At least one assumption must be relinquished.

This is a theorem, not an interpretation, so it constrains the McGucken framework as it constrains every framework: one of the four must be given up. The framework's commitments fix which one. Assumption (1) is retained — $dx_4/dt = ic$ applies at every scale, with no collapse threshold (in contrast to the objective-collapse models, which relinquish (1)). Assumption (3) is retained — the framework is not superdeterministic. The assumption relinquished is (2), locality, and it is relinquished with a physical mechanism rather than as a bare posit.

Brukner's locality is the statement that a setting choice on one wing does not influence the distant outcome. In the McGucken framework two entangled systems created at a common event $E$ are one $x_4$-coincident object: their wavefronts share the accumulated $x_4$-advance of $E$ and remain $x_4$-coincident as the expansion carries them outward (Proposition VIII.1; the First Law of Nonlocality, all nonlocality begins in locality). A setting choice on one wing is therefore not a spacelike influence transmitted to a separate distant system; it is a measurement performed on one $3$-spatial cross-section of a single object that is undivided in $x_4$. The framework is, in Brukner's classification, nonlocal — in the same category as de Broglie–Bohm, which Brukner names as relinquishing assumption (2) — but the nonlocality is the $x_4$-coincidence of the outbound expansion, not action across a spatial gap. The $S = 2\sqrt{2}$ that Brukner derives is the Tsirelson value the framework independently derives as the maximum $SO(3)$-Haar-weighted correlation on the spherically symmetric expansion (Proposition VIII.2; [MG-QM, Theorem 13]); it is the framework's own prediction, not a tension within it.

Relinquishing (2) is what permits the framework to retain (4) — the theorem forbids only the conjunction of all four, and with (2) dropped, observer-independent facts are admissible. The framework retains them in a definite form: the measurement outcome is a physical first-contact collision event at a definite spacetime point (§XI.5-bis), a Geometric Channel event with definite coordinates that occurs whether or not it is observed. This is the sense in which the framework keeps observer-independent facts where the relational and QBist readings relinquish assumption (4) instead: Wigner and his friend do not hold irreducibly observer-relative facts; they read different $3$-spatial cross-sections of one $x_4$-extended state (Proposition V.1), and the cross-sections are guaranteed mutually consistent by $x_4$-coincidence (§V.6.2). The objective fact is the collision event and the single $x_4$-extended state of which both observers' descriptions are slices; what is not observer-independent is only the cross-section each observer has access to, which is a statement about restricted access, not about the reality of the underlying event.

The cost of relinquishing locality is the standard one: a nonlocal theory sits in apparent tension with the no-preferred-frame content of special relativity. The framework's answer is the Cloaking Theorem (Theorem 39 of the corpus [MG-Cloaking], referenced in the four-velocity discussion): the preferred $x_4$-foliation to which the coincidence is referred is locally undetectable, its bookkeeping quantities cancelling from every local invariant measurement, so the nonlocality carries no signal (Proposition VIII.2, exact no-signaling) and produces no operational conflict with Lorentz invariance. This is the same foliation-relative commitment that the four-velocity bookkeeping quantities carry (Appendix on the four $x_4$-rate quantities): real, referred to the cosmic-comoving frame, and cloaked from local metrology.

The Frauchiger–Renner extension [FrauchigerRenner2018] sharpens Brukner's result: it targets the *self-consistency* of single-world frameworks across nested observers, proving that no theory can jointly satisfy compliance with quantum theory (QT), single-world (SW), and self-consistency (SC). The McGucken framework is single-world — one Geometric Channel collision per event, no Everett branches — so it retains (SW) and the argument applies to it. Its route to consistency is the same cross-section structure: the nested statements of $F_1$, $F_2$, $A$, and $W$ are readings of one $x_4$-extended state, and their consistency is enforced by $x_4$-coincidence rather than by comparing truth values across the mutually incompatible measurement contexts whose comparison the Frauchiger–Renner argument requires. The framework's diagnosis coincides with Brukner's own reading of Frauchiger–Renner: the self-consistency property (SC) illegitimately promotes one observer's knowledge of another observer's context-bound outcome into a joint Boolean algebra, and the promotion fails precisely because the outcomes live on different cross-sections of the $x_4$-extended state. What the framework adds is the physical referent for that failure — the cross-sections are $3$-spatial slices of one four-dimensional object, not competing accounts requiring reconciliation in a single context. The two-observer Wigner-friend case is worked in §V.6.2; the full four-observer Frauchiger–Renner nested chain is not carried through term by term here, and its explicit completion — showing that each nested inference is a cross-section reading and that the apparent contradiction is the comparison of incompatible slices — is a derivation the framework supports in principle and which remains to be written out in full.

## V.bis. Fields in the McGucken Framework

Section V established that the wave function $\psi$ is a derived geometric object — the complex amplitude carried by an $x_4$-spherical wavefront, with every aspect of its mathematical form being a theorem of $dx_4/dt = ic$ rather than an interpretive choice on a postulated entity. The structural significance of that result extends naturally to the broader question of what *fields* are in the McGucken framework.

The present section addresses the question directly. In standard physics, "field" is a polysemous term encompassing at least four structurally distinct kinds of object: classical fields (the electromagnetic field $F_{\mu\nu}$, the metric $g_{\mu\nu}$, hydrodynamic and temperature fields), quantum wave functions treated as fields (the historical Schrödinger reading of $\psi$ as a literal field on configuration space), quantum fields in QFT (operator-valued distributions $\hat{\phi}(x)$ on Fock space), and gauge fields (connections on principal bundles mediating the Standard Model interactions). A complete account of "what is a field?" requires addressing all four senses and explaining how they connect.

The McGucken framework's account is structurally uniform across the four senses: every kind of field is a *derived* object — a structure carrying values on the McGucken-derived spacetime $\mathcal{M}_{1,3}$ (or its substrate-scale and Fock-space refinements), with the value-space, the dynamics, and the gauge structure descending from the source-tuple $F_M = (\Sigma_M, \mathcal{G}_M, \mathcal{M}_G, D_M, \mathcal{S}_M, \mathcal{A}_M)$ as theorems rather than being postulated independently. This parallels the McGucken account of the wave function in §V.1: the strategic move is *derivation rather than postulation*, with the meaning of each derived object fixed by the derivation that produces it.

The structural unification across the four senses of "field" sits in sharp contrast to standard physics, where each kind of field is postulated as primitive and the connections between them (why electromagnetism is U(1), why the strong force is SU(3), why fermions satisfy Dirac, why gauge fields have curvature equations) are either independent postulates or empirical-input choices. The present section establishes how the four senses of field arise as theorems in the McGucken framework, contrasts the McGucken account with the seven major prior interpretive programmes plus standard QFT, and identifies which aspects of the field structure are settled in the corpus and which are programmatically in place pending further formalization.

### V.bis.1 Classical fields as cross-section structures of $\mathcal{M}_G$

The deepest structural reading of classical fields in the McGucken framework is that they are *cross-section structures* on $\mathcal{M}_G$ — smooth assignments of values to each point of the McGucken-derived spacetime $\mathcal{M}_{1,3}$, where the assigned values carry McGucken-derived geometric content. The field is not an independent entity coexisting with spacetime; it is a feature of the spacetime structure that descends from $\mathcal{M}_G$.

For the **electromagnetic field** specifically, the McGucken framework's account runs through the gauge-bundle derivation of [MG-McGuckenSpace, §16.7] together with the McGucken Symmetry [MG-FatherSymmetry]. The U(1) gauge structure is a theorem: it descends from the phase-freedom of $\psi$ under the local action $\psi(x) \to e^{i\alpha(x)} \psi(x)$, and this phase freedom is itself a structural feature of $i$ being the perpendicularity marker of $x_4$ in the McGucken Principle. The vector potential $A_\mu$ is the connection one-form on the McGucken-derived U(1) principal bundle; the field strength $F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu$ is the curvature two-form. Maxwell's equations $dF = 0$ and $d\star F = J$ follow from the Bianchi identity (a structural identity of any connection one-form's curvature) plus the Yang-Mills sector $\mathcal{L}_{\rm YM}$ of the McGucken Lagrangian [MG-Lagrangian]. The electromagnetic field is therefore, in the McGucken framework, *the curvature of the U(1) connection that descends from the phase-freedom of $x_4$-wavefronts via the McGucken-derived gauge-bundle structure*.

For the **gravitational field**, the structural picture is even cleaner. The metric $g_{\mu\nu}$ on spacetime $\mathcal{M}_{1,3}$ is what the McGucken constraint $\Phi_M = x_4 - ict = 0$ produces when projected onto the spatial-temporal slice — the metric is a derived feature of how $\mathcal{M}_G$'s four-dimensional structure restricts to its constraint locus, with the Lorentzian signature emerging from the imaginary unit $i$ in $dx_4/dt = ic$ converting the Euclidean four-metric into Minkowski signature [MG-GR; MG-McGuckenSpace, §16.2]. The Einstein field equations $G_{\mu\nu} = 8\pi G T_{\mu\nu}$ are derived from the Einstein-Hilbert sector $\mathcal{L}_{\rm EH}$ of the McGucken Lagrangian, with the stress-energy tensor $T_{\mu\nu}$ being the source of metric curvature sourced by the $x_4$-extended states whose configurations populate $\mathcal{M}_G$ [MG-Lagrangian; MG-GR]. The gravitational field is therefore *the curvature of the McGucken-derived spacetime metric, with curvature sourced by stress-energy of $x_4$-extended states* — and crucially, *no graviton is required*, because the metric is not a quantum field but a structural feature of the constraint-projection of $\mathcal{M}_G$ onto $\mathcal{M}_{1,3}$.

The structural unification across classical fields in the McGucken framework is that *every classical field is the curvature or potential of some structure that descends from $\mathcal{M}_G$ via McGucken-derived bundle/connection machinery*. The bundles are not postulated; the connections are not postulated; the field equations are not postulated. They all descend from the source-tuple via specific theorems whose statements appear in [MG-McGuckenSpace, MG-Lagrangian, MG-GR, MG-FatherSymmetry] and whose content is the structural derivation of classical-field theory from the single primitive law $dx_4/dt = ic$.

### V.bis.2 The wave function as a complex scalar field on $\mathcal{M}_G$

This sense of "field" was already addressed in §V.1: the wave function $\psi(\mathbf{x}, t)$ is a smooth complex-valued assignment to each point of spacetime, and as such it qualifies as a complex scalar field in the classical-field sense. What §V.1 establishes is that the McGucken-derived wave function is *more* than a field on spacetime alone — the underlying geometric object is the four-dimensional structure $\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4)$ on $\mathcal{M}_G$, with the standard 3D wave function being its cross-section reading at the constraint locus $x_4 = ict$.

The historical Schrödinger hope — that quantum mechanics is fundamentally a field theory and $\psi$ is a literal complex field on spacetime, with quantum probabilities being statistical readings of a continuous wave structure — is essentially correct in the McGucken framework. Schrödinger lacked the additional structural ingredient that the McGucken framework supplies: the four-dimensional underlying structure of which the 3D wave function is a cross-section. With that ingredient added, the Schrödinger reading becomes precise: $\psi$ is a field, but its foundational existence is on $\mathcal{M}_G$ rather than on $\mathcal{M}_{1,3}$, and what physicists work with as the "3D wave function" is the spatial-slice cross-section of this 4D field.

This is the simplest McGucken-derived field, and it provides the template for understanding the more elaborate quantum fields of QFT (§V.bis.3) as $D_M$-flow structures on multi-particle Fock-space liftings of the basic single-particle wave-function-as-field structure.

### V.bis.3 Quantum fields in QFT as $D_M$-flow on Fock space

This is structurally the deepest of the four senses, and the McGucken framework's account here connects to what [MG-McGuckenSpace, §16.6] establishes about Fock space being downstream in the derivational hierarchy of physical-arena spaces.

A quantum field $\hat{\phi}(x)$ in standard quantum field theory is an operator-valued distribution on spacetime, expandable as

$$\hat{\phi}(x) = \int \frac{d^3k}{(2\pi)^3 \sqrt{2\omega_k}} \left[ \hat{a}_k\, e^{-ik\cdot x} + \hat{a}_k^\dagger\, e^{ik\cdot x} \right]$$

with creation and annihilation operators $\hat{a}_k^\dagger, \hat{a}_k$ acting on Fock space $\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{H})$. In standard QFT, this entire construction is postulated: the Hilbert space is postulated, the Fock-space lifting is postulated, the canonical commutation relations $[\hat{\phi}(x), \hat{\pi}(y)] = i\hbar\,\delta^3(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y})$ are postulated, and the equations of motion (Klein-Gordon, Dirac, Maxwell, Yang-Mills) are postulated separately for each field type with structurally-independent Lagrangians.

In the McGucken framework, every component of the QFT construction is derived as a theorem:

- **The single-particle Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$** is a theorem (Proposition XIII.1 of the present paper, plus [MG-McGuckenSpace, Theorem 12.1]). The Hilbert space is not postulated; it is the structural completion of complex amplitudes on $x_4$-wavefronts under the SO(3)-Haar-measure inner product (Proposition XIII.4).
- **The Fock space $\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{H}) = \bigoplus_n \mathcal{H}^{\otimes_s n}$** for many-particle states is a theorem [MG-McGuckenSpace, §16.6]. The symmetric (or antisymmetric) tensor algebra over the single-particle Hilbert space descends from N copies of $\mathcal{M}_G$ joined by McGucken-Sphere structure, with the $x_4$-coincidence connection (Proposition VIII.1 of the present paper) supplying the structural origin of multi-particle entanglement.
- **The creation and annihilation operators $\hat{a}_k^\dagger, \hat{a}_k$** are restrictions of $D_M$'s flow to specific momentum modes — they are theorems via the source-operator's action on Fock-space slots [MG-McGuckenOperator]. The "particle-creating" character of $\hat{a}_k^\dagger$ is the structural feature of $D_M$'s flow lifting an N-particle configuration to an (N+1)-particle configuration on the Fock-space hierarchy, with the momentum mode $k$ specifying the McGucken-Sphere wavefront direction.
- **The canonical commutation relations** $[\hat{\phi}(x), \hat{\pi}(y)] = i\hbar\,\delta^3(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y})$ are theorems (Proposition XIII.5 of the present paper, plus the two structurally-independent routes of [MG-CCR-Comp]). The canonical $i\hbar$ in $[\hat{q}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ is the same $i$ that is the perpendicularity marker of $x_4$ in $dx_4/dt = ic$, and the structure is forced by $D_M$'s commutator action on cross-sections.
- **The equations of motion** for each sector — Klein-Gordon for scalars, Dirac for fermions, Maxwell for U(1), Yang-Mills for non-abelian gauge fields — are derived from the corresponding sector of the McGucken Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}_{\rm McG} = \mathcal{L}_{\rm kin} + \mathcal{L}_{\rm Dirac} + \mathcal{L}_{\rm YM} + \mathcal{L}_{\rm EH}$ [MG-Lagrangian]. The four-sector decomposition is itself forced — no fewer, no more — by eleven minimal consistency conditions on $dx_4/dt = ic$, per [MG-Lagrangian, Theorem 1].

A quantum field in the McGucken framework is therefore, structurally, *a momentum-mode decomposition of $D_M$'s flow on Fock space, with the Fock space being the symmetric or antisymmetric tensor algebra over the single-particle Hilbert space derived from $\mathcal{M}_G$, and the field's equation of motion descending from the corresponding sector of the McGucken Lagrangian*. Every component descends from the source-tuple $F_M$. The seemingly disparate field types of standard QFT — bosons and fermions, gauge fields and matter fields, massless and massive — are unified as different sectors of the same source-flow $D_M$ acting on different Fock-space liftings.

### V.bis.4 Gauge fields as connections on McGucken-derived principal bundles

The Standard Model's gauge group $G_{\rm SM} = U(1)_Y \times SU(2)_L \times SU(3)_c$ has, in the McGucken framework, a structurally explicit derivation route via [MG-FatherSymmetry] together with [MG-McGuckenSpace, §16.7] and the substrate-scale identifications of [MG-Connes, Theorem H]. The structural picture, with the gap between *settled* and *programmatically in place* identified explicitly:

**The U(1) gauge structure is settled.** It descends from the phase-freedom of $x_4$-wavefronts: the wave function $\psi$ has the local symmetry $\psi(x) \to e^{i\alpha(x)} \psi(x)$ because $i$ is the perpendicularity marker of $x_4$, and the local nature of the phase freedom forces a connection one-form $A_\mu$ on the U(1) principal bundle. This is the electromagnetic potential, with the field strength $F_{\mu\nu}$ being the curvature two-form. Both the bundle structure and the connection are theorems of [MG-McGuckenSpace, §16.7], not postulates.

**The SU(2)\_L gauge structure descends programmatically.** The structural route runs through the Cl(1,3) Clifford algebra of the McGucken-Dirac construction [MG-Dirac]: the McGucken-Dirac equation forces a four-component spinor structure decomposing canonically into Weyl components $\psi_L \in S^+$ and $\psi_R \in S^-$, with the $x_4$-reversal $\Theta_{x_4}: x_4 \to -x_4$ acting as charge conjugation $C: \psi_L \leftrightarrow \overline{\psi_R}$. The McGucken-Sphere SO(3) symmetry, acting on the two-component irreducible representation of the even subalgebra Cl(1,3)$^+$ (which is isomorphic to the algebra of complex 2×2 matrices), lifts canonically to an internal SU(2) action on left-handed Weyl doublets. The chirality structure — that SU(2) acts on left-handed components only — descends from the $\Theta_{x_4}$-non-commutativity of the McGucken-Sphere action on Cl(1,3)$^+$ chirality eigenspaces. This route is structurally laid out in [MG-FatherSymmetry] but the explicit theorem statement (call it FS-2 in [MG-GaugeGroups]) is research-program-active.

**The SU(3)\_c colour gauge structure is the deepest open derivation.** The structural route runs through the substrate-scale identifications of [MG-Connes, Theorem H], where Planck-volume four-spheres tile the noncommutative four-manifold via the higher Heisenberg commutation relation of [Chamseddine-Connes-Mukhanov2014]. The colour SU(3) is conjecturally the symmetry of how substrate-scale McGucken Spheres pack at the Planck scale, with the three-fold internal structure descending from the three-fold irreducible decomposition of the higher Heisenberg relation. This conjecture (FS-3 in [MG-GaugeGroups]) is genuine open research; the structural route is laid out, but the explicit theorem is not yet written.

**The hypercharge U(1)\_Y descends as a structural combination.** The full U(1)\_Y of hypercharge descends as a combination of the $x_4$-phase-freedom U(1) (which becomes the McGucken-derived U(1)\_em after electroweak symmetry breaking) and a residual internal U(1) emerging from the SU(2)\_L × SU(3)\_c bundle structure. The Weinberg angle $\theta_W$ would be a structural consequence of the relative McGucken-Sphere-saturation rates of the SU(2) and U(1) sectors at substrate scale (FS-4 in [MG-GaugeGroups]).

**The structural prediction of no GUT.** A specific structural feature distinguishing the McGucken framework from grand-unified theories (SU(5), SO(10), $E_6$, $E_8$, etc.) is that the gauge group is forced to be *exactly* $U(1)_Y \times SU(2)_L \times SU(3)_c$ — no larger embedding group is structurally necessary. The structural reason: in the McGucken framework, the gauge group descends from specific geometric features of $\mathcal{M}_G$ and its substrate (Cl(1,3)$^+$ for SU(2), substrate-scale McGucken-Sphere packing for SU(3), $x_4$-phase-freedom for U(1)). There is no geometric feature of the framework that would naturally produce a single embedding group of dimension twelve or larger. GUT gauge groups are mathematically compelling embeddings of $G_{\rm SM}$ but are not *forced* by any deeper geometric principle — and the McGucken framework, by deriving $G_{\rm SM}$ directly from geometric features, has no structural need to embed it in a larger group. This generates the testable prediction of *no proton decay*: if the framework's no-GUT structure is correct, there is no gauge boson connecting quarks to leptons, and proton decay is forbidden. The current experimental lower bound $\tau_p > 10^{34}$ years is consistent with this prediction and in increasing tension with minimal SU(5).

A gauge field in the McGucken framework is therefore *a connection on a principal bundle whose Lie-group structure descends from the McGucken Symmetry's internal action on Cl(1,3)$^+$ spinor structure (SU(2)), substrate-scale McGucken-Sphere packing (SU(3)), or $x_4$-phase-freedom (U(1)), with the bundle's base manifold descending from $\mathcal{M}_G$ and the Lie-algebra-valued curvature two-form descending from the corresponding sector of the McGucken Lagrangian*. Connections are not postulated; bundles are not postulated; the gauge group is not postulated. Each piece is a theorem (settled for U(1); programmatically in place for SU(2); open research for SU(3) via the substrate-scale Connes-descent route).

### V.bis.5 Comparison with prior interpretive programmes and standard QFT

The seven major interpretive programmes of quantum mechanics treated in the master comparison table — Copenhagen, Many-Worlds, Bohmian, GRW, Decoherence + einselection, RQM, QBism — each operate within standard QFT for any sufficiently relativistic application. None of them addresses the foundational question of *what fields are* at the level of the present paper's analysis of *what the wave function is* (§V.1). The interpretive programmes accept fields as primitive structural data of QFT and dispute the meaning of the wave function only; the question "what is a quantum field?" is treated as already-answered by the standard QFT formalism, with the field operator $\hat{\phi}(x)$ taken as primitive and the canonical commutation relations and equations of motion postulated together.

Standard quantum field theory itself, taken as a foundational programme rather than as a calculational toolkit, is the closest competitor to the McGucken framework's account of fields. Its structural commitment is that the field operator $\hat{\phi}(x)$ is primitive, with its locality, its commutation relations, its Lagrangian, its gauge invariances, and its symmetries being either postulates or empirical-input choices. The most rigorous formulation — algebraic QFT [Haag1996] — replaces the field operator with the local algebra $\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{O})$ associated to spacetime regions $\mathcal{O}$, and treats locality as a categorical axiom rather than a derived feature. Algebraic QFT gives the most mathematically precise standard-physics account of fields, but as Connes-style noncommutative-geometry analysis [MG-Connes] establishes, the algebraic-QFT spectral structure is itself a downstream descent image of McGucken Source-Tuple structure via the descent functor $F_{\rm Spec}$. Algebraic QFT is thus, structurally, a Sense-1 categorical equivalence (in the language of §XIII.13.12) — bidirectional in the re-encoding sense, not in the co-generation-from-primitive-law sense — and the McGucken framework supplies the prior third structure (the primitive law $dx_4/dt = ic$) that standard QFT, including algebraic QFT, lacks.

The field-comparison table:

| Question about fields | Standard QFT | Algebraic QFT | Copenhagen / standard interpretations | **McGucken** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Is the field operator $\hat{\phi}(x)$ postulated or derived? | postulated | postulated as local algebra $\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{O})$ | postulated (via standard QFT) | **derived: $D_M$-flow on Fock space** |
| Origin of canonical commutation $[\hat{\phi}, \hat{\pi}] = i\hbar\,\delta^3$ | postulated | postulated (as algebraic relation) | postulated | **theorem: $i$ from perpendicularity, $\hbar$ from $D_M$ commutator (Prop. XIII.5)** |
| Origin of Hilbert space and Fock space | postulated | postulated (GNS construction over algebra) | postulated | **theorem (Prop. XIII.1; [MG-McGuckenSpace, §16.5–16.6])** |
| Origin of equations of motion (KG, Dirac, Maxwell, YM) | postulated separately for each field type | postulated as local-algebra structure | postulated | **theorem: four sectors of $\mathcal{L}_{\rm McG}$ forced by 11 conditions [MG-Lagrangian]** |
| Origin of gauge group $U(1) \times SU(2) \times SU(3)$ | postulated (empirical input) | postulated | postulated (via standard QFT) | **theorem (settled for U(1); programmatic for SU(2), SU(3))** |
| Origin of locality / microcausality | postulated as axiom | postulated as axiom | postulated | **theorem: $x_4$-coincidence light-cone structure (Prop. VIII.1)** |
| Spacetime on which fields live | postulated (Minkowski / curved) | postulated | postulated | **theorem: $\mathcal{M}_{1,3}$ from constraint-projection of $\mathcal{M}_G$ [MG-McGuckenSpace, §16.2]** |
| Treatment of gravity | excluded (no graviton in standard QFT) or postulated (perturbative graviton) | excluded or postulated | excluded or postulated | **structural: metric is constraint-projection feature, no graviton needed [MG-GR]** |
| Need for renormalization | required (UV divergences) | required (in interacting theories) | required | **substrate-scale cutoff supplied by McGucken-Sphere granularity [MG-Connes, Theorem H]** |
| Three matter generations | postulated (empirical input) | postulated | postulated | **open research; structurally expected to descend from source-tuple feature [MG-Generations programmatic]** |

The pattern is the same as in the wave-function comparison of §V.1: every entry in the McGucken column is a theorem (settled or programmatically in place); every entry in every other column is a postulate or an empirical-input choice or a feature accepted as primitive. The categorical asymmetry is total. The McGucken framework derives where standard QFT and the interpretive programmes postulate.

### V.bis.6 What is settled and what is open

In intellectual honesty, the McGucken account of fields has different completeness levels for different sectors of the picture. The present subsection identifies these levels explicitly so the reader has a clear map of where the framework is settled, where it is programmatically in place, and where it is genuine open research.

**Settled in the corpus.** The wave function as the McGucken-derived complex amplitude of the $x_4$-wavefront [MG-QM, §V.1 of the present paper]. The U(1) gauge structure descending from $x_4$-phase-freedom [MG-McGuckenSpace, §16.7]. The Hilbert space and Fock space derivations [MG-McGuckenSpace, §16.5–16.6]. The canonical commutation relations and Schrödinger equation [MG-QM]. The four-sector decomposition of the McGucken Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}_{\rm McG} = \mathcal{L}_{\rm kin} + \mathcal{L}_{\rm Dirac} + \mathcal{L}_{\rm YM} + \mathcal{L}_{\rm EH}$ [MG-Lagrangian]. The gravitational field as McGucken-derived metric curvature with no graviton required [MG-GR]. The Connes spectral-triple as descent image of the source-tuple via $F_{\rm Spec}$ [MG-Connes].

**Programmatically in place but with details to be filled in.** The full SU(2)\_L × SU(3)\_c derivation from the McGucken Symmetry's internal action — the structural derivation route is laid out in [MG-FatherSymmetry], but the explicit construction of why SU(2) and SU(3) specifically (and not other Lie groups) descend is research-program-active rather than fully formalized in a single paper, with [MG-GaugeGroups] as the projected dedicated treatment. The exact correspondence between the Chamseddine-Connes-Mukhanov "quanta of geometry" and the McGucken Spheres at substrate scale [MG-Connes, Theorem H] — this connects fields-on-spacetime to the noncommutative-geometry image of fields, with the descent functor $F_{\rm Spec}$ doing the structural work, but the explicit substrate-scale identifications need further formalization. The empirical-input encoding of the Standard Model parameters (Yukawa couplings, mixing angles, mass spectrum) — the structural framework is present in [MG-Lagrangian] but the explicit fitting of internal-algebra empirical inputs to observed parameter values is its own program.

**Genuinely open.** A complete derivation of why the matter sector has three generations from the McGucken framework alone — this is open in standard physics too, but the McGucken framework would predict that the three-generation structure descends from a specific feature of the source-tuple, and identifying which feature is open work [MG-Generations]. The full derivation of dark matter and dark energy as McGucken-cosmological consequences [MG-Lambda, MG-DarkMatter] is in progress; whether dark matter is a separate field, an artifact of the McGucken-cosmological geometry, or something else entirely is an active research question.

The structural picture is therefore clear in outline and settled in detail for several specific cases, with active research filling in the gaps for full Standard Model and cosmological coverage. The framework's commitment is uniform across the four senses of "field": *every aspect of every field type is ultimately a theorem of $dx_4/dt = ic$*. The work in progress is the explicit derivation of the remaining pieces, with the SU(3) substrate-scale derivation being the deepest open frontier.

### V.bis.7 The McGucken definition of "field"

If pressed for a one-sentence definition that fits the framework: a field in the McGucken framework is a smooth assignment of values from a McGucken-derived value-space (complex scalars, spinors, vectors, tensors, Lie-algebra elements) to points of $\mathcal{M}_G$ or its constraint-projected spacetime $\mathcal{M}_{1,3}$, with the assignment's dynamics governed by $D_M$'s flow restricted to the relevant sector of the McGucken Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}_{\rm McG} = \mathcal{L}_{\rm kin} + \mathcal{L}_{\rm Dirac} + \mathcal{L}_{\rm YM} + \mathcal{L}_{\rm EH}$ — with the value-space, the dynamics, and the gauge structure all descending from the source-tuple $F_M = (\Sigma_M, \mathcal{G}_M, \mathcal{M}_G, D_M, \mathcal{S}_M, \mathcal{A}_M)$ as theorems rather than being postulated independently.

Compared to the standard "a field is a tensor-valued map from spacetime" definition, the McGucken definition adds the structural content that *what counts as a field, and what dynamics it satisfies, is itself derivable* rather than being a postulated input. This is the same strategic move that the framework makes for the wave function in §V.1: not interpreting a postulated object, but deriving the object so its meaning is fixed by the derivation.

**Definition V.bis.1 (The McGucken field).** *A field $\Phi$ in the McGucken framework is a section of a fibre bundle $E \to \mathcal{M}_{1,3}$ whose fibre value-space is a McGucken-derived structure (complex scalar, spinor representation of Cl(1,3), vector or tensor representation, Lie-algebra-valued one-form), with the bundle structure descending from $\mathcal{M}_G$ via the universal derivability principle of [MG-McGuckenSpace], the field's dynamics governed by $D_M$'s flow restricted to the relevant Lagrangian sector, and the field's gauge symmetries (if any) descending from the McGucken Symmetry's internal action [MG-FatherSymmetry] — with each component of the construction being a theorem of $dx_4/dt = ic$ rather than an independent postulate.*

The structural payoff of this definition is that the four senses of "field" — classical, wave-function, QFT-operator, gauge — are unified as different bundle and value-space realizations of the same underlying derivation, rather than being four structurally-independent kinds of object that happen to share the name "field." In the McGucken framework, a field is what $D_M$'s flow on a McGucken-derived bundle produces, and the apparent diversity of field types in standard physics is a structural feature of which sector of the McGucken Lagrangian governs the flow.

The wave function is what $x_4$'s spherical expansion produces. The classical fields are the curvatures of the bundles that the McGucken Symmetry produces. The quantum fields are the $D_M$-flow on the Fock space that the multi-particle $x_4$-coincidence structure produces. The gauge fields are the connections on the principal bundles that the McGucken Symmetry's internal action produces. Every kind of field descends from the same primitive law, and the McGucken framework supplies the structural unification that standard physics treats as four distinct subjects.
