## VI. The Irreversibility of Measurement

### VI.1 The thermodynamic arrow

The irreversibility of measurement is the same irreversibility that characterizes the second law of thermodynamics throughout physics. In the McGucken framework, both are theorems of x₄'s monotonic advance.

### VI.2 Proposition VI.1 (Measurement irreversibility from x₄-monotonicity)

**Proposition VI.1 (The irreversibility of measurement is the same x₄-monotonicity that grounds the second law).** *The apparent irreversibility of (R) — that once a measurement has been made, the system cannot return to its premeasurement superposition — is a Grade-2 theorem of x₄'s monotonic advance, identical in structural origin to the second law of thermodynamics. No separate stochastic dynamics is required.*

**Proof.** From [MG-Entropy] and [MG-Horizon, §7], the second law of thermodynamics has a dynamical origin in x₄'s monotonic advance: at the initial moment t = 0 of any process, no x₄-advance has occurred and the accessible phase-space volume is minimal; as x₄ advances at rate ic, the accessible phase-space volume grows continuously, driving entropy increase. The arrow of time is the arrow of x₄'s monotonic advance.

A measurement is a specific instance of this general process. Consider the von Neumann measurement scheme of §II.1: prior to the measurement interaction, the system is in a superposition Σ\_i c\_i |s\_i⟩ and the apparatus is in the ready state |A\_0⟩. After the measurement interaction at time t > 0, the system-apparatus state is the entangled superposition Σ\_i c\_i |s\_i⟩ ⊗ |A\_i⟩, with the apparatus pointer state |A\_i⟩ correlated with the system eigenstate |s\_i⟩.

The unitary evolution preserves information: the entangled superposition contains the same information as the original superposition plus the apparatus's correlation structure. To "undo" the measurement — to restore the premeasurement superposition — would require reversing the unitary evolution and disentangling the apparatus from the system. This is *in principle* possible (since (U) is reversible) but *practically* impossible: the apparatus has been entangled with the environment via Compton-frequency coupling (Convention I.5.4 and [MG-QM, Theorem 22]), and disentangling all the environmental degrees of freedom would require precise control over them — control that x₄'s monotonic advance has dispersed across an exponentially large phase space.

The irreversibility is therefore not a feature of a separate (R) law; it is the same x₄-monotonic dispersion that drives the second law. As x₄ advances, the entangled state spreads through the environmental phase space at rate proportional to the Compton frequencies of the environmental constituents (Theorem 22 of [MG-QM]). For a macroscopic apparatus with N ∼ 10²³ environmental degrees of freedom each oscillating at Compton frequencies ω\_C ∼ 10²⁴ rad/s for nucleons (and ∼ 10²¹ rad/s for electrons), the dispersion timescale is Planck-short — far below any observational timescale. The "collapse" appears irreversible because the practical reversibility timescale exceeds the age of the universe by factors involving the entropy of the apparatus.

The structural identification with the second law is precise: both are Grade-2 theorems of dx₄/dt = ic via the same monotonic-advance mechanism. The apparent (R) irreversibility is one consequence of the universal x₄-monotonicity that also produces thermodynamic entropy increase, the cosmological arrow of time, and the radiative arrow [MG-Entropy, MG-Horizon]. There is one arrow of time, with multiple manifestations. **∎**

### VI.3 Comparison with prior accounts

**Standard quantum mechanics + thermodynamics.** Standard quantum mechanics treats (U) reversibility and (R) irreversibility as a foundational tension, often "resolved" by appealing to thermodynamic-statistical arguments without specifying the underlying mechanism. The McGucken framework supplies the mechanism: x₄'s monotonic advance, the same mechanism that produces the second law.

**Decoherence accounts (Zurek).** The standard environmental-decoherence account explains irreversibility as information leakage to an environmental phase space too large to track. This is correct as far as it goes but does not specify *why* the environment has the requisite size and structure to produce irreversibility, and does not connect the measurement arrow to other thermodynamic arrows. The McGucken framework supplies the connection: the environmental phase-space size is set by the Compton-frequency coupling of environmental constituents to x₄'s expansion, and the various arrows of time are unified as manifestations of x₄'s monotonic advance.

**GRW.** The Ghirardi-Rimini-Weber programme adds explicit stochastic terms to (U) to produce (R) directly, with phenomenological parameters for the localization rate. The McGucken framework requires no additional dynamics: irreversibility emerges from the same (U) plus the geometric structure of x₄'s expansion.

**Past Hypothesis (Albert, Penrose).** The Albert-Penrose Past Hypothesis posits a brute-fact low-entropy initial condition for the universe to ground the thermodynamic arrow. The McGucken framework replaces this brute fact with a dynamical mechanism [MG-Horizon, §7]: entropy starts low because x₄-advance starts (no phase-space growth has yet occurred at t = 0), and entropy increases because x₄-advance continues. The same mechanism grounds the measurement arrow.

## VII. The Preferred Basis Selected by Compton-Frequency Decoherence

### VII.1 The preferred-basis problem

Standard quantum mechanics does not specify a preferred basis. The reduced density matrix ρ\_S = Tr\_A |Ψ⟩⟨Ψ| of the post-measurement state is diagonal in the eigenbasis of the measured observable, but it is *also* diagonal in any unitary transformation of that basis. Why does the observer see definite outcomes in the eigenbasis of (say) position rather than some superposition basis?

The standard decoherence answer (Zurek, Joos, Zeh) is that the system-environment coupling diagonalizes ρ\_S in a specific basis — the *pointer basis* — determined by which observables of the system commute with the system-environment interaction Hamiltonian. The pointer basis is the basis "monitored by the environment," and the preferred basis problem reduces to specifying the environmental coupling.

This shifts the problem rather than solving it: which environmental coupling is the right one? The McGucken framework supplies a specific physical mechanism — environmental Compton-frequency coupling to x₄ — that fixes the preferred basis from first principles.

### VII.2 Proposition VII.1 (Preferred basis from environmental Compton-frequency decoherence)

**Proposition VII.1 (The preferred basis is selected by environmental Compton-frequency coupling to x₄'s expansion).** *In the McGucken framework, the preferred basis observed by macroscopic observers is the position basis (and the energy basis for stationary states), and the cut between quantum and classical regimes is the scale at which environmental Compton-frequency coupling to x₄'s expansion produces decoherence faster than coherent dynamics. The cut is specified by a concrete physical mechanism — the Compton frequency of environmental constituents — rather than left arbitrary.*

**Proof.** From Convention I.5.4 (Compton coupling), every massive particle of rest mass m couples to x₄'s expansion at its Compton angular frequency ω\_C = mc²/ℏ. For the constituents of a macroscopic environment — nucleons (m\_p c²/ℏ ≈ 1.4 × 10²⁴ rad/s), electrons (m\_e c²/ℏ ≈ 7.8 × 10²⁰ rad/s), and atomic and molecular systems — the Compton frequencies are extremely high, and the coupling to x₄'s expansion produces extremely rapid phase oscillations.

When a quantum system S interacts with an environmental constituent E, the system's reduced density matrix ρ\_S acquires off-diagonal terms that oscillate at the difference frequencies of the system and environment Compton couplings. For macroscopic environments with N ∼ 10²³ constituents, the off-diagonal terms accumulate phase contributions from all N constituents, producing an effective decoherence rate

  Γ\_dec ≈ Σ\_{i=1}^{N} ω\_{C,i} (g\_{S,i})² / ℏ

where g\_{S,i} is the system-environment coupling strength to constituent i. The mass-dependence of Γ\_dec therefore has two sources: the explicit factor ω\_{C,i} ∝ m\_i, and any mass-dependence carried by the coupling g\_{S,i} itself. The cross-species prediction below (T\_dec ∝ ω\_C^{−2}) requires that the dominant system-side coupling scale as g\_S ∝ ω\_C^{1/2}, so that Γ\_dec ∝ ω\_C²; this scaling of the coupling is a structural assumption of the Compton-coupling model [MG-QM, Theorem 22], stated here explicitly rather than derived in the present paper, and is the load-bearing premise of the empirical test of §VII.2. For typical macroscopic systems, Γ\_dec is enormous on either the linear or the quadratic reading — far greater than any coherent dynamical timescale — so off-diagonal terms decay to zero on Planck-short timescales relative to the observer's timescale.

The basis in which Γ\_dec is *not* enormous — the basis whose elements minimize off-diagonal coupling to environmental Compton oscillations — is the *position basis* (and, for stationary states, the energy basis). Position eigenstates are localized in space and have well-defined spatial relations to environmental constituents at each point of space; their off-diagonal couplings are the smallest possible. This is the structural reason why macroscopic observers see definite spatial configurations and definite energies, but never superpositions of spatial configurations or energies.

The cut between quantum and classical regimes is therefore specified by a concrete physical scale: the scale at which the system's coherent dynamical timescale T\_coh exceeds the Compton-frequency decoherence timescale T\_dec = 1/Γ\_dec. For microscopic systems (e.g., a single atom), T\_coh ≪ T\_dec, so quantum behavior is observable. For macroscopic systems (e.g., a brick), T\_coh ≫ T\_dec, so classical behavior dominates. The crossover scale is determined by the physical sizes and Compton couplings — no arbitrary cut is required.

The Compton-frequency decoherence mechanism makes a specific empirical prediction (Theorem 22 of [MG-QM]): the cross-species ratio of decoherence times for different masses is

  T\_{dec,A} / T\_{dec,B} = (m\_B / m\_A)² = (ω\_{C,B} / ω\_{C,A})²,

where m\_i is the rest mass and ω\_{C,i} = m\_i c² / ℏ is the Compton angular frequency of species i. The mass-squared scaling follows from Γ\_dec ∝ ω\_C² under the coupling assumption g\_S ∝ ω\_C^{1/2} stated in the proof above, and contrasts with thermal decoherence's 1/m scaling. The prediction is testable in cold-atom systems at ultra-low temperatures, where thermal effects are suppressed and Compton-frequency coupling becomes the dominant decoherence channel; a measured scaling departing from (m\_B/m\_A)² would falsify the coupling assumption and with it this sector of the model. **∎**

### VII.3 Comparison with standard decoherence

The Zurek/Joos/Zeh decoherence programme correctly identifies that environmental coupling produces apparent classicality, but does not specify *which* environmental coupling is the foundational one. Different system-environment couplings produce different pointer bases; the framework requires additional input to fix the coupling.

The McGucken framework fixes the coupling from first principles: every massive constituent of every environment couples to x₄'s expansion at its Compton frequency, and the position basis is the basis that minimizes this coupling for spatially-localized environmental constituents. The preferred basis is therefore *forced* by the geometric structure of x₄'s expansion, not selected by phenomenological choice of system-environment Hamiltonian.

This is a substantive advance over standard decoherence: where the standard programme has free parameters (the system-environment coupling), the McGucken framework has a specific mechanism (Compton-frequency coupling) that fixes the preferred basis from first principles. The cross-species mass-independence test (Theorem 22 of [MG-QM]) provides an empirical discriminator between the two accounts.

## VIII. Quantum Nonlocality from x₄'s Spherical Expansion

### VIII.1 The Bell phenomenon and the standard puzzle

Bell's theorem [Bell1964] and the CHSH inequality [CHSH1969] establish that quantum correlations cannot be reproduced by any local hidden-variable theory. Aspect's experiments [Aspect1982; Aspect2015] confirmed quantum nonlocality up to the Tsirelson bound 2√2 [Tsirelson1980], and the loophole-free experiments of [Hensen2015; Giustina2015; Shalm2015] closed the remaining locality and detection loopholes.

The standard formalism reports the violation and proves the no-signalling theorem (entangled measurements cannot transmit information faster than light), but supplies no geometric mechanism for how distant entangled particles maintain correlations consistent with relativistic causality. This is the (P5) sub-problem of §II.2.

### VIII.2 Proposition VIII.1 (Nonlocality from six-sense null-surface identity)

**Proposition VIII.1 (Quantum nonlocality is the geometric consequence of x₄-mediated correlation through the six-sense null-surface identity of the McGucken Sphere).** *Two entangled particles created at a common spacetime event E share six-sense null-surface identity with respect to E, with the identity preserved along subsequent null-geodesic propagation. The Bell-violating correlations between the particles are not faster-than-light spatial signaling but the geometric expression of this preserved shared identity, with the spacelike separation of the spatial cross-sections leaving the x₄-coupled state coherent. The First Law of Nonlocality — all nonlocality begins in locality — supplies the structural account.*

**Proof.** From [MG-Susskind, §II.4] and Convention I.5.6, two distinct points p, q on the same McGucken Sphere centered on a common emission event E share geometric identity in six independent mathematical senses with respect to E: foliation theory (both on the same leaf of the null-cone foliation), level sets (both at the same metric distance cτ from E), caustics/Huygens (both on the same wavefront from E), contact geometry (both on the same Legendrian section), conformal/inversive (both invariant under the same Möbius pencil structure), and null-hypersurface (both on the same spacelike cross-section of the future light cone of E).

The corollary established in [MG-Susskind, §II.4]: **the six-sense identity is preserved under null-geodesic propagation**. If p and q share six-sense identity with respect to E, and if their null geodesics from E are continued forward to new points p′, q′, then p′ and q′ still share the same six-sense identity structure with respect to E. The reason: null geodesics are precisely the trajectories that preserve null-hypersurface membership, and each of the six senses is a property of pairs of points on null hypersurfaces from a common emission event.

A pair of entangled particles is created at a common spacetime event E (e.g., a photon-pair source, a parametric down-conversion crystal, an atomic decay). The two particles propagate along null or near-null worldlines from E. By the six-sense corollary, they retain six-sense identity with respect to E throughout their propagation, even as their spatial separation increases.

When the two particles are measured at spacelike-separated detectors A and B at time t after the emission event, the measurement outcomes correlate because the particles are *the same object* with respect to E in six independent geometric senses. The correlations are not the result of faster-than-light signaling between A and B at the time of measurement; they are the result of the shared geometric identity that has persisted from the emission event onward. There is no faster-than-light signal because there is no signal at all — the correlation is a structural feature of the four-dimensional geometry of the McGucken Sphere from E.

The CHSH violation up to 2√2 is the quantitative expression of this shared geometric identity. By [MG-QM, Theorem 13] (CHSH and Tsirelson bound), the bound 2√2 is the maximum CHSH score achievable through SO(3) Haar-measure averages on the spherical symmetry of x₄'s expansion. The Tsirelson bound is therefore a Grade-2 theorem of dx₄/dt = ic, not a separate quantum postulate.

The First Law of Nonlocality [MG-Nonloc]: all nonlocality begins in locality. Two particles are nonlocally correlated *because* they originated locally at a common spacetime event. There is no nonlocality without a shared local origin. The framework predicts no "spooky action at a distance" between particles with no shared causal past — and standard quantum mechanics, conformingly, predicts no Bell violations between such particles. The First Law unifies the empirical fact (only entangled pairs violate CHSH) with the geometric mechanism (only pairs with shared local origin share six-sense identity).

The mediated case — entanglement swapping and quantum teleportation [Pan1998] — extends the structure: each locally-created entangled pair carries its own McGucken Sphere from its own local origin, and entanglement is transferred at the local intersection of those spheres. The resulting correlations trace through a chain of intersecting McGucken Spheres back to local creation events, in accord with the First Law. **∎**

### VIII.3 Why this is geometrically distinct from prior accounts

The McGucken account of nonlocality is structurally distinct from the four prior approaches:

**Copenhagen.** Treats nonlocality as a feature of the wavefunction's holistic character, with no geometric mechanism. The McGucken framework supplies the mechanism: six-sense identity preserved along null geodesics.

**Bohmian mechanics.** Provides a nonlocal hidden-variable account: the guidance equation depends on the global wavefunction, producing nonlocal influences on hidden particle positions. The McGucken framework requires no hidden variables; the nonlocality is a structural feature of the four-dimensional state's projection onto spatial slices.

**Many-Worlds.** Treats correlations as preserved across branches by the unitary evolution; no geometric mechanism is given for the correlations themselves. The McGucken framework supplies the mechanism: shared six-sense identity at emission, preserved along propagation.

**Relational Quantum Mechanics.** Treats correlations as relational features of the wavefunction across observers. The McGucken framework treats correlations as objective features of the four-dimensional geometry, observer-independent.

**The structural payoff.** Among the surveyed frameworks, the McGucken framework is distinctive in supplying a *geometric mechanism* for nonlocality consistent with (i) relativistic causality (no faster-than-light signaling), (ii) the Tsirelson bound (the specific quantitative limit on CHSH violations), and (iii) the First Law of Nonlocality (the empirical fact that only entangled pairs with shared local origin exhibit Bell violations). All three are theorems of dx₄/dt = ic.

### VIII.4 Proposition VIII.2 (Probability cloaks nonlocality: the no-signaling theorem as a property of the physical apparatus)

The standard no-signaling theorem of quantum mechanics [GhirardiRiminiWeber1980; Eberhard1978; Bussey1982] states that no observer can transmit a message faster than light using entangled pairs, even though the entangled pair exhibits the instantaneous nonlocal correlations of Proposition VIII.1 violating Bell–CHSH up to the Tsirelson bound 2√2 [Tsirelson1980]. The standard derivation is purely algebraic: it follows from the linearity of quantum mechanics combined with the trace-preserving property of completely positive maps. The marginal probability P(a | x) = ∑\_b P(a, b | x, y) at one detector is independent of the distant setting y because the partial trace over the distant subsystem returns the same reduced density matrix regardless of what local operation the distant observer performs. This is a theorem of the algebraic apparatus; it has no geometric content. The derivation works equally well in a flat-space algebraic formalism with no metric, no light cone, and no specific spacetime structure — which is exactly why no-signaling has historically appeared as an unmotivated coexistence between nonlocality (which seems to require relativistic violation) and relativistic causality (which forbids superluminal signaling). Shimony coined the resulting puzzle "peaceful coexistence" [Shimony1978]: quantum mechanics is genuinely nonlocal, yet relativity is preserved, and the standard formalism offers no geometric reason why the two should be calibrated to coexist.

The McGucken framework reformulates the no-signaling picture by locating nonlocality and probability on one geometric object rather than treating them as independent algebraic inputs. The same expansion dx₄/dt = ic that produces the instantaneous nonlocal correlation between distant entangled measurements (Proposition VIII.1) also fixes, through the Born-rule statistics derived in Proposition III.1, the form of the marginal at each detector. The instantaneous correlation is real and geometric (the shared null hypersurface of the past McGucken Sphere); the marginal statistics at each detector are the SO(3)-Haar intensity of the local wavefront, and their independence of the distant setting — no-signaling proper — is the partial-trace property of the shared state. The result is that the nonlocal channel exists and is geometric, yet is cloaked by probability statistics so that no message is ever transmitted, with both features carried by the one wavefront. This is the *physical-geometric* reading of the no-signaling situation.

**Proposition VIII.2 (Probability cloaks nonlocality; the no-signaling theorem as a Grade-2 theorem of dx₄/dt = ic).** *Let A and B be two systems on a shared McGucken Sphere Σ₊(p₀) emitted from a common source event p₀. Let ρ\_AB be the joint state inherited from the wavefront identity at p₀ (Proposition VIII.1), and let {M^A\_a}, {M^B\_b} be local measurement settings at A and B parameterized by x and y respectively. Then three structural facts hold simultaneously and as theorems of the same primitive law dx₄/dt = ic:*

*(i) **Geometric nonlocality.** The joint statistics*

  *P(a, b | x, y) = Tr[(M^{A,x}\_a ⊗ M^{B,y}\_b) ρ\_AB]*

*exhibit the full Tsirelson-bound violation of CHSH (singlet correlation E(a,b) = −â · b̂) as a geometric consequence of shared null-hypersurface origin at p₀, by Proposition VIII.1.*

*(ii) **Marginal flatness.** The marginal probability at each detector is independent of the distant setting:*

  *P(a | x) = ∑\_b P(a, b | x, y) = |ψ^A\_x|²,    P(b | y) = ∑\_a P(a, b | x, y) = |ψ^B\_y|²,*

*by the SO(3) symmetry of Σ₊(p₀) (Convention I.5.2) and the Born rule applied separately to each subsystem (Proposition III.1).*

*(iii) **Cancellation.** The nonlocal channel of (i) carries no usable information: the geometric nonlocality is exactly cloaked by the wavefront-intensity statistics of (ii). This is the no-signaling theorem stated as a property of the physical apparatus (ℳ\_G, F\_M) itself, not of the algebraic formalism. The exactness of the cancellation is forced by the fact that nonlocality and probability are two readings of the same wavefront on the same McGucken Sphere, with the SO(3) symmetry of dx₄/dt = ic calibrating the two readings to cancel.*

**Proof.** *(i)* is Proposition VIII.1 specialized to the singlet wavefront on Σ₊(p₀): the two systems share six-sense null-surface identity with respect to p₀, preserved along null-geodesic propagation, with the CHSH bound 2√2 the maximum SO(3)-Haar-weighted score on the spherically symmetric expansion of x₄ from p₀ ([MG-QM, Theorem 13]).

*(ii)* The marginal at A is the diagonal of the reduced density matrix ρ\_A = Tr\_B(ρ\_AB). Its independence of the distant setting y is the standard partial-trace fact: for any local CPTP operation at B parameterised by y, Tr\_B is unchanged, so P(a | x) = Tr(M^{A,x}\_a ρ\_A) carries no dependence on y. What the McGucken geometry contributes is the *value* and *shape* of that marginal: by the SO(3) symmetry of Σ₊(p₀) under x₄'s spherically symmetric expansion (Convention I.5.2), the reduced state ρ\_A is the SO(3)-Haar-weighted intensity of the local wavefront, so P(a | x) = |ψ^A\_x|² (Proposition III.1, Piece 3). The same statement with A and B exchanged gives the marginal at B. The y-independence (no-signaling proper) is therefore inherited from the partial-trace structure of the shared state; the geometry supplies the Born-rule form of the marginal, not the y-independence itself.

*(iii)* is the conjunction of (i) and (ii). The geometric content is that the *same* object — the wavefront Σ₊(p₀) — carries both the nonlocal correlation (through its identity structure, (i)) and the marginal probability (through its SO(3)-Haar intensity, (ii)). On the McGucken reading, nonlocality and the Born-form marginal are two readings of one wavefront rather than two independent ingredients that must be checked for compatibility. The y-independence that constitutes no-signaling proper is the partial-trace property of the shared state, as in the standard treatment; what the McGucken framework adds is the structural reason the two features are automatically co-present and co-calibrated — they are inscribed on a single SO(3)-symmetric object generated by dx₄/dt = ic — rather than two separately-postulated facts. **∎**

**Corollary VIII.2.1 (What the geometric reading adds to no-signaling).** *The no-signaling theorem of conventional quantum mechanics is exact — not approximate, not a low-energy effective statement. Its exactness, as the y-independence of the marginal, is the exactness of the partial-trace identity and is shared by the McGucken and algebraic treatments alike. What the McGucken framework adds is structural: the wavefront Σ₊(p₀) is the one object on which both nonlocality and the marginal probability live, so the co-presence and mutual calibration of the two features are automatic rather than separately posited.*

This is the structural reason the saturation of the Tsirelson bound 2√2 on Σ₊(p₀) and the flatness of the marginal appear together across forty years of Bell experiments at separations from millimeters [Aspect1982] to 1200 km [Yin2017]: both are features of one SO(3)-symmetric wavefront. The standard algebraic derivations of no-signaling [GhirardiRiminiWeber1980; Eberhard1978; Bussey1982] establish the y-independence directly from linearity and partial trace, and the McGucken framework agrees with that derivation of no-signaling proper; what the algebraic route does not provide, and the geometric route does, is the account of *why* the nonlocal correlation and the marginal probability are inscribed on a single object and therefore co-occur. The specific value 2√2 of the saturated correlation is established separately, via the SO(3)-Haar-weighted maximum of [MG-QM, Theorem 13], and is not re-derived here.

**Corollary VIII.2.2 (Two faces of one expansion).** *The two "strange features" of quantum mechanics historically taken as independent — instantaneous nonlocal correlation [EPR1935; Bell1964; Aspect1982] and irreducible probability [Born1926; Heisenberg1927] — are not two features but one. Each is a face of the single expansion dx₄/dt = ic: nonlocality is the wavefront's identity, probability is the wavefront's intensity, and the relation between them is precisely the no-signaling theorem stated geometrically (Proposition VIII.2). Nonlocality and probability are not two postulates of nature; they are two faces of the McGucken Sphere generated by the principle.*

#### VIII.4.1 Why the standard no-signaling theorem cannot supply the geometric content

The Ghirardi–Rimini–Weber, Eberhard, and Bussey derivations of no-signaling proceed entirely within the algebraic formalism: linearity of QM, completely positive trace-preserving maps, partial trace reducing to the same density matrix regardless of distant operations. These ingredients establish the y-independence of the marginal — no-signaling proper — exactly and without approximation, and the McGucken framework inherits that same partial-trace fact (Proposition VIII.2(ii)). What the algebraic ingredients do not carry is any account of *why* the nonlocal correlation and the marginal probability are features of a single object, and therefore why they co-occur and are mutually calibrated. The standard derivation works as a formal theorem of the algebraic apparatus; the McGucken reading adds the structural content that both features are inscribed on one SO(3)-symmetric wavefront Σ₊(p₀). The specific saturation value 2√2 is supplied separately by the SO(3)-Haar maximum of [MG-QM, Theorem 13]; the no-signaling bound of 4 and the algebraic derivation of y-independence are common to both treatments.

#### VIII.4.2 The physical-apparatus reformulation

Under the McGucken framework, the no-signaling theorem becomes a property of the physical apparatus (ℳ\_G, F\_M) itself — the McGucken Space and the associated frame fields generated by dx₄/dt = ic at every event. The algebraic apparatus of QM (Hilbert space, density matrices, CPTP maps) is the *the dx₄/dt = ic Algebraic Channel* formalism on ℳ\_G (Convention I.5.5; Proposition XIII.1 of the present paper); the geometric apparatus (Sphere wavefronts, SO(3) symmetry on Σ₊(p₀), past-Sphere chain identity) is the *the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel* reading of the same physical content. The standard no-signaling theorem is the Algebraic Channel reading; the McGucken physical-apparatus no-signaling theorem (Proposition VIII.2) is the dual-channel reading, with the cancellation between nonlocality and probability statistics being forced by the geometric calibration on the McGucken Sphere rather than by the algebraic apparatus.

The reformulation has structural consequences. In the algebraic reading, no-signaling is a derived consequence of linearity plus partial trace. In the geometric reading, the *single* object Σ₊(p₀) carries both features: the wavefront's identity carries nonlocality, the wavefront's intensity carries probability, and the SO(3) symmetry of x₄'s expansion fixes the Born form of the marginal. The y-independence that makes no-signaling hold remains the partial-trace fact in both readings; what the geometric reading supplies is the reason the two features are co-inscribed on one object and therefore automatically co-present, rather than two ingredients whose compatibility must be separately verified.

#### VIII.4.3 Empirical signature

Every Bell experiment performed since Aspect 1982 has confirmed three facts simultaneously: (i) maximally nonlocal correlations saturating Tsirelson at 2√2 [Aspect1982; Hensen2015; Giustina2015; Shalm2015]; (ii) exact no-signaling at the marginal level [Bell1990 review]; (iii) the joint structure of (i) and (ii) being precisely calibrated. The McGucken framework predicts the *conjunction* of (i), (ii), and (iii) as a single geometric theorem; standard quantum mechanics has them as three independent algebraic facts whose joint exactness has no underlying explanation. The forty-year empirical record of Bell experiments is therefore the empirical signature of dx₄/dt = ic acting at every emission event with full SO(3) symmetry on the resulting McGucken Sphere, with the probability-cloaks-nonlocality calibration being the conjunction of nonlocality and no-signaling that the geometry forces.

#### VIII.4.4 Why this resolves the "peaceful coexistence" puzzle

The historical puzzle — Shimony's "peaceful coexistence" of relativity and nonlocality [Shimony1978] — is that QM is genuinely nonlocal yet relativity is preserved, with no apparent geometric reason for the calibration. The McGucken framework explains the coexistence as not a coincidence but a single geometric fact: nonlocality and no-signaling are two readings of the same Sphere wavefront, with the wavefront identity carrying the nonlocal correlation and the wavefront intensity carrying the marginal probability statistics, and the calibration between them being forced by the SO(3) symmetry of dx₄/dt = ic acting at the source event. The coexistence is peaceful because both features are projections of one object; the standard formalism has them as two facts to be independently reconciled, while the McGucken framework has them as one fact viewed through two channels.

This completes the structural diagnosis of nonlocality at the foundational level. Proposition VIII.1 establishes the *mechanism* of nonlocal correlation — six-sense null-surface identity preserved along null-geodesic propagation. Proposition VIII.2 establishes the *cloaking* of that correlation by Born-rule probability — the same SO(3) symmetry that produces the nonlocality produces the marginal flatness, so the channel exists geometrically but transmits no information. Together, the two propositions reduce the full Bell-phenomenology — entanglement, Tsirelson saturation, no-signaling, peaceful coexistence — to theorems of the single primitive law dx₄/dt = ic.

### VIII.5 The expanding fourth dimension as the physical mechanism, and its relation to prior programs

The propositions above make a claim stronger than a correspondence: the expanding fourth dimension is the physical carrier of nonlocality. As x₄ advances at rate c from every event, a single emission event is co-present across the extended spatial wavefront it generates, so that a correlation observed between spatially separated systems is the projection of one event's persistence at a shared accumulated x₄-advance X₄ (Appendix A (R4)). The expansion distributes locality into nonlocality — locality being the single emission event, nonlocality being the extended correlated wavefront — and the distribution is a physical process, not a bookkeeping relation. This subsection states the mechanism at its sharpest and places it against the programs in physics and mathematics that share part of its architecture, marking in each case what is shared and what is not, so that the framework's distinctive claim is neither overstated nor conflated with weaker cousins.

**The mechanism at a point.** Two systems co-emitted at a common event p₀ each ride the McGucken Sphere at |v| = c. On a null worldline the worldline's share of the advance vanishes (v_{x₄} = 0, the standard time-dilation factor c·dτ/dt at v = c), so each system is at rest in x₄: dτ = 0 pointwise, the accumulated x₄-advance X₄[γ] = ic·τ[γ] (proper time up to the factor ic) keeps its emission value along the null worldline, and the coordinate rate dx₄/dt = ic holds at every event the system crosses (Appendix A, (R1) and (R4)). The two systems therefore share the same accumulated x₄-advance, ΔX₄ = 0, independent of their spatial separation. They are separated in the three spatial dimensions while coincident in x₄; the measured correlation is the three-dimensional shadow of the four-dimensional x₄-coincidence. This is the pointwise content of the six-sense identity of Proposition VIII.1, and it is a geometric identity rather than a signaling channel — the marginals are independent (Proposition VIII.2), so no message is carried.

**What the mechanism is, against what the literature supplies.** The relevant literature on quantum nonlocality supplies existence results and reformulations, not a physical mechanism for what produces the correlation. Bell's theorem and the experimental record from Aspect (1982) through the loophole-free experiments (2015) establish that nonlocality is real and irreducible — an existence result, not a mechanism. Maudlin's *Quantum Non-Locality and Relativity* [Maudlin1994] works through every candidate for explaining the correlation away and concludes that nonlocality is real and cannot be reduced; that conclusion establishes that a mechanism is needed and legitimate to seek, and supplies none. The programs that offer geometric or informational content for nonlocality supply correspondences and pictures: the entanglement-geometry program (van Raamsdonk 2010; Ryu–Takayanagi 2006) establishes that entanglement entropy tracks geometric connectivity — a dictionary between structures that vary together, not an account of what produces the correlation; ER=EPR (Maldacena–Susskind 2013) offers a geometric picture in which entangled particles are joined by a non-traversable bridge that carries no signal — a restatement of the correlation, not a causal account; twistor theory (Penrose) trades locality for causality and builds the spacetime point from nonlocal null primitives — a reformulation of the geometric substrate in which locality is derived, not a mechanism for the quantum correlation. The extra-dimension-mediator proposals come closest to the shape of the McGucken claim in routing nonlocality through an extra dimension, but they add a further dimension as a mediator, supply no superluminal causal channel, and contain nothing that expands. The distinction is exact: these programs share with the McGucken framework the single commitment that locality is not fundamental — a genuine intellectual lineage for that inversion — and none proposes a dynamical fourth dimension whose expansion at rate c is the physical carrier that distributes locality into nonlocality. That mechanism is the framework's own.

**Maudlin's Theory of Linear Structures: shared architecture, opposite treatment of locality.** Maudlin's mathematical program [Maudlin2014, *New Foundations for Physical Geometry*] is the closest cousin on one axis and a clean contrast on another. On the shared axis, it derives spatial geometry from primitive temporal-directional structure: its primitive object is the directed line, and for relativistic spacetime the primitive is a two-place "earlier than" relation from which the light-cone structure is recovered without metrical input, with proper time added as a length along the directed lines. Maudlin states the resulting thesis directly — "the whole geometry of space-time derives from temporal structure; instead of spatializing time, Relativity temporalizes space" — which is the same inversion the McGucken framework makes (temporal structure primitive, spatial geometry and causal structure derived, proper time as an accumulated advance X₄[γ] = ic·τ[γ]). On the contrasting axis, Maudlin's primitive is static and local: the "earlier than" relation is a fixed order on a set of points, nothing expands, and his stated reason for preferring lines over long-range constructions is that facts about long-range relations among points are extrinsic and non-fundamental. His geometry therefore contains no nonlocality, seeks none, and by its own commitment excludes the long-range as fundamental; separately, his physics establishes that nonlocality is real but supplies no geometric mechanism for it and does not connect it to his geometry. Maudlin is thus a cousin on the derive-space-from-time architecture and a contrast, not a cousin, on nonlocality: his geometry has none, while the McGucken expanding fourth dimension distributes locality into nonlocality.

**Mathematical programs that take a derived point as primitive.** Two mathematical frameworks take the point as derived rather than primitive, and predate the physics. Pointless topology (locale theory; Stone 1930s, Menger, Ehresmann, Johnstone) replaces the open set with the lattice of opens as the primitive notion, with points recovered as derived maps and non-trivial locales existing with no points at all — the rigorous mathematical statement of the inversion the McGucken mechanism enacts physically (extended structure primitive, point derived). Noncommutative geometry (Connes), through Gelfand duality, sharpens this into a statement about spaces without points: commutative C*-algebras correspond to point-spaces, and the passage to a noncommutative algebra is the passage to a geometry carried by the algebra rather than by an underlying point-set, with locality acquiring a Fourier-conjugate meaning that matches the framework's own uncertainty structure. Neither contains an expanding dimension, a rate, or a dynamical process; they are static frameworks, and they are not cousins of the McGucken mechanism. What they establish is that the inversion the mechanism enacts — extended structure primitive, locality derived — is a rigorous and well-developed position in mathematics, so that the framework's treatment of locality as derived stands in a recognized tradition even though its dynamical, physical realization of that inversion is its own.

The uniform result: every program surveyed shares at most the inversion that locality is not fundamental; none contains a dynamical fourth dimension whose expansion distributes locality into nonlocality. The physics programs supply correspondences, pictures, and reformulations; the mathematical programs supply static frameworks in which the point is derived; Maudlin supplies a static, local geometry that derives space from time and excludes the long-range. The expanding-dimension mechanism — nonlocality carried by the fourth dimension's active advance, with the spatial correlation as its three-dimensional shadow, cloaked by the Born statistics of Proposition VIII.2 so that no signal is carried — is, on the present survey of the literature, the McGucken framework's own.

### VIII.6 Einstein's Bubble and the EPR handshake: the two phenomena that founded the Transactional Interpretation, resolved without an advanced wave

The Transactional Interpretation began, by Cramer's own account [Cramer2016, Ch. 1], in two moments. The first was a mid-lecture insight while teaching the Einstein's Bubble paradox: the quantum wavefunction spreading from an emitter as an inflating spherical bubble must somehow "know" to vanish everywhere at the instant the particle is detected at one location. Cramer's resolution was that the advanced and retarded waves present throughout the quantum formalism could perform Wheeler–Feynman handshakes, so that only those retarded offer waves that received advanced-wave echoes would transfer a particle. The second moment, a month later, applied the same handshake picture to the Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen experiments then testing Bell's inequalities: the "V" diagram in which offer waves travel from a source to two detectors and confirmation waves travel back, forming a three-vertex transaction only when the detections are compatible with conservation at the source. Both phenomena — the collapsing bubble and the EPR correlation — were, for Cramer, explained by advanced waves returning from the future. The McGucken framework resolves both by the expansion of x₄, with no advanced wave.

**Einstein's Bubble.** The paradox assumes a spherical wavefunction spreading through 3-space that must instantaneously vanish from all locations except the detection point when the particle is found. On the McGucken reading the spreading object is the McGucken Sphere, the wavefront of x₄'s spherically symmetric expansion at rate c from the emission event A. Every point on that wavefront is x₄-coincident with A: the expansion carries the emission event's locality across the whole expanding surface (§XII.4, the expanding surface of nonlocality). The bubble does not need to send a signal to its own distant parts telling them to vanish, because the distant parts are not causally separate regions that must be updated — they are one geometric object, the single wavefront, every point of which shares the origin's locality through x₄-coincidence. Detection is the first-contact collision of that wavefront with an absorber's wavefront (§XI.5-bis), a single pointlike event at which the x₄-momentum cancels and localizes the particle. The rest of the wavefront does not "pop" by a propagating instruction; the single four-dimensional object is registered at one first-contact point, and the 3D appearance of a bubble vanishing everywhere at once is the cross-section reading (Proposition V.1) of that one four-dimensional registration. Where Cramer needs an advanced confirmation wave returning from the detector to the source to enforce that only one detection occurs, the McGucken framework needs only that the wavefront is one x₄-coincident object and that its registration is a single first-contact event — both forward, neither retrocausal.

**The EPR handshake and the Bell experiments.** Cramer's "V" diagram requires offer waves outbound to two detectors and advanced confirmation waves inbound from them, forming a transaction only when the two detections conserve angular momentum at the source. The McGucken account of the same Freedman–Clauser and Aspect correlations is Proposition VIII.1: the two entangled particles are created at a common event E and share six-sense null-surface identity with respect to E, preserved along null-geodesic propagation, so that their measured correlation is the geometric expression of a shared identity generated at the local origin and carried outward — not a signal exchanged between the detectors at measurement time, and not a handshake reaching back from the future. This is the content of the First Law of Nonlocality [MG-Nonloc]: all nonlocality begins in locality, meaning the nonlocal correlation is *generated from* a local origin by the outbound expansion of x₄. The direction is outbound: x₄'s advance at rate c from E carries the local creation event outward into an extended surface every point of which remains x₄-coincident with E, so the correlation is produced as the wavefront expands, and the "separated" particles are, in x₄, still at their common origin. The nonlocality is not a pre-existing link later traced back to a shared source; it is created, outward, by the expansion — locality becoming nonlocality through the advance of x₄. The Bell-violating correlation therefore exists precisely because the pair had a shared local origin from which the expansion carried the identity outward, and no correlation is predicted between particles with no common causal past, because there is no shared origin for the expansion to carry outward. The spatial separation measured in the laboratory is the 3D cross-section of a state that is undivided in x₄. The Tsirelson bound 2√2 is the maximum SO(3)-Haar-weighted correlation on the spherically symmetric expansion ([MG-QM, Theorem 13]), and the no-signaling that accompanies the correlation is the probability-cloaking of Proposition VIII.2 — the same SO(3) symmetry that produces the correlation produces the marginal flatness, so the channel is real and geometric yet carries no message. The entire Bell phenomenology that Cramer accounts for with the advanced-wave V-diagram is here accounted for by one forward, outbound expansion: the correlation generated from shared origin as x₄ advances, its magnitude from the SO(3) measure, its non-signaling from the same measure's marginal flatness.

**Why the expansion does the work the advanced wave was introduced to do.** Cramer's advanced wave exists to supply two things: the enforcement that a spreading wavefunction produces exactly one detection (the bubble), and the correlation between spatially separated entangled detections (EPR). In the McGucken framework both are supplied by the single fact that x₄'s expansion makes the wavefront one x₄-coincident object rather than a collection of causally separate spatial regions. For the bubble, one object registered at one first-contact event needs no instruction propagated to its distant parts. For EPR, one object undivided in x₄ needs no signal exchanged between its distant cross-sections. The advanced wave was Cramer's device for restoring, across a pre-given spacetime, the connectivity that the expansion of x₄ supplies intrinsically. The connectivity is real — this is genuine nonlocality, saturating Tsirelson and confirmed from Freedman–Clauser through the loophole-free experiments — but it is the connectivity of a single expanding four-dimensional object, carried forward by dx₄/dt = ic, rather than a handshake reaching backward from future absorbers. The founding intuition of the Transactional Interpretation — that quantum mechanics contains a real nonlocal connective structure and that the wavefunction is a physical spreading object — is correct and is preserved here; what the McGucken framework removes is the backward-in-time wave Cramer introduced to implement it, replacing it with the forward expansion of the fourth dimension.

### VIII.7 The six nonlocality questions Cramer poses, answered from dx₄/dt = ic

Cramer sets out six questions about nonlocality that he holds Copenhagen cannot answer, and states that the Transactional Interpretation is the only interpretation that answers all six [Cramer2016, §3.4 and Appendix A.2]. Each is answered here from the McGucken Principle, with the answer drawing on the propositions established above rather than on an advanced wave.

*Can the quantum wavefunctions of entangled systems be objects that exist in normal three-dimensional space?* The four-dimensional object is the McGucken Sphere — the wavefront of x₄'s expansion — and it does not live in 3-space; it lives in the four dimensions x₁x₂x₃x₄. What exists in normal 3-space is its cross-section: the wavefunction ψ(x,t) is the 3D spatial slice of the x₄-extended wavefront (Proposition V.1). For a composite system the joint wavefront is the product of the constituent constraint surfaces, so the N-particle wavefunction is the cross-section of an object living in the product of N four-dimensional arenas — which is why the entangled wavefunction appears to require a high-dimensional configuration space rather than 3-space. The answer is therefore precise: the entangled wavefunction is not an object in 3-space, and it need not be, because it is the 3D cross-section reading of a wavefront whose home is the four-dimensional expansion. The apparent puzzle — that ψ seems to demand a space larger than the 3-space we inhabit — is resolved by identifying the larger space as the x₄-extended manifold and the 3-space object as its slice.

*What are the true roles of the observers and measurements in quantum processes involving several separated measurements on entangled subsystems?* The observer has no special role and the measurement no special status (a commitment shared with TI). A measurement is a physical first-contact collision between the system's wavefront and an absorber's wavefront (§XI.5-bis), a Geometric Channel physical event with definite spacetime coordinates that occurs whether or not anyone observes it. For several separated measurements on an entangled system, each measurement is a local collision event on the shared wavefront, and their outcomes correlate because the wavefront is one x₄-coincident object generated at the common source (Proposition VIII.1). The observer enters only as a system whose records become correlated with one collision outcome; the ordering of the separated measurements is immaterial, because the correlation is carried by the shared x₄-coincidence of the common origin, not by a signal exchanged at measurement time. This is the content of Wigner's-friend consistency (§V.6): different observers reading different spatial slices of the one wavefront report mutually consistent outcomes, guaranteed by x₄-coincidence.

*What is wavefunction collapse, and how does it occur, particularly for entangled systems?* There is no separate collapse law (Proposition IX.1). What is called collapse is the 3D cross-section reading of the x₄-extended state (Proposition V.1): when a first-contact collision localizes the system at one event (§XI.5-bis), the observer's spatial slice thereafter intersects the branch consistent with that localization, and the wavefunction description updates accordingly — a change in which cross-section is being read, not a physical process propagating through space. For entangled systems the update is the same reading applied to the shared wavefront: a collision localizing one subsystem fixes the cross-section for the whole x₄-coincident object, so the partner's description updates without any influence traveling between them, because they were never separate objects in x₄. The "collapse" of the distant partner is the cross-section update of one undivided wavefront, not a signal.

*How can quantum nonlocality be understood?* As the outbound expansion of x₄ generating nonlocality from locality (First Law of Nonlocality; Theorem XII.A.4). An entangled pair is created at a local event E; x₄'s advance at rate c carries that local event outward into an extended wavefront every point of which remains x₄-coincident with E. The pair's correlation is understood as the persistence of that shared origin across the expanding wavefront: the systems are spatially separated in the 3D cross-section while undivided in x₄. Nonlocality is thus not action at a distance but the shared locality of a common origin carried outward by the expansion — locality becoming nonlocality through the advance of x₄.

*How can quantum nonlocality be visualized?* Directly, as an expanding sphere. The McGucken Sphere is a spherical wavefront expanding at c from the source event; every point on its surface shares the accumulated x₄-advance X₄ of the source, because X₄ = ∫ic dτ does not grow along the null rays from the source (sphere-surface x₄-locality, Theorem XII.A.2; Appendix A (R4)). The visualization is the growing sphere whose whole surface carries the one accumulated x₄-advance of the event where it began — so two detectors sitting on that surface, however far apart in 3-space, are reached at the same accumulated x₄-advance. This is the visualization Cramer sought and found in the transactional handshake diagram, supplied here by a single forward-expanding sphere rather than a pair of advanced-and-retarded waves: one growing surface, every point of it x₄-coincident with the origin.

*What are the underlying physical processes that make quantum nonlocality possible?* One process: dx₄/dt = ic, the outbound expansion of the fourth dimension at rate c from every event. This is the physical mechanism — not a correspondence, not a picture, not an advanced wave. The expansion generates the McGucken Sphere; the sphere's surface is x₄-coincident with the origin; the coincidence is the physical basis of the correlation; the SO(3) symmetry of the expansion fixes its magnitude at the Tsirelson bound (Proposition VIII.1) and cloaks it with the Born-form marginal so no signal is carried (Proposition VIII.2). The underlying physical process is the advance of x₄ itself, and every feature of the Bell phenomenology — the correlation, its Tsirelson magnitude, its no-signaling, its restriction to pairs with a common origin — is a consequence of that one outbound expansion.

Cramer holds that TI is the only interpretation answering all six. The McGucken framework answers all six as well, from a single principle, and with two differences of kind: the answers derive the formalism they use rather than interpreting a given formalism (§XI.3.9), and the physical process invoked is the forward, outbound expansion of x₄ rather than a wave propagating backward in time from future absorbers. The nonlocal connective structure Cramer correctly identified is retained; the mechanism supplied for it is the expansion of the fourth dimension.

### VIII.8 Nonlocality and probability as physical realities contained in the premise

The nonlocality of quantum mechanics, and the probability that is observed through it, are not anomalies to be explained away; they are physical realities already contained in the statement of the McGucken Principle. The premise itself carries them: the fourth dimension expands as a *spherically symmetric* wavefront at rate $c$, with a foundational wavelength proportional to the Planck action $h$. For a dimension to expand in a spherically symmetric manner is for it to be nonlocal — one expansion event is co-present across the whole sphere it generates. Nonlocality is therefore stated in the premise, in the word *spherically*; it is not added downstream. Probability then arises from this nonlocality: what is observed in measurement, and especially across the many observations that reveal a statistical distribution, is the imprint of the nonlocal surface, distributed by the isotropy of the expansion (§V.5-bis). Nonlocality is the physical fact; probability is how the nonlocal surface presents itself to repeated measurement.

That a dimension can move, stretch, and behave differently in one region than another is not a novelty of this framework. General relativity established it: near a mass, the dimensions bend, curve, stretch, and their rate of advance differs from the rate far from the mass. The active, position-dependent behaviour of the spatial and temporal dimensions is a century-old part of accepted physics. The McGucken Principle extends the same recognition to the fourth dimension's expansive motion: that $x_4$ expands, spherically and at $c$, is of a piece with general relativity's teaching that dimensions are dynamical. The expansive, nonlocal motion of $x_4$ should occasion no more surprise than the curving and stretching of space near a mass.

The recognition that the photon expands as a spherically symmetric wavefront while not ageing already commits us to its preserving a form of locality in spacetime — the photon carries its emission event's locality across the expanding surface (Theorem XII.A.2). This connects to a limit long recognised in relativity. As an object approaches the velocity of light — $0.999999999\,c$ — the intervals of space and time it traverses in its own reckoning contract toward zero, so that in that limit two distant events are brought closer and closer together; the fast object augments a form of nonlocality, its own clock and ruler contracting as $v \to c$. The germ of this recognition is Einstein's earliest thought experiment, recalled in his *Autobiographical Notes*: "a paradox upon which I had already hit at the age of sixteen: If I pursue a beam of light with the velocity $c$ ... I should observe such a beam of light as an electromagnetic field at rest though spatially oscillating. There seems to be no such thing, however, neither on the basis of experience nor according to Maxwell's equations" [Einstein1949, pp. 52--53]. The teenage Einstein was right to ask what it would be like to catch a light beam; the question was the seed of special relativity.

The recognition that the photon is a physical tracer of the fourth dimension follows from two facts already accepted, joined into one deduction. First, an emitted photon propagates through the three spatial dimensions as a spherically symmetric probability wavefront expanding at $c$ — the content of the double-slit experiment and of the elementary description of single-photon emission. As P. J. E. Peebles put the latter to the author at Princeton, a photon has an equal chance of being detected anywhere on the surface of a sphere expanding at $c$ (the setup made quantitative in §V.5-bis) [Peebles1992; McGucken2008]. Second, relativity dictates that the photon, ageless and timeless, is at rest in the fourth dimension (v_{x_4} = 0; §II, Appendix on the four $x_4$-rate quantities), as J. A. Wheeler emphasised to the author. Joining the two: if the photon's observed behaviour is that of a spherically symmetric wavefront expanding at $c$ through the three spatial dimensions, and the photon is at rest in $x_4$, then the expanding spherical wavefront that is observed is the wavefront of $x_4$ itself — the photon rides it without advancing in it, and so traces its motion. The double-slit experiment is therefore not only a display of the photon's wave nature; it is a display of the motion of the fourth dimension, read through the one object that is stationary with respect to it. This deduction, developed by the author from the Princeton exchanges with Wheeler and Peebles and first recorded in [McGucken2008], is the physical route by which $dx_4/dt = ic$ was recognised: it begins in experience — the double-slit result and the photon's agelessness — and ends in the physical statement that $x_4$ expands at $c$. J. Taylor, advising the author's junior work on entanglement, framed the target that the same expansion answers: the source of entanglement is the source of the quantum, since, as Schrödinger held, entanglement is the characteristic trait of quantum mechanics [McGucken1990]. The expansion of $x_4$ supplies both — entanglement as the shared $x_4$-origin carried outward (Proposition VIII.1), the quantum of action as the geometry the expansion carves (§III.1-bis).

The physicist has the right to ask this question, and its analogue for the fourth dimension. The photon, the velocity of light, and the fourth dimension are as physically real as the electron and the three spatial dimensions. It is therefore a legitimate physical question — not a forbidden one — to ask "what is the photon doing relative to the fourth dimension?" exactly as one asks "what is the photon doing relative to the three spatial dimensions?" and "what is the photon doing relative to spacetime?" The answer is definite and, importantly, well-posed where the naive question is not. Special relativity correctly holds that a photon has no inertial rest frame: the Lorentz boost is singular at $v = c$ and proper time is undefined along a null worldline, so "the photon's proper-time frame" does not exist. But the framework's question concerns the photon's *share* of the $x_4$-advance --- a quantity distinct from the proper-time frame and well-defined at $v = c$ by direct substitution: $v_{x_4} = \sqrt{c^2 - v^2} = 0$ (the four-velocity budget of §II; Appendix on the four $x_4$-rate quantities). The photon is at rest in $x_4$ — not in the forbidden sense of a comoving inertial frame, but in the defined sense that its share of the expansion vanishes. The framework can answer the question relativity had to leave undefined, precisely because $v_{x_4} = 0$ is defined on the null boundary where the proper-time frame is not.

Once the photon's $x_4$-rest is recognised, the apparent paradoxes resolve together. The twin "paradox" is the difference in accumulated $x_4$-advance along worldlines of different $v_{x_4}$ (Appendix, worked example); the isotropy of the microwave background and the existence of a cosmic-comoving frame are the foliation to which the $x_4$-share is referred, cloaked from local metrology (Proposition VIII.2, the Cloaking Theorem); and on the quantum side, nonlocality, entanglement, the double slit, and probability are the manifestations of the spherically symmetric $x_4$-expansion catalogued in §V.5-bis and §VIII. Quantum mechanics, general relativity, and thermodynamics descend as theorem chains from the one principle: the Born rule and nonlocality from the isotropic expansion (§III, §VIII), the Lorentzian metric and its dynamics from $x_4 = ict$ and its curvature response [MG-QM, MG-Minkowski], the arrow of time and the second law from the strict $+ic$ monotonicity of the advance (Proposition VI.1; [MG-Entropy]). The physicist's right to ask what the photon does relative to $x_4$ — the question relativity's pedantic inheritors declared out of bounds — is the doorway through which the paradoxes evaporate and the three frameworks are seen to share one foundational source.

### VIII.9 The first task of a physical theory: a source for nonlocality and entanglement

That physical theory would have to incorporate nonlocality and probability has been apparent since the beginning of quantum mechanics, and the recognition sharpened at a series of definite milestones. In 1935 Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen introduced the nonlocal correlations of entangled systems as a theoretical paradox, intending to show that quantum mechanics was incomplete [EPR1935]. In 1964 Bell converted the question into mathematics, proving that no local hidden-variable theory can reproduce the quantum predictions [Bell1964]. In 1972 Freedman and Clauser performed the first experimental Bell test, showing entanglement and nonlocality to be real physical phenomena [Freedman1972]. In 1982 Aspect, Grangier, and Roger closed the locality loophole by switching the measurement settings while the photons were in flight [Aspect1982]. Between 2015 and 2017 the loophole-free experiments ruled out any local-realistic alternative simultaneously on the detection and locality loopholes [Hensen2015; Giustina2015; Shalm2015]. In 2022 the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Clauser, Aspect, and Zeilinger for this collective demonstration [NobelPrize2022]. What EPR posed as a paradox intended to refute quantum mechanics became, over eighty-seven years, the confirmed and honoured physical fact the theory must now supply a source for.

Nonlocality and entanglement are established empirical facts, confirmed across a century of experiment and honoured by the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics, awarded to Alain Aspect, John F. Clauser, and Anton Zeilinger "for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell inequalities and pioneering quantum information science" [NobelPrize2022]. The experimental record is continuous and unambiguous. The single-photon and low-intensity interference experiments established that a probabilistic wavefront passes through both slits at once: Taylor's 1909 feeble-light interference [Taylor1909], and the single-electron buildup of the interference pattern by Tonomura and collaborators [Tonomura1989]. The Bell-inequality tests established entanglement and the failure of local hidden variables: Freedman and Clauser's first experimental violation in 1972 [Freedman1972], Aspect, Grangier, and Roger's time-varying-analyzer experiment in 1982 [Aspect1982], and the three independent loophole-free tests of 2015 — Hensen and collaborators with electron spins separated by 1.3 km [Hensen2015], Giustina and collaborators with entangled photons [Giustina2015], and Shalm and collaborators [Shalm2015] — closing the detection and locality loopholes simultaneously. Nonlocality has been a physical fact since the double-slit experiment; entanglement has been a physical fact since Freedman–Clauser; and the Nobel Prize records the settled status of both.

If nonlocality and entanglement are physical facts, then the first task of any physical theory is to supply a physical source for them, alongside its account of general relativity, quantum mechanics, thermodynamics, and the symmetries and conservation laws. A framework that takes nonlocality as a brute feature of the formalism, or as an interpretive posture, has not discharged this task; it has deferred it. The McGucken framework discharges it directly: nonlocality is the spherically symmetric expansion of $x_4$ carrying a local event outward into an extended $x_4$-coincident surface (§VIII.8, §V.5-bis), entanglement is the persistence of a shared origin across that outbound surface (Proposition VIII.1), and the probability observed in the double slit and the Bell tests is the isotropic $SO(3)$-Haar measure of the one nonlocal surface (Proposition III.1). The same principle supplies the source for the general-relativistic metric, the quantum formalism, the arrow of time, and the conservation laws (Noether on the $x_4$-symmetries), so that nonlocality and entanglement are derived alongside everything else from $dx_4/dt = ic$, rather than left as unexplained residue.

This is the standard the founders of the discipline set, and it should not be abandoned. Three statements fix it:

> The grand aim of all science is to cover the greatest number of empirical facts by logical deduction from the smallest possible number of hypotheses or axioms. — Albert Einstein

> Behind it all is surely an idea so simple, so beautiful, so compelling that when --- in a decade, a century, or a millennium --- we grasp it, we will all say to each other, "Oh, how could it have been otherwise!" — John Archibald Wheeler

> We are to admit no more causes of natural things than such as are both true and sufficient to explain their appearances. To this purpose the philosophers say that Nature does nothing in vain, and more is in vain when less will serve; for Nature is pleased with simplicity, and affects not the pomp of superfluous causes. — Isaac Newton, *Principia*, Rule I [Newton1687]

Newton's second statement of the same criterion — "Truth is ever to be found in simplicity, and not in the multiplicity and confusion of things" — states the measure by which the present account asks to be judged: not whether it interprets the formalism agreeably, but whether it covers the greatest number of empirical facts, nonlocality and entanglement among them, by deduction from the fewest hypotheses. The McGucken framework offers one: $dx_4/dt = ic$. Nonlocality, entanglement, the Born rule, the double-slit interference, the Bell violations, the Lorentzian metric, the arrow of time, and the conservation laws are its consequences, and the empirical facts the Nobel Prize honours are, on this account, deductions from the single principle rather than brute features admitted without a source.

### VIII.10 Philosophy of physics begins and ends in experiment

Philosophy of physics, like physics, begins and ends in experiment. The foundations-of-physics tradition sets its own mandate as the identification of the ontology behind the formalism — what the world must be like for the formalism to be true (Maudlin, Albert, Myrvold, Wallace, Saunders, and the post-Bell literature). The McGucken framework meets that mandate directly and by the tradition's own standard of evidence. The argument is an inference to the best explanation operating at the foundational level. The orthodox formal-coordinate reading of $x_4 = ict$ and the physical-expansion reading $dx_4/dt = ic$ agree with experiment equally at the level of relativity's predictions; they part on productivity. The formal-coordinate reading produces no foundational quantum-mechanical content. The physical-expansion reading produces the Hilbert space, the Born rule, the canonical commutator, the uncertainty principle, and the Schrödinger equation as theorems (§III, §XIII, and the companion derivations of [MG-Minkowski-Hilbert]). The question at the foundational level is not which ontology agrees with experiment — both do for relativity — but which ontology also explains why the world carries the additional structure of quantum mechanics. The physical-expansion ontology explains it; the formal-coordinate ontology does not. The world has to be such that the fourth dimension is expanding at $c$ from every event, because that ontology forces the quantum formalism as theorem.

The measure that separates physics from its speculative shadow is testability, the demarcation criterion of the empirical tradition from Galileo through Popper. A framework earns its standing by exposing itself to falsification; a program that yields no observable it could fail forfeits that standing, and forfeits more of it the longer it stays unfalsifiable. By this measure the McGucken framework stands on the empirical side: it makes falsifiable predictions, several of them sharp. The identification of $\hbar$ as the Lorentz-invariant substrate-tick action of the expansion predicts that no inertial frame will register a deviation of $\hbar$ from Lorentz-invariance — a prediction held to the seventh through twelfth significant digit across seventy years of precision quantum electrodynamics (electron $g-2$, the Lamb shift, atomic-clock stability across gravitationally boosted platforms), any deviation falsifying the identification ([MG-Minkowski-Hilbert, Remark 2.2.bis.1]). The First Law of Nonlocality predicts that two systems that have never shared a local origin nor interacted through a chain of local contacts cannot be entangled — the operationally testable "New York–Los Angeles" prediction [MG-Nonloc]. The Weak Equivalence Principle, confirmed to one part in $10^{15}$ by MICROSCOPE, becomes a test of $dx_4/dt = ic$ rather than an independent input. These are observables the framework could fail.

Against this stand the programs that produce internally consistent mathematics while yielding, by construction, no observable that could distinguish them from the alternatives: the Everett multiverse, whose branches are inaccessible in principle; the string landscape, with its many free parameters and no derived low-energy prediction; and the reconciliation programs whose status as the "central open problem" has persisted for ninety years without a decided observable. A program of this kind stands unrefuted, yet its claim on the title of physics weakens as the years of unfalsifiability accumulate, and the criterion that measures the weakening is the same one Galileo established: theory answers to experiment, or it is not yet physics. Einstein stated the standard exactly:

> All knowledge of reality starts from experience and ends in it. Propositions arrived at by purely logical means are completely empty as regards reality. Because Galileo saw this, and particularly because he drummed it into the scientific world, he is the father of modern physics --- indeed, of modern science altogether. — A. Einstein, "On the Method of Theoretical Physics" (1934) [Einstein1934]

The highest philosophy of physics is therefore proper physics: a physical ontology that forces the formalism and exposes itself to experiment. The McGucken framework asks to be judged by that standard and by the simplicity criterion the founders set — the greatest coverage of empirical facts by deduction from the fewest hypotheses (Einstein), the single simple idea behind it all (Wheeler), and Nature's economy of causes (Newton, *Principia*, Rule I) — and it offers, for that judgment, one principle: $dx_4/dt = ic$.

### VIII.11 Causal set theory: its motivations resolved, and the McGucken derivation of Lorentz invariance together with nonlocality (transcribed in full from [MG-Gravity-Born, §5.8], in the author's language; internal section-references are to that paper's numbering)

**Table 5.8a. The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic versus causal set theory (Sorkin–Dowker lineage).**
