## XI. The Joint Derivation of Superposition and Collapse: The Structural Punchline

The development of the present paper has now reached a point where the structural significance of the McGucken framework can be stated in its sharpest form. This section makes the structural punchline explicit, develops it in detail, and supports it with the rigorous joint analysis that the foundational status of the claim requires.

### XI.1 The structural punchline

The standard Dirac–von Neumann axiomatization of quantum mechanics rests on six independent postulates Q1–Q6. Of these six, two are foundational in a deeper sense than the others, in that the remaining four either presuppose them or follow naturally from them once they are in place:

**(Q1) Linear superposition (the Hilbert-space postulate).** The state space of a quantum system is a complex separable Hilbert space ℋ, and physically realizable states are unit vectors in ℋ defined up to overall phase. The linearity of ℋ — the fact that for any |ψ⟩, |φ⟩ ∈ ℋ and α, β ∈ ℂ with |α|² + |β|² = 1 the linear combination α|ψ⟩ + β|φ⟩ is also a physically realizable state — is the foundational structural feature that distinguishes quantum mechanics from classical mechanics. Without (Q1), there is no superposition, no interference, and no quantum theory; there is only classical statistical mechanics.

**(Q3) The Born rule.** The probability of measurement outcome a given the wavefunction ψ is |⟨a|ψ⟩|². The squared-amplitude form of (Q3) is what converts the Hilbert-space amplitudes of (Q1) into empirical probabilities. Without (Q3), the Hilbert-space formalism is mathematically well-defined but empirically empty; quantum mechanics has no testable predictions.

These two postulates — (Q1) and (Q3) — are the structural core of quantum mechanics. The other four postulates (Q2 self-adjoint operators, Q4 Schrödinger evolution, Q5 canonical commutation, Q6 tensor product structure) are derivable from (Q1) and (Q3) together with standard structural commitments shared with all reasonable physical theories: real-valuedness of observables forces (Q2), Stone's theorem applied to spacetime translations forces (Q5), Lorentz-covariance plus the rest-mass-phase factor forces (Q4), and the linearity of Hilbert space combined with subsystem decomposition forces (Q6). The structural foundation of quantum mechanics is therefore really *two* postulates: linearity (Q1) and the Born rule (Q3).

**The structural punchline of the McGucken framework.** Both of these foundational postulates are derived as theorems of one geometric principle. (Q1) is forced by Proposition IV.1 (superposition as geometric overlap of McGucken-Sphere wavefronts); (Q3) is forced by Proposition III.1 (Born rule as squared-amplitude geometry of x₄-wavefront cross-sections). The remaining apparent (R) postulate — wave function collapse — is reduced to a theorem of the same principle by Proposition V.1 (apparent collapse as 3D cross-section reading) and Proposition VI.1 (irreversibility from x₄-monotonicity). The McGucken framework therefore moves the foundational base of quantum mechanics from the postulate column toward the theorem column: linearity, the Born rule, and the apparent collapse are presented as consequences of dx₄/dt = ic. The Born-rule derivation is closed by Lemma 7.1 and Theorem 7.2 of [MG-BornCentury], with five routes to the exponent 2 (§III.4.5); the superposition derivation is Grade-2, resting on the empirically anchored conditions D3 and D4 of Proposition IV.1 (§IV.2), so the reduction is conditional on that one bridge.

This is a structural reduction without parallel in the foundations of quantum mechanics. No prior framework — Copenhagen, Many-Worlds, Bohmian mechanics, GRW, decoherence-plus-environmental-selection, RQM, QBism, or any combination — derives both (Q1) and (Q3) from a single underlying principle. Each prior framework either takes both as postulates, takes one as primitive and derives the other from auxiliary assumptions, or modifies the dynamics to incorporate one and leaves the other primitive. Among the surveyed frameworks, the McGucken framework is the exception: it derives both from one geometric postulate (the superposition derivation Grade-2, §IV.2).

### XI.2 Why this is structurally novel

Three sub-claims must be established to ground the structural punchline.

**(SP-I)** The linearity of the Hilbert-space postulate (Q1) is not foundational in the McGucken framework; it is a derived structural feature.

**(SP-II)** The Born rule (Q3) is not foundational in the McGucken framework; it is a derived structural feature.

**(SP-III)** The joint derivation of (Q1) and (Q3) from a single principle is unique to the McGucken framework among all known quantum interpretations.

**(SP-I)** is established by Proposition IV.1: the superposition principle is forced by the geometric overlap of McGucken-Sphere wavefronts in four-dimensional spacetime, with three structural pieces — multiple wavefronts can coexist (because x₄'s uniform advance does not select between sources), linear addition with complex coefficients is the unique combination operation (because of the four conditions D1–D4), and the perpendicularity marker i encodes relative phase (because x₄ = ict). The Hilbert-space linearity of (Q1) is the algebraic consequence of these three geometric facts, not the source of them.

**(SP-II)** is established by Proposition III.1: the Born rule is forced by the squared-amplitude geometry of the McGucken-Sphere cross-section, with three structural pieces — complex character of ψ from i as perpendicularity marker (Piece 1), quadratic exponent forced by the four conditions C1–C4 on probability density (Piece 2), and SO(3) Haar-measure shape forced by spherical symmetry of x₄'s expansion (Piece 3). The Born rule is the unique probability density consistent with these three structural facts.

**(SP-III)** is the comparative claim and is the substantive content of the present section. It is established by surveying all known quantum interpretations and showing that none of them simultaneously derives both (Q1) and (Q3) from a single underlying principle. The next two subsections develop this comparison in detail.

### XI.3 Why prior frameworks cannot derive both (Q1) and (Q3) from one principle

The seven major interpretive programmes are surveyed under the joint criterion: does the framework derive *both* (Q1) and (Q3) from a single underlying principle? The answer is uniformly negative for all seven prior frameworks. We develop the analysis programme by programme.

**XI.3.1 Copenhagen.** Copenhagen takes both (Q1) and (Q3) as postulates. The Hilbert-space structure is accepted as given; the Born rule is accepted as the operational rule for measurement probabilities. The framework explicitly declines to provide a foundational source for either postulate, treating them as primitive elements of the formalism. There is no claim of derivation from a deeper principle, single or otherwise. **Result: derives neither (Q1) nor (Q3) from any underlying principle.**

**XI.3.2 Many-Worlds.** Many-Worlds takes (Q1) as foundational — the universal wavefunction evolves unitarily on a Hilbert space, and all branches are equally real. The framework attempts to derive (Q3) from auxiliary frameworks: decision theory (Deutsch1999; Wallace2012) requires rationality axioms (independence, transitivity, dominance) plus the Many-Worlds ontology; envariance (Zurek2005) requires symmetry properties of system-environment entangled states with a specific coupling structure. Critics [Albert2010; Kent2010; Saunders2010] have argued at length that the rationality axioms and envariance assumptions themselves require justification not present in the framework, and that the derivations of (Q3) are circular or incomplete. Even granting the most charitable reading of these derivations, (Q1) remains foundational and (Q3) is derived only from auxiliary postulates (rationality axioms, envariance, etc.) that are not themselves derived from a deeper physical principle. **Result: takes (Q1) as foundational; derives (Q3) only from auxiliary postulates that are themselves foundational.**

**XI.3.3 Bohmian mechanics.** Bohmian mechanics takes (Q1) as foundational — the guidance wave ψ evolves unitarily on a Hilbert space — and adds hidden variables (definite particle positions) plus the guidance equation. (Q3) is derived from the equilibrium hypothesis: particles are initially distributed according to |ψ|². Valentini [Valentini1991, Valentini2001] showed that quantum non-equilibrium distributions are stable under Bohmian dynamics, so the equilibrium hypothesis is an *additional* postulate not derivable from the Bohmian dynamics alone. The framework therefore takes (Q1) as foundational and derives (Q3) only by adding the equilibrium hypothesis as a separate postulate. **Result: takes (Q1) as foundational; derives (Q3) only by adding the equilibrium hypothesis as a separate postulate.**

**XI.3.4 GRW spontaneous localization.** GRW modifies (U) by adding stochastic terms with phenomenological parameters λ (rate) and a (localization width). The modified dynamics produces an effective Born rule in the long-time limit, but the modification itself is the additional postulate, and the parameters are phenomenological (set to match observed quantum-classical behavior). (Q1) remains foundational at the level of the unmodified Schrödinger equation; (Q3) is derived from the modified dynamics, but only by adding parameters that are not themselves derived. **Result: takes (Q1) as foundational; derives (Q3) only by adding stochastic dynamics with phenomenological parameters.**

**XI.3.5 Decoherence-plus-environmental-selection.** The Zurek/Joos/Zeh decoherence programme takes both (Q1) and (Q3) as foundational and supplements them with an account of how environmental coupling produces apparent classicality. The framework correctly explains why off-diagonal terms in ρ\_S decay rapidly, but does not derive (Q1) or (Q3) from any deeper source. The diagonal weights |c\_i|² are taken as primitive; the linearity of Hilbert space is taken as primitive. **Result: takes both (Q1) and (Q3) as foundational, supplemented with environmental coupling but not derived from a deeper principle.**

**XI.3.6 Relational Quantum Mechanics.** RQM relativizes both (Q1) and (Q3) to observers — different observer-systems may assign different states (and different probabilities) to the same physical situation. The framework takes the Born rule and the Hilbert-space structure as relational primitives, accepting that there is no observer-independent answer to the question "what state is the system in?" The framework is a coherent philosophical position but does not derive (Q1) or (Q3) from a deeper physical principle. **Result: takes both (Q1) and (Q3) as relational primitives; no derivation from underlying principle.**

**XI.3.7 QBism.** QBism takes (Q1) as a feature of the agent's choice of representation (the Hilbert space is a tool for organizing the agent's beliefs about measurement outcomes) and (Q3) as a normative coherence requirement on the agent's beliefs (justified by Dutch-book arguments). The framework explicitly declines to derive either postulate from a deeper physical principle, treating them as primitive coherence requirements on agent reasoning. **Result: takes both (Q1) and (Q3) as agent-relative primitives; no derivation from underlying principle.**

**XI.3.8 Barandes: the indivisible stochastic-quantum correspondence.** Jacob Barandes's stochastic-quantum correspondence [Barandes2023; Barandes2025] is the most recent entry in the configuration-space stochastic tradition (Nelson 1966; Yasue 1981; Guerra–Morato 1983), and it warrants separate treatment because Barandes is a philosopher of physics whose diagnostic of the orthodox formalism coincides at several points with the present paper's. Barandes resolves the Wallstrom obstruction [Wallstrom1989] — that Nelson's Markovian stochastic mechanics cannot reproduce the multivalued Madelung phase — by generalizing from Markovian to *indivisible* (non-Markovian) stochastic processes whose transition matrices admit a unistochastic decomposition. The Schrödinger equation is recovered as the Hilbert-space representation of an indivisible process on configuration space, with the wavefunction demoted from a primary ontological ingredient to a derived mathematical tool. His five objections to the Dirac–von Neumann formalism — observers in the base axioms, the abstract Hilbert space disconnected from physical space, the unclear ontological status of the wavefunction, the collapse postulate as a separate primitive, and Markovianity as an unjustified assumption — constitute the sharpest recent critique of the orthodox axiomatization, and each names a problem the present framework also identifies.

Barandes takes neither (Q1) nor (Q3) as a primitive Hilbert-space postulate; both are reconstructed from the indivisible process. This appears to place his program alongside the McGucken framework as a joint reconstruction of both from a deeper base. The comparison requires the reverse-engineering question, which is the same one Barandes presses against Everett via Norton's principle — that the conclusion of a derivation cannot be stronger than its premises. Applied to the stochastic-quantum program: a generic stochastic process yields classical probability — Markov chains, diffusion, ordinary noise — and reproduces neither interference, nor complex phase, nor the non-commutative operator structure, nor the Born rule with its cross terms. To recover those, the process must be exactly the indivisible, unistochastically-decomposable kind that reconstructs a Hilbert space. If the sole motivation for indivisibility is that it lands on quantum mechanics, then Hilbert-space quantum mechanics is the target being fitted, and the quantum content resides in the reconstructed Hilbert-space structure rather than in the stochastic process; the process is a relabelling of the answer rather than a derivation of it. The devastating question for the program is therefore not "where is the Hilbert space" — Barandes reconstructs it and would rightly deny lacking it — but "what independently motivates indivisibility, other than that it reproduces the Hilbert space the program set out to eliminate."

The McGucken framework is not exposed to this objection at the same point, for a reason internal to the present paper rather than a general appeal. Barandes's indivisibility — the non-Markovian memory his processes require — is, on the McGucken reading, the projection-residual of a 4D-Markovian dynamics. The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic is first-order in the evolution parameter and Markovian on the 4D constraint surface; when the dynamics is projected onto a 3D spatial slice, the perpendicular x₄-direction is integrated out, and the memory that a 3D observer must encode as non-Markovianity is the trace of that integrated-out direction. Barandes's indivisibility is thus the operational shadow of x₄-advance projected onto configuration space. The independent motivation for the non-Markovian memory that Barandes posits is, in the McGucken framework, the perpendicular fourth dimension — a physical primitive specified without reference to the quantum-mechanical target: the i is the perpendicularity marker of x₄ (Proposition III.1, Piece 1), the ℏ is the action quantum of x₄-advance, and the complex linear structure is forced by the geometry of the expanding perpendicular axis rather than selected to make the reconstruction yield quantum mechanics. The quantum structure is produced from a physical primitive, not fitted to a known answer.

One qualification bounds the claim. Barandes can reply that indivisibility is independently natural as a clean mathematical class, not gerrymandered toward quantum mechanics; whether that independent naturalness holds is the crux of the debate about his program, and it is not settled here. What the McGucken framework contributes is a concrete alternative in which the corresponding property is derived rather than posited — indivisibility as the projection-residual of a stated 4D-Markovian principle, its independent motivation exhibited (the perpendicular x₄-axis) rather than asserted. The claim is scoped accordingly: the McGucken framework supplies the independent motivation the reverse-engineering objection demands, at the mechanism level established by the projection-residual identification, not a step-by-step reconstruction of Barandes's indivisibility class, which remains a distinct direction of work. **Result: reconstructs both (Q1) and (Q3) from an indivisible stochastic process, but the indivisibility that carries the quantum content is motivated by the reconstruction target unless supplied from outside; the McGucken framework supplies it as the x₄-projection-residual of a 4D-Markovian principle.**

**Barandes's causally-local proposal, and why probability and nonlocality cannot be separated.** Barandes's program turns on a further move that sharpens the engagement: rather than accept nonlocality as a physical feature, he seeks to reclassify quantum theory as *causally local*. In "New Prospects for a Causally Local Formulation of Quantum Theory" (2024) he proposes that a theory is causally local when, for two systems at spacelike separation, "there's a clean factorization of the conditional probabilities between them," supporting this with the no-signaling theorem (the steering "cannot deliberately send controllable messages"), Reichenbachian common-cause factorization, and the suggestion that if "there's no causation there's no superluminal causation and then the problem is just solved" [Barandes2024; Barandes2025]. His stated motivation is to take probability seriously — to found quantum theory on ordinary probability over configurations with definite values at all times, demoting the wavefunction to bookkeeping ("there's no wave function... the wave function is whatever your choice of configurations are"). That motivation is correct and is shared by the present framework as a starting recognition: the Born measure is a genuine physical probability, the SO(3)-Haar state-count of the expanding McGucken Sphere (Proposition III.1).

The asymmetry in Barandes's program is that it accepts one experimentally established feature of nature — its probabilistic character — as the foundation, while resisting a second experimentally established feature — its nonlocality, confirmed by the Bell-inequality violations of §VIII.9 — which it seeks to reclassify as causal locality. But probability and nonlocality stand on the same experimental footing: both are what measurement shows, and the singular/plural analysis of §X.8-ter shows both to be the plural, Geometric Channel content of the same expansion. The McGucken framework supplies the reason the two cannot be separated: probability and nonlocality are co-generated by the one act, the expansion of $x_4$ at $c$. The expansion turns each local emission event into an extended $x_4$-coincident surface — this is the creation of nonlocality (the outbound First Law of Nonlocality, §VIII.6) — and the same expanding surface carries the SO(3)-Haar state-count whose antipodal overlap is the Born measure (§III.1-ter, the head-on meeting of two Spheres). Two entangled photons from a common source are one expanding McGucken Sphere measured at two points, so their nonlocal correlation and their Born probabilities are the same Sphere read two ways (Proposition VIII.1; Proposition VIII.2, where the same isotropic measure that constitutes the correlation cloaks it in the flat marginal). The nonlocality is the expanding surface; the probability is the state-count of that surface; they are one object seen twice. This is why Barandes's program can honor probability but cannot consistently shed nonlocality: in the mechanism from which both descend, to take the probability is to take the nonlocality, because the expanding surface that is the one is the expanding surface that is the other. Barandes, like the entropic-gravity originators (§XI.3.11-bis), is candid that his foundation is not yet supplied — on ontology, "if we think there's never going to be some fundamental theory at the bottom of all of this... that's an open question," and on quantum gravity, that a fluctuating spacetime leaves him "a gap." The framework's answer to both is the same expansion: the substrate is the fourth dimension advancing at $c$, and probability and nonlocality are its co-generated readings.

**How Barandes argues the reclassification, and why the argument leaves the geometric nonlocality intact.** Barandes's route to "causally local" is more specific than a factorization claim, and stating it exactly shows both its force and where it does not reach [Barandes2025]. His argument is that Bell's theorem cannot be given a fundamental physical statement, because it depends on a notion of causation that has no fundamental referent. Bell's theorem, the EPR argument, and the GHZ argument, he holds, all "help themselves to interventionist causation" — the account on which "$A$ causally influences $B$" means "if an agent intervenes on $A$, then $B$ changes." That account requires agents performing interventions: an Alice and a Bob who make measurements. But a fundamental microphysical theory is, in his words, "just atoms doing the things that they're doing, with no agents, no interventions, no measurements," and at the level of atoms "I don't even know what this theory of causation is supposed to mean." He then invokes the Laplacian and Russellian picture: the universe is one global state evolving by a single differential equation forward and backward, in which "there's no place for causation... at a fundamental microphysical level," citing Russell's remark that causation is "a relic" [Russell1913] and Norton's thesis that "causation is folk science" [Norton2003]. The conclusion he draws is that "if there's no causation there's no superluminal causation and then the problem is just solved" — Bell's nonlocality is non-local *causation*, and if fundamental causation does not exist, Bell's theorem has nothing to be about.

Two responses follow, and together they are the McGucken framework's engagement with the argument. The first is that the argument turns on an internal tension in Barandes's own position. To dissolve Bell he adopts the Laplacian–Russellian metaphysics: a single global state, a Markovian differential equation, deterministic, time-symmetric, evolving forward and backward, with no fundamental causation. But the thesis of his own program is that the fundamental dynamics is genuinely probabilistic and *indivisible* — non-Markovian, with the probabilities law-like and fundamental — which is the negation of the Markovian deterministic block he invokes to remove causation. The move that dissolves nonlocality (a deterministic, time-symmetric, causation-free Laplacian block) and the move that founds the program (an irreducibly probabilistic, non-Markovian, indivisible process) pull in opposite directions: the first is Laplace's, the second is against Laplace. A foundation cannot be Markovian-deterministic-enough to make causation disappear and non-Markovian-probabilistic-enough to make the Born rule fundamental at the same time. The asymmetry — accept probability as fundamental, reclassify nonlocality away — is purchased by holding both halves of a contradiction.

The second response grants Barandes the causation-elimination move in full and shows that the nonlocality survives it. Suppose fundamental causation is indeed a folk-scientific relic, as Russell and Norton urge; suppose there is no fundamental "$A$ causes $B$." What Bell's theorem then loses is its reading as *non-local causation* — a controllable influence propagated from one wing to the other. That reading the McGucken framework never asserted: by Proposition VIII.2 the correlation carries no signal, and by the outbound First Law of Nonlocality (§VIII.6) the correlation's source is the common $x_4$-origin carried outward by the expansion, not a causal signal exchanged between the wings. The McGucken nonlocality is *common-origin geometric structure*, not superluminal causation. Eliminating causation therefore removes the causal *description* of the correlation while leaving the correlation and its geometric source untouched: two systems created at a common event share the $x_4$-coincidence of one expanding Sphere and share one accumulated $x_4$-advance $X_4$ (Appendix A (R4); Proposition VIII.1), and this is a fact about the geometry of the expansion, not about any agent's intervention or any signal. The Bell-inequality violation — the empirical fact confirmed from Freedman–Clauser through the loophole-free tests (§VIII.9) — is a statistical fact about coincidence counts across many pairs, requiring no notion of causation to state, and it remains exactly as it was after causation is declared folk science. Barandes's argument, at its strongest, shows that the *causal gloss* on nonlocality is dispensable; it does not touch the geometric nonlocality that the expanding Sphere carries, because that nonlocality was never a causal signal. The correlation stays, its common-origin geometric source stays, and its inseparability from the Born probability stays — all three being readings of the one expansion — so the reclassification removes a word for the phenomenon without removing the phenomenon. What Barandes correctly senses (that "non-local causation" is a problematic notion) the McGucken framework already grants, and it supplies the non-causal account of the nonlocality he is reaching for: not a causal influence to be explained away, but the shared $x_4$-locality of a common origin, carried outward by $dx_4/dt = ic$.

**What the programme keeps and what it discards.** Stated plainly, the indivisible-stochastic programme keeps the mathematics of quantum mechanics and discards the nonlocality the experiments demonstrate. Barandes accepts the Bell-inequality violations in full — the correlations are real, the experiments correct, the confirmations decisive (§VIII.9) — and reproduces them in his formalism as a non-factorizable joint probability distribution; what he removes is the reading of that violation as nonlocality, relabelling it "causally local." He accepts the double-slit interference in full — the fringe pattern, the single-photon buildup — and reproduces it as the discrepancy between the indivisible evolution and its Markov approximation; what he removes is the wave, relabelling it "the non-Markovian correction." In both cases the mathematical carrier is retained and the physical mechanism is deleted: the Bell correlation kept, its nonlocality discarded; the interference kept, its wave discarded. The reproduction succeeds because the mathematics is imported from the standard formalism — the stochastic matrix is the mod-square of the unitary, so the wave's phase content and the entangled joint distribution's correlation strength are present in the inputs — and are then renamed rather than derived. This is the reverse-engineering signature stated above, now at the level of the two decisive experiments: the programme presupposes the quantum structure it sets out to replace, keeps that structure's numbers, and strips the physical facts — the wave and the nonlocality — that the numbers record. No physical substrate is supplied in their place, because the programme has none to supply (its author states that what is "at the bottom" is "an open question").

The McGucken framework accepts the identical experimental outcomes and takes the opposite course: it keeps the physics and derives the mathematics. The double-slit interference is the antipodal self-overlap of the physical McGucken Sphere, the wavefront of $x_4$'s expansion ([MG-Minkowski-Hilbert, Theorem 7.12]; §III.1-ter); the wave is exhibited as the expanding wavefront the double slit displays (§III.1-bis), rather than relabelled away. The Bell correlation is the shared $x_4$-coincidence of one expanding Sphere from the common origin (Proposition VIII.1), with its Tsirelson strength derived from the SO(3)-Haar measure and its no-signaling derived from the same measure's flat marginal (Proposition VIII.2); the nonlocality is derived as the geometry of the expansion, rather than relabelled away. Where the indivisible-stochastic programme imports the unitary and deletes the wave and the nonlocality it carries, the framework derives the unitary, the wave, the Born measure, and the nonlocal correlation from $dx_4/dt = ic$. The demonstrated nonlocality of nature — what the Bell experiments show and the 2022 Nobel Prize honours — is, on the one account, a word to be removed while the correlations are kept, and on the other, a physical fact derived from the expansion of the fourth dimension. Probability, nonlocality, and interference are kept together in the framework because they are one expansion read three ways; they can be separated in the indivisible-stochastic programme only because, lacking the expansion, it never had them as one thing to begin with.

**The decisive question: where do the probability and the nonlocality come from?** The programme's deflationary claim is that it removes the strangeness of quantum mechanics by recasting it as an ordinary stochastic process. It does not remove the strangeness; it relocates the two strangest facts of nature — that the world is irreducibly probabilistic and that separated systems are correlated beyond every classical bound — into the axioms of the stochastic process, where they sit unexplained. The demonstration is direct, in two parts.

*Probability has no origin in the programme; it is the primitive.* The stated foundation of the indivisible-stochastic approach is to begin with ordinary probability — to treat quantum theory as a genuine stochastic process from the start. Probability is therefore the ground floor of the construction, the thing assumed, not the thing derived. The programme does not ask why nature is probabilistic rather than deterministic; it posits a probabilistic process and proceeds. The question "why is there probability at all?" has no answer within the framework, because the framework's first move is to write probability down as given. This is not a defect the programme could repair by further work: probability is constitutive of what an indivisible stochastic process is, so the theory cannot derive its own foundation.

*Nonlocality has no origin in the programme; it is imported by hand.* The Bell correlations enter the formalism as a non-factorizable joint probability distribution over the two systems' configurations — a joint distribution that does not split as $P(a,b) = P(a)\,P(b)$. That non-factorizability is an input. It is written down because the experiments require it, and it is obtained by mod-squaring the entangled unitary of the standard formalism. Nothing in the programme explains why the joint distribution is non-factorizable rather than factorizable, why the correlation reaches the Tsirelson value $2\sqrt{2}$ rather than a weaker classical value, or why the correlated systems were correlated in the first place. The correlation is transcribed from the quantum formalism and installed as a brute feature of the joint distribution. The reclassification as "causally local" changes the name of this feature; it supplies no origin for it. So the programme has, for the nonlocality, exactly what it has for the probability: an unexplained input.

The programme therefore supplies no source for either of the two facts it is built to accommodate. Probability is assumed as the primitive; nonlocality is imported as a non-factorizable distribution; and the interference that the double slit displays is the mod-square of a unitary taken as given. The strangeness of quantum mechanics is not dissolved by this construction — it is demoted to a set of unexamined axioms and left there. The author is candid that the substrate is not supplied: what is "at the bottom" is, in his words, "an open question," and "I don't know." That admission is the exact measure of the programme: it does not explain where probability and nonlocality come from, and it does not claim to.

The McGucken framework answers precisely the question the programme leaves open, and answers it for both facts from the one principle. Probability has an origin: when $x_4$ expands, no spatial direction is preferred, because $x_4$ is perpendicular to all three spatial dimensions equally (§I.4.1-bis), so the advance is isotropic, and an isotropic advance from a point is a sphere — a local point becomes a sphere of expanding locality. The particle is equivalently locatable anywhere on that expanding surface, with no point preferred because no direction is preferred, so the registration point is drawn from the unique isotropic $SO(3)$-Haar measure on the surface, which is $|\psi|^2$ (Proposition III.1). Probability is the isotropic measure of the expanding surface, existing because the expansion of $x_4$ has no preferred direction, rather than a primitive assumed at the outset. Nonlocality has an origin: the expansion carries the local emission event outward into an extended surface every point of which shares the emission event's accumulated $x_4$-advance $X_4$ (Theorem XII.A.2; Appendix A (R4)), so the surface is one $x_4$-coincident object — a single locality distributed across a region, which is nonlocality by construction (the outbound First Law of Nonlocality). Two systems created at a common event ride one such surface and share one accumulated $x_4$-advance $X_4$ (Proposition VIII.1; Appendix A (R4)); the correlation reaches the Tsirelson value because that value is the maximum SO(3)-Haar-weighted correlation on the isotropic surface, and it carries no signal because the same isotropic measure flattens the marginal (Proposition VIII.2). Nonlocality is the geometry of the expanding surface, derived rather than imported. And the two origins are one origin: the isotropic surface whose measure is the probability is the $x_4$-coincident surface whose identity is the nonlocality — the same expansion of the fourth dimension read as intensity and as extent. Where the indivisible-stochastic programme installs probability and nonlocality as two unexplained axioms, $dx_4/dt = ic$ derives both as two readings of the one expanding McGucken Sphere. That is the difference between relocating the strangeness and explaining it.

**The Maudlin–Barandes debate: three demands, and the single-outcome problem.** The 2025 Maudlin–Barandes discussion [Maudlin2025b] brings the central assumption of the programme into the open and states three demands the McGucken framework meets and the stochastic reading leaves owed. First, the category problem: Barandes identifies quantum expectation values with classical averages, and Maudlin objects that this is stipulated rather than earned — "it's not enough just to put little brackets around a quantity and say it's an average and then say that therefore it's the same kind of average that we would think of classically; there's more work that needs to be done" [Maudlin2025b]. The framework does the work: $|\psi|^2$ is the physical state-count $\Omega$ of the expanding McGucken Sphere — the head-on $x_4$-collision of two Spheres (§III.1-ter) — a definite physical quantity, not a classical average asserted by placing brackets around it. Second, the ontology question: Maudlin presses "what is the ontology? what is the theory saying exists?", noting that an indivisible stochastic process is a formal recipe rather than an account of what exists. The framework answers: what exists is the expanding fourth dimension, the McGucken Sphere at every event (§I.4.1-bis, §III.1-bis), the physical substrate the stochastic recipe lacks. Third, the imposition charge, which the programme's own description exhibits: at a measurement, in Barandes's words, "the indivisible unistochastic matrix factorizes across the two times and suddenly we get the spontaneous generation of a new division event that wasn't there before" [Maudlin2025b] — a division event introduced where the theory needs an outcome to actualize, rather than derived. The framework has no such insertion: the indivisibility Barandes must posit is, physically, the unity of one expanding Sphere — an entangled pair is one Sphere measured at two points (§VIII.6), so the joint process is indivisible because it is literally one object, and the definite outcome is the physical first-contact collision localizing that one Sphere (§XI.5-bis), not a spontaneously generated division event.

The sharpest form of the imposition charge is the single-outcome problem, and it is the sphere-of-detectors case of §V.5-bis: a source at the centre of a sphere of detectors, every detector reached with identical weight, exactly one firing. The indivisible process assigns the outcome probabilities, but the actualization of one detector rather than another is carried by the "spontaneous generation of a new division event" — a device that records that one outcome occurs without supplying what selects it. This is the same gap that appears in the Transactional Interpretation's symmetric handshake (§XI.3.9) and in the collapse postulate both were meant to replace: the probabilities are given, the single actualization among equal alternatives is left as a primitive. The framework supplies the physical selection — the first-contact collision, the one point at which the two expanding wavefronts meet head-on and the $x_4$-momenta cancel (§V.5-bis, §XI.5-bis) — locating the actualization in the collision geometry, with only the seed (which first-contact point on a given trial) left open, the determinism-versus-chance fork every framework shares (§V.5-bis). Where Barandes inserts a division event to record the outcome and the Transactional Interpretation posits a handshake to complete it, the framework exhibits the physical event at which the one Sphere localizes.

**Probability's origin is ontic, and it carries an empirical signature.** The programme takes probability as the primitive (above); the framework derives it, and the derivation fixes its character as geometric and ontic rather than epistemic [MG-Gravity-Born, §4.1.0bis]. Orthodox quantum mechanics can read probability as epistemic ignorance of a definite underlying value; the framework reads it as the geometric consequence of coupling to a nonlocal expansion. The identity at work is that in $dx_4/dt = ic$ the rate $c$ is the speed of the advance and the imaginary unit $i$ is the nonlocality of the advance ($i$-as-nonlocality, $c$-as-rate): the $x_4$-expansion carrying $i$ proceeds as a spherically symmetric wavefront in all directions at once, with no single local direction, so a massive particle coupled to it is dragged by a process that has no definite local direction, and the direction of each displacement is drawn from the uniform measure on the sphere precisely because the expansion it couples to is nonlocal and cannot single out one spatial direction. The randomness is the shadow, on the local particle, of the nonlocality of the expanding $x_4$; probability over detection directions and displacement direction are the one nonlocality read at the event and along the trajectory. Because this ontic origin differs from the epistemic reading, it carries a falsifiable consequence the epistemic reading forbids: a residual, temperature-independent diffusion of a massive particle coupled to the expansion, $D_x = \varepsilon^2 c^2 \Omega / 2\gamma^2$, which the epistemic reading predicts to be exactly zero ([MG-Gravity-Born, §6.2.1]; [MG-Entropy]). The nonlocality that is the $i$ of $dx_4/dt = ic$ is thus the common physical source of the random walk, the Second Law, and the Born measure — and it stakes the account on a measurable number, where the programme that takes probability as primitive stakes nothing.

**XI.3.9 Cramer's Transactional Interpretation: a level distinction, not a head-to-head.** Cramer's Transactional Interpretation (TI) [Cramer1986; Cramer2016] is the closest existing program to the present framework's measurement account, and the comparison must be set up correctly, because a naive head-to-head on derivation is a category error that would misstate both programs. TI and the McGucken framework agree on the decisive ontological commitments: the wavefunction ψ is a physical wave with spatial extent rather than a knowledge-representation; the complex conjugate ψ* is equally physical; measurement is a physical two-wave event (Cramer's transaction; the McGucken Sphere-collision of §XI.5-bis) rather than an observer-triggered collapse; and the Born density ψ*ψ is the product of a forward wave and a conjugate wave, both physically real. On these points TI is the correct comparison — the one prior program that located the ontology of the wave correctly — and the present framework inherits the same commitments.

The two programs differ in *level*, and the level difference is itself the comparison rather than a common axis along which one out-performs the other. TI is, by Cramer's explicit and repeated statement, an *interpretation* that derives no structure: "the mathematics is (and should be) exclusively contained in the standard quantum formalism itself; the function of the interpretation is to interpret that mathematics, not to introduce any new additional mathematics" [Cramer2016, §on transaction formation]. Cramer hardens this into a criterion for what counts as an interpretation at all, classifying Bohmian mechanics and GRW as "not interpretations of standard quantum mechanics at all, but rather alternative theories" precisely because they add or modify mathematics. By this criterion TI is constitutively committed to deriving nothing: it takes the Hilbert space, the Schrödinger equation, the Born rule, and the Minkowski spacetime background as given inputs, and supplies an ontological reading (real offer and confirmation waves) on top of them.

Two consequences follow, and they are the substance of the comparison.

First, on the structures the present paper derives, TI takes each as a primitive input. The Hilbert space is taken wholesale — the offer wave ψ *is* the standard state vector and ψ* *is* the standard Bra; TI reinterprets the ontological status of these objects without asking why the state space is complex, linear, and sesquilinear. Cramer in fact treats the "many-dimensional Hilbert hyperspace" as elegant mathematics that "provides little assistance in visualizing what is really going on," and offers the transactional spacetime picture as a visualization aid while retaining Hilbert space as the calculational engine. The present framework derives the Hilbert space rather than taking it: ℋ = L²(ℳ_G) with the complex structure from i as the perpendicularity marker of x₄ (Proposition III.1, Piece 1), the sesquilinear inner product from the rank-2 metric, and the composite-system tensor product from the product of constraint surfaces (Theorem XIII cogeneration cascade). The Minkowski spacetime that TI treats as a fixed background is likewise a derived structure here: x₄ = ∫ ic dt = ict, the metric from squaring (ic)² = −c², the light cone as the locus the wavefront traces, and the causal orientation from the +ic sign (Proposition II.1.2).

Second, and sharper: TI's central mechanism *presupposes* precisely the structure the present framework derives, and cannot state itself without it. The advanced/retarded distinction on which the entire transactional handshake rests is definable only on a pre-given Minkowski spacetime with a pre-given time-orientation — "advanced" means backward along an already-fixed time direction, "retarded" forward along it. TI must be handed the causal orientation to say which wave is which. The present framework generates that causal orientation from the +ic sign of the advance (Proposition II.1.2 and the Algebraic/Geometric Channel modulus boundary of Remark II.1.3) and then reads the conjugate factor off it. TI presupposes what the McGucken framework produces.

This bears directly on the confirmation wave. TI's confirmation wave ψ* is an *advanced* solution: it leaves the absorber and arrives back at the source at the instant of emission, propagating in the negative time direction, with the transaction forming "atemporally." The backward-in-time wave is TI's central posit, and it carries the retrocausation that most resists physical motivation; its only role is to supply the ψ* factor of the Born density. The present framework supplies the same ψ* factor without any backward-in-time wave: the conjugate factor is the absorber's own *forward* +ic-expansion viewed in the emitter's frame, where it reads as −ic along the shared axis (§XI.5-bis and the frame-relational sign structure), or equivalently the PT-antipodal hemisphere of a single forward-expanding Sphere. Every wave in the McGucken account propagates forward; the −i is a frame-relational sign, not a time-reversed propagation. The framework obtains TI's entire explanatory payoff — a physical ψ*, a physical two-wave measurement event, no special observer, natural accounts of delayed-choice and quantum-eraser experiments — while replacing the posited advanced wave with a forward expansion read relationally, a strictly smaller ontological commitment.

The retrocausal commitment carries three specific problems that Cramer inherits from the Wheeler–Feynman absorber theory and documents in the opening chapter of *The Quantum Handshake* [Cramer2016, Ch. 1], and the McGucken framework resolves each by the orientation of the primitive rather than by any absorber boundary condition. Cramer recounts that Larry Biedenharn set him on the path to TI by pressing the absorber theory's difficulties: Wheeler and Feynman had built a time-symmetric formalism and then imposed the observed causal arrow through a boundary condition — the assumed dominance of future absorbers — with retarded waves from a present emitter answered by advanced waves from future absorbers [WheelerFeynman1945; Cramer2016, Ch. 1].

The first problem is the retrocausal integration. The advanced wave is a backward-in-time solution, so a calculation requires integrating over the absorber distribution of the entire future universe. The McGucken framework carries no advanced wave: the conjugate factor is the absorber's own forward +ic-expansion read in the emitter's frame (§XI.5-bis), so there is no future absorber distribution to integrate over, and the calculational obstruction does not arise — it is removed at its source rather than made tractable.

The second problem is the one Biedenharn raised and Cramer reports as having looked "fishy" to him [Cramer2016, Ch. 1]: the Wheeler–Feynman arrow requires future absorbers to dominate over past absorbers, yet the universe is expanding and growing less dense as time advances, so the future is *less* absorptive than the past. The absorber asymmetry the theory needs runs opposite to cosmology. The McGucken framework does not require future-absorber dominance at any point, because its arrow is not an absorber asymmetry: it is the sign of the primitive, dx₄/dt = +ic, an expansion that is intrinsically oriented with no −ic branch in the physical fact. The expanding universe that undermines the Wheeler–Feynman absorber asymmetry is, on the McGucken reading, the very expansion that constitutes the arrow — the feature Biedenharn used against the absorber theory becomes the mechanism rather than a threat to it. (The identification of the x₄-advance with the observed cosmological expansion is developed in the McGucken cosmology corpus and is cited here rather than re-derived; the point requires only that the +ic orientation is primitive and directional, established in the arrow-of-time results of [MG-Entropy].)

The third problem is the deepest and is the same diagnosis Proposition II.1.2 gives: the Wheeler–Feynman formalism is time-symmetric, and the causal arrow must be imposed on it by hand through the absorber boundary condition. A time-symmetric formalism is sign-blind on the direction of time and cannot produce the arrow from within; it must import it. The McGucken framework's primitive is not time-symmetric — dx₄/dt = +ic is oriented before any metric or boundary condition exists — so the causal order, the retarded-over-advanced propagator selection (+ic → +iε → G_ret), the thermodynamic arrow, and the radiative arrow are readings of the one oriented sign rather than consequences of an imposed boundary condition. Where Wheeler–Feynman and TI locate the arrow in a boundary condition on a symmetric formalism, the McGucken framework locates it in the orientation of the primitive.

The one genuinely successful element of the Wheeler–Feynman handshake — the account of radiative recoil and the transfer of energy and momentum between emitter and absorber — is retained here, but as a forward two-sphere collision at the emission–absorption event, with the recoil supplied by the x₄-momentum cancellation of §XI.5-bis rather than by a handshake across time. The recoil is derived; the backward-in-time wave that Wheeler–Feynman introduced to account for it is not needed.

The comparison therefore cannot be run as "which program derives Hilbert and Minkowski space better," because TI declines to derive by definition. Where the two programs genuinely meet is the count-of-posits criterion (§XIV-bis). TI posits the full Hilbert-space formalism, the Minkowski spacetime background, the Schrödinger equation, the Born rule, and a backward-in-time advanced wave — deriving none of them and adding one retrocausal primitive on top. The McGucken framework posits dx₄/dt = ic and derives the Hilbert space, the Minkowski metric, the Schrödinger equation (Theorem XIII.E), the Born rule (Proposition III.1), the causal orientation, and the conjugate factor as a forward relational sign. On Einstein's criterion of the fewest irreducible elements, TI operates entirely downstream of the structures the McGucken framework derives, and requires one of those structures — the Minkowski causal orientation — merely to define its own central mechanism.

One element of TI has no counterpart yet developed in the present framework, and it is named here rather than passed over. Cramer supplies a worked dynamical model of transaction *consummation* — the Mead coupled-dipole-resonator avalanche [Mead2000, §5.4], a tractable calculation with hydrogen-atom wavefunctions showing the exponential build-up of a completed transaction. This is a model of how the handshake avalanches to completion in time, and the McGucken collision account (§XI.5-bis) derives the pointlike first-contact and the conservation-forced localization without yet supplying the equivalent worked consummation dynamics. The distinction to draw is exact: the Mead model is detailed machinery for consummating a process whose basis is the backward-in-time advanced wave, so it is not an independent advantage but development of the very retrocausal structure the McGucken framework removes. A forward-time consummation dynamics for the Sphere-collision — coupled-resonator machinery of the Mead type, but with both spheres expanding forward and the coupling building at the first-contact event rather than through an advanced wave — is a well-defined direction of work that would supply the good part of Mead's calculation on a forward-time basis. **Result: TI interprets the standard formalism without deriving it, taking Hilbert space, Minkowski spacetime, Schrödinger, and Born as inputs and adding a backward-in-time advanced wave; it presupposes the Minkowski causal orientation its own mechanism requires. The McGucken framework derives all of these from dx₄/dt = ic and obtains the conjugate factor as a forward relational sign, positing one principle where TI posits the entire formalism plus a retrocausal primitive.**

**XI.3.10 Vedral: the Many-Worlder who wants the Born rule derived.** Vlatko Vedral's position [Vedral2023, in conversation with Greene] is included because it states, from inside the Many-Worlds programme, the precise dissatisfaction the McGucken framework addresses. Vedral is a Many-Worlder who does not regard the Born rule as adequately derived. On the decision-theoretic derivation of Deutsch and Wallace he says it "is as best as we can do so far," but asked whether it satisfies him, "Not quite… if you really claim that probabilities come out of amplitudes and there is nothing else there, then I'd like to see a more minimalistic derivation. I think there's still far too many extra assumptions." He notes the opposing Many-Worlds camp (Vaidman) holds the Born rule "impossible to derive" and takes it as given, and states his own wish plainly: "I would like the Born postulate to follow more naturally from quantum mechanics, but I don't think we have a way to do that."

His complaint is specific — the extant derivation carries too many auxiliary assumptions (rationality axioms, betting/economics postulates) — and it is the first-person form of the XI.3.2 critique. The McGucken framework answers exactly this. The Born form P = |ψ|² is derived from the geometry of dx₄/dt = ic with no decision-theoretic input: the exponent 2 is forced by the elimination of |ψ|¹, |ψ|³, Re(ψ), Im(ψ) as candidate measures and by the rank-2 metric structure (Proposition III.1), and independently by the unique SO(3)-invariant Haar measure on the spherical expansion (Proposition III.1, Piece 3; [MG-QM, Theorem 13]). Where Deutsch supplies rational-agent axioms and Wallace supplies branch-weighting decision theory, the McGucken derivation supplies the metric rank and the rotational symmetry of the wavefront — the "more minimalistic derivation" Vedral asks for, with the assumptions reduced to the geometry of the expansion. The single open element is the seed (which first-contact outcome is realized on a given trial, §XI.5-bis), not the form of the measure.

Vedral also raises, unprompted, the Many-Worlds probability problem in its sharpest form: if all branches are equally real, then the cat in a one-in-a-billion-amplitude branch "feels alive as much as if the amplitude was much" larger, so probability cannot arise from branches that all occur with certainty — a tension he concedes is real. This tension is a cost of the branch-realist ontology and the McGucken framework does not carry it: the framework is single-world (one Geometric Channel first-contact collision per event, §XI.5-bis), the amplitude is the SO(3)-measure density over which collision occurs, and the low-amplitude outcome occurs rarely rather than occurring with certainty in a low-weight branch. The probability problem Vedral concedes is dissolved by not adopting the many-branches ontology that generates it.

Two further positions of Vedral's coincide with the framework. He rejects any special status for observers — "observers should have no special status in our theory; they're just another collection of Q numbers" — and rejects Vaidman's self-locating-uncertainty route because it makes the probabilities intelligible only after the observer "opens their eyes," whereas the probabilities are stated before (Greene's "too late in the story" objection). The framework supplies the physical content Vedral wants here: measurement is a first-contact collision (§XI.5-bis), an event requiring no observer, and the Born probability is the SO(3)-measure density fixed by the expansion geometry before any detection, not an observer's post-hoc self-location among copies. He also rejects the epistemic/QBist reading as "the other extreme"; the framework agrees, taking |ψ|² as an objective geometric fact rather than an agent's belief (§XI.3.7 and §V.6.4).

The one genuine divergence is the direction of derivation. Vedral, with Greene, places quantum "Q numbers" (or entanglement) at the foundation and treats spacetime as emergent from them — "reality consists of these Q numbers," and in the entanglement-stitches-spacetime picture, "Einsteinian space and time is not there, and yet quantum mechanics seems to persist." The McGucken framework reverses this: dx₄/dt = ic is the primitive, and both the Lorentzian metric and the quantum formalism — Hilbert space, the complex structure, the non-commutativity of the Q numbers, entanglement as x₄-coincidence — descend from it (Propositions III.1, XIII.1–XIII.6; §VIII). The non-commutativity Vedral takes as the abstract bottom is, in the framework, a theorem: the i is the perpendicularity marker of x₄, and [q̂, p̂] = iℏ follows from D_M (Proposition XIII.5). Where Vedral's programme puts Q numbers first and derives spacetime, the McGucken framework puts the expanding fourth dimension first and derives both the Q numbers and spacetime. (The identification of the x₄-expansion with the structure the entanglement-first programme treats as emergent is developed in the corpus and cited here rather than re-derived.) **Result: a Many-Worlder who states the exact dissatisfaction — too many assumptions in the Born derivation, no special observer status, no epistemic retreat — that the framework's geometric Born derivation answers; the framework further dissolves the branch-probability tension Vedral concedes, and differs from him only on which structure is primitive.**

**XI.3.11 Maudlin: the three measurement problems, and why the framework meets the standard set by the most exacting philosopher of physics.** Tim Maudlin is the interlocutor whose standards the present framework most wants to meet, because his demands are precisely the ones the framework is built to satisfy: a real solution to the measurement problem requires *new physics* with a *specified primitive ontology* and *stated dynamics*, judged by whether it delivers definite outcomes, the Born statistics, and the forward influence of a measurement on later measurements. Maudlin's foundational work has three pillars, and the framework engages each.

*Maudlin's first pillar: the three measurement problems.* In "Three Measurement Problems" [Maudlin1995] Maudlin shows that what is usually called "the" measurement problem is three distinct problems, and that most proposed solutions fail at least one. The first is the *problem of outcomes*: the three claims

- (1.A) the wave-function of a system is complete — it specifies, directly or indirectly, all physical properties of the system;
- (1.B) the wave-function always evolves by a linear dynamical equation (e.g. the Schrödinger equation);
- (1.C) measurements always (or usually) have determinate outcomes

are mutually inconsistent, by the Schrödinger-cat symmetry argument: feed a measuring device an electron in an x-spin eigenstate (a superposition of z-up and z-down); by (1.B) linearity the device evolves into the entangled superposition $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}(|z\text{-up}\rangle|{\rm UP}\rangle + |z\text{-down}\rangle|{\rm DOWN}\rangle)$; by (1.A) completeness that wave-function is the whole physical story; but the two terms enter symmetrically, so nothing in the complete description makes the pointer read UP rather than DOWN — contradicting (1.C). A solution must reject one: reject (1.A) → *additional-variables* theory (Bohm); reject (1.B) → *non-linear* theory (GRW); reject (1.C) → *multiverse* theory (Everett). The second is the *problem of statistics*: even granted definite outcomes, one must recover the Born probabilities, and a deterministic complete theory (2.A completeness + 2.B deterministic evolution) gives identical outcomes from identical wave-functions, contradicting the observed Born statistics (2.C). Here Maudlin delivers the verdict on Many-Worlds that the framework's §XI.3.10 engagement with Vedral already invoked: on the multiverse reading "there is simply nothing for the numbers generated by Born's rule to be probabilities of," because every branch occurs and no observer goes down any one branch, so the frequencies-approach-one argument is a *petitio principii*. The third is the *problem of effect*: the outcome of a first measurement must influence the future — a second measurement of the same observable must agree — and Maudlin shows the modal interpretations fail it, because the outcome is codified in neither the (uncollapsed) wave-function nor a forward-propagating additional variable, leaving it "empirically superfluous." His conclusion: only additional-variables theories (Bohm) and non-linear collapse theories (GRW) survive all three; "any real solution demands new physics," and any candidate that fails must be committed "to the flames, for it can contain nothing but sophistry and illusion."

*The framework is not one of Maudlin's three boxes, because it denies the shared premise of all three.* It is tempting to file the McGucken framework as an additional-variables theory — the four-dimensional $x_4$-extended state carries more than the 3D wave-function ψ (which is its spatial cross-section, Proposition V.1), so ψ is incomplete and (1.A) is denied. That filing is half right and half misleading. The framework does deny (1.A) as a statement about the 3D ψ; but it does not add a variable *alongside* an otherwise-intact linear evolution in the manner of Bohm, whose corpuscles ride a wave that still evolves by the unmodified linear Schrödinger equation. The deeper point is that Maudlin's trilemma, and the taxonomy of three escapes built on it, silently assumes that "the evolution" is a single object — the linear Schrödinger evolution (1.B) — so that the only freedom is whether one adds variables, adds a collapse law, or adds worlds. The framework rejects that shared assumption. Under $dx_4/dt = ic$ the linear unitary Schrödinger evolution is the *Algebraic Channel reading* of a two-faced physical process whose *Geometric Channel reading* is the expanding, dissipative, monotonically oriented McGucken Sphere; the modulus operation $|\cdot|^2$ is the boundary between the two channels (Proposition II.1.2). Linearity (1.B) is therefore true *of the evolution operator between measurements* and is not the whole of the realized physical process, which begins with an oriented emission and ends with a projective absorption. The framework escapes the trilemma not by paying one of its three costs — it adds no hidden variable riding an intact linear wave, no non-linear collapse term, and no branching worlds — but by exhibiting that (1.B), read as a claim about the realized process rather than the between-measurements operator, is false. Quantum mechanics is not strictly unitary as a description of what physically happens.

That last claim is demonstrated, not merely asserted, in the minimal system that can carry it, transcribed here in full from the corpus. The two-atom double slit strips the double-slit experiment to one atom on each side of a two-aperture partition and one excitation — no room, screen, thermal bath, detector, or ensemble — and shows that the retarded selection of a time-symmetric field equation is a single sign, that the sign is fixed by the $+$ of $+ic$, and that the realized emission-propagation-absorption process is not the unitary operator even though the operator is unitary. The complete construction and every proof follow.

*The two-atom double slit (transcribed in full from [MG-TwoAtom] and the companion flagship [MG-Minkowski-Hilbert, §10.12septies]; theorem and equation labels are local to this transcribed block).*

The Wheeler–Feynman subsection above located the time-orientation contribution of $dx_4/dt = ic$ against absorber theory. This subsection gives the argument in full, self-contained, as the minimal exhibition of the Principle’s arrow: a two-atom system in which the retarded selection of a time-symmetric field equation is shown to be a single sign, and that sign is derived from $+ic$. The construction and all results transcribe the companion paper \[MG-TwoAtom\]; the theorems are renumbered here as 10.12S.1–10.12S.11 to avoid collision with the flagship numbering, and the equation labels are local to this subsection.

*The thought experiment.* Take the double-slit experiment and remove everything removable: the room, the glass, the screen, the thermal bath, the detector electronics. What remains is a partition with two apertures, one atom $A$ on side $M$, one atom $B$ on side $N$, and one excitation. Atom $A$ emits; the photon passes the partition; atom $B$ absorbs. Run it the other way — atom $B$ emits — and ask whether the photon retraces its path to $A$. Two readings must be separated: whether $A$ ever absorbs, and whether the forward process is run backward. It reaches $A$ with the forward interference weight (Theorem 10.12S.5) and retraces the forward wave history with probability zero. The system is minimal by construction: two degrees of freedom and one field, no ensemble, no coarse-graining, no entropy count. Whatever irreversibility survives here is present before thermodynamics begins, and the conclusion is that it is the choice of the retarded solution of a time-symmetric field equation, a sign on the time coordinate, and that $dx_4/dt = ic$ is the single statement from which that sign follows.

*Setup.* Let side $M$ be the half-space $z<0$, side $N$ the half-space $z>0$, and the partition the plane $z=0$ with aperture function $T(x,y) = 1$ on $S_1 \cup S_2$ (the two slits) and $0$ otherwise. Atom $A$ sits at $\mathbf{r}_A$ with $z_A<0$; atom $B$ at $\mathbf{r}_B$ with $z_B>0$. Work first with a scalar field for a monochromatic excitation, $\psi(\mathbf{r},t) = U(\mathbf{r})\,e^{-i\omega t}$, $k=\omega/c$; the spatial part obeys the inhomogeneous Helmholtz equation with the emitting atom as source,
$$(\nabla^2 + k^2)\,U(\mathbf{r}) = -\delta(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_{\rm src}). \tag{S.1}$$
The analysis carries over verbatim to the vector Maxwell field and to the Schrödinger wave of a massive particle, each being time-reversal invariant in the sense of Theorem 10.12S.1 with retarded and advanced Green’s functions related as in (S.3). The barrier is reflecting in the first five theorems and absorbing in Theorem 10.12S.8; the two cases differ, and the difference is part of the content.

**Theorem 10.12S.1 (T-invariance).** *The wave equation $\square\,\psi = -4\pi\rho$, the source-free Maxwell equations, and the Schrödinger equation with real potential are each invariant under time reversal: if $\psi(\mathbf{r},t)$ is a solution, so is $\psi(\mathbf{r},-t)$ (wave; Maxwell with $\mathbf{B}\to-\mathbf{B}$) or $\psi^*(\mathbf{r},-t)$ (Schrödinger).*

*Proof.* For the wave equation $\partial_t^2$ is even in $t$. For Maxwell, the substitution $t\to-t$, $\mathbf{E}\to\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{B}\to-\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{j}\to-\mathbf{j}$ maps the equations to themselves. For Schrödinger, complex conjugation of $i\partial_t\psi = H\psi$ with $H$ real gives $-i\partial_t\psi^* = H\psi^*$, the original equation in $-t$. ∎

This is standard (Jackson §6.10; Sakurai §4.4); it is stated because the rest turns on it — the equation does not orient time, so whatever orients time is added to it. The Helmholtz equation (S.1) has two Green’s functions,
$$G_\pm(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}') = \frac{e^{\pm ik|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}'|}}{4\pi|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}'|}, \tag{S.2}$$
which with the time factor $e^{-i\omega t}$ are the retarded (outgoing, $G_+$) and advanced (incoming, $G_-$) solutions, related by
$$G_-(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}') = G_+(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}')^*. \tag{S.3}$$
Both satisfy (S.1); the equation is indifferent between them. This is the Ritz–Einstein point of 1909.

**Proposition 10.12S.2 (Forward amplitude).** *Atom $A$ emits the retarded solution $U_A(\mathbf{r}) = G_+(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}_A)$. With a reflecting barrier, the field on side $N$ is given by the Rayleigh–Sommerfeld integral over the aperture plane,*
$$U_A(\mathbf{r}_N) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\iint T(x,y)\,U_A(x,y,0^-)\,\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\!\left(\frac{e^{ikL_N}}{L_N}\right) dx\,dy, \qquad L_N = |\mathbf{r}_N - (x,y,0)|, \tag{S.4}$$
*and the probability that $B$ absorbs is proportional to $|U_A(\mathbf{r}_B)|^2$, the two-slit interference weight at $\mathbf{r}_B$.*

*Proof.* Kirchhoff–Rayleigh–Sommerfeld diffraction for an aperture in a plane screen (Born and Wolf §8.3); the restriction to $S_1 \cup S_2$ is the two-source coherence producing interference at $\mathbf{r}_B$. ∎

Denote the forward field on all of side $N$ by $U_A|_N$; it is an extended field determined on the entire half-space by the aperture data, and $U_A(\mathbf{r}_B)$ is one value of it.

**Theorem 10.12S.3 (Exact reversal requires the advanced solution).** *The time-reverse of the forward process is the solution $U_A^*$. On side $N$ it is the incoming, phase-conjugate field $U_A^*|_N$, which converges through the apertures onto $\mathbf{r}_A$; it is the advanced solution $G_-(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}_A)$ restricted to the two-slit geometry.*

*Proof.* Apply Theorem 10.12S.1 to the forward solution: $\psi_A(\mathbf{r},t) = U_A(\mathbf{r})e^{-i\omega t}$ maps to $\psi_A(\mathbf{r},-t)$, spatial part $U_A^*(\mathbf{r})$; by (S.3), $U_A^* = G_-(\cdot,\mathbf{r}_A)$ filtered by $T$, incoming on $\mathbf{r}_A$. ∎

**Theorem 10.12S.4 (A point emitter produces the retarded solution).** *Atom $B$ re-emitting produces $U_B(\mathbf{r}) = G_+(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}_B)$, the outgoing spherical wave centered on $\mathbf{r}_B$, its restriction to the aperture plane $z=0^+$ having phase fixed by the distance from $\mathbf{r}_B$ to each point of $S_1\cup S_2$.* Which of $G_\pm$ describes emission is a property of the emitter, and it is the retarded one.

**Theorem 10.12S.5 (Non-retracing).** *With a reflecting barrier, the re-emission from $B$ does not retrace the forward path. The field on side $M$ is*
$$U_B(\mathbf{r}_M) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\iint T(x,y)\,U_B(x,y,0^+)\,\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\!\left(\frac{e^{ikL_M}}{L_M}\right)dx\,dy, \tag{S.5}$$
*an extended diffraction pattern over side $M$. The probability that $A$ absorbs is proportional to $|U_B(\mathbf{r}_A)|^2$, and by Helmholtz reciprocity $U_B(\mathbf{r}_A) = U_A(\mathbf{r}_B)$, so the return probability equals the forward interference weight at $B$, which is strictly less than the total weight over side $M$.*

*Proof.* By Theorem 10.12S.3, exact retracing requires the boundary data $U_A^*|_{z=0^+}$, the conjugate of the forward field, an extended converging wavefront. By Theorem 10.12S.4, $B$ supplies $U_B|_{z=0^+}$, the restriction of an outgoing spherical wave. The two agree at no point in general; the overlap of $U_B|_N$ with $U_A^*|_N$ is the single complex number $\langle U_A^*, U_B\rangle \propto U_A(\mathbf{r}_B)^{*}$, one component of the continuum exact reversal requires. The remainder of $U_B$ diffracts afresh through the apertures and spreads over side $M$ by (S.5); reciprocity $G_+(\mathbf{r}_A,\mathbf{r}_B) = G_+(\mathbf{r}_B,\mathbf{r}_A)$ gives the return amplitude. ∎

**Corollary 10.12S.6 (The asymmetry is not geometric).** *The map from the field on side $M$ to the field on side $N$ through a reflecting two-slit partition is unitary on the transmitted subspace and is inverted exactly by the conjugate boundary data of Theorem 10.12S.3. The double-slit geometry therefore does not produce the irreversibility; its role is to spread the boundary data exact reversal requires over an extended aperture, so the mismatch between the required incoming wavefront and the outgoing wavefront a point atom supplies is visible at every point of the aperture plane.*

*Proof.* The reflecting barrier conserves the field norm; transmitted and reflected components are orthogonal projections. Phase conjugation of the transmitted field, propagated back, reconstructs $U_A$ on side $M$ (Theorem 10.12S.3); this is realized experimentally by time-reversal mirrors (Fink 1992). ∎

The reading in which the partition “discards information” so that geometry alone forbids reversal is therefore wrong: with a reflecting barrier nothing is discarded, the blocked component returns into side $M$ and remains in the system, and reversal fails for one reason only — the emitter is oriented.

**Theorem 10.12S.8 (Absorption adds non-unitarity).** *If the barrier absorbs, the blocked component $U_A\,[1-T]$ leaves the two-atom-plus-field system. The forward evolution restricted to that system is non-unitary, and the reverse process initiated by $B$ has no access to the absorbed component; exact reversal then fails even with conjugate boundary data on side $N$.*

*Proof.* The absorbed component is transferred to barrier degrees of freedom outside the system; a reversal prepared on side $N$ alone reconstructs at most the transmitted component $U_A\,T$, and the reconstructed field on side $M$ differs from $U_A$ by the back-propagation of $U_A[1-T]$. ∎

Theorems 10.12S.5 and 10.12S.8 are independent: the first holds with a reflecting barrier and no absorption, the second with conjugate boundary data and no point-emitter restriction. Only the first survives when everything removable is removed, and it is the one the thought experiment isolates.

**Theorem 10.12S.10 (Retarded selection is a sign choice).** *The retarded and advanced Green’s functions of the wave operator are the two boundary values of the same analytic function,*
$$\tilde G(\mathbf{k},\omega) = \frac{1}{k^2 - \omega^2/c^2}, \qquad G_{\rm ret} \leftrightarrow \omega \to \omega + i\varepsilon, \quad G_{\rm adv} \leftrightarrow \omega \to \omega - i\varepsilon, \tag{S.6}$$
*and the choice between them is the sign of the infinitesimal imaginary displacement of the frequency, equivalently the sign of the imaginary part of the time coordinate in the Fourier kernel $e^{-i\omega t}$.*

*Proof.* The poles of (S.6) at $\omega = \pm ck$ are displaced into the lower half $\omega$-plane by $+i\varepsilon$, so the inverse transform vanishes for $t<0$ (retarded); the opposite displacement gives vanishing for $t>0$ (advanced). ∎

This is the exact location of the asymmetry: the equation is symmetric (Theorem 10.12S.1), emission is oriented (Theorem 10.12S.4), and the orientation is the sign in (S.6). Every account of irreversibility at the level of a single emission event must supply that sign, and the accounts differ in what they add to the field equation to supply it — Ritz (1908–1909) adds a rule, use $G_+$; Wheeler–Feynman (1945) adds a perfect-absorber boundary condition on the totality of absorbers; the standard thermodynamic account adds a low-entropy initial condition. None derives the sign from a prior kinematic fact about events.

**Theorem 10.12S.11 (The Principle selects the retarded propagator).** *Under $dx_4/dt = ic$, the Fourier kernel of time evolution acquires the imaginary displacement of Theorem 10.12S.10 with the sign fixed by the $+$ of $+ic$, so that the Green’s function selected is $G_{\rm ret}$. Emission from a point atom is therefore outgoing as a consequence of the Principle.*

*Derivation.* The Principle identifies the direction of advance in $x_4$ with the direction of increasing $t$ through $x_4 = ict$: as $t$ increases, $x_4$ moves in the $+i$ direction. The Wick substitution $t \to -i\tau$, $\tau = x_4/c$, is under the Principle the coordinate identification between $t$ and the advance in $x_4$ rather than an analytic continuation (Theorem 6 of the Wick-necessity companion \[MG-Wick\]). The $+i\varepsilon$ prescription of (S.6) is the infinitesimal form of that identification: displacing $\omega$ by $+i\varepsilon$ is equivalent to giving $t$ a small imaginary part of sign fixed by the orientation of $x_4$-advance, and $+ic$ fixes that orientation as $+$. With the displacement sign fixed, Theorem 10.12S.10 yields $G_{\rm ret}$, and a point source then emits the outgoing wave $G_+$, which is Theorem 10.12S.4. ∎

**Corollary 10.12S.12 (The two-atom double slit exhibits the Principle’s orientation).** *In the two-atom experiment, non-retracing (10.12S.5) follows from point emission being outgoing (10.12S.4), which follows from 10.12S.11, which follows from $dx_4/dt = ic$. The experiment therefore exhibits, in a single emission event with no environment and no statistics, the time orientation that the Principle yields.* Under the Principle the same $+ic$ that orients emission generates the expanding McGucken Sphere from every event, and the interference weight $|U_A(\mathbf{r}_B)|^2$ of Proposition 10.12S.2 is the Born weight carried by the SO(3)-Haar measure on that Sphere (Remark 7.17), so in this system the orientation of emission and the interference weight at $B$ have a common origin.

The comparison of accounts is set out in Table 10.12S.A, McGucken far-left.

  Account                          What is added                                Level                        Sign origin         In two-atom system
  -------------------------------- -------------------------------------------- ---------------------------- ------------------- -----------------------------------------
  McGucken, $dx_4/dt = ic$         One kinematic statement about every event    Prior to Green’s functions   The $+$ in $+ic$    Yes (Theorem 10.12S.11)

  Ritz, retarded-only              A rule: use $G_+$                            Green’s-function level       Postulated          Yes, as postulate
