## XII. The Feynman Path Integral as the 3D Shadow of x₄'s Expanding Wavefront: The Geometric Content of "Every Path"

### XII.1 Feynman's mystery and its dissolution

Richard Feynman's 1948 reformulation of quantum mechanics expressed the propagator as a sum over all paths connecting an initial event A to a final event B, with each path weighted by exp(iS/ℏ) where S is the classical action [Feynman1948]:

$$K(B;A) = \int \mathcal{D}x(t)\, \exp\!\left(\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_A^B L\,dt\right).$$

The path integral is calculationally equivalent to the Schrödinger and Heisenberg formulations and has become the standard tool of quantum field theory. Yet the *physical* content of "the particle follows every path" has remained mysterious for nearly eighty years. Feynman himself acknowledged the strangeness: in his Nobel lecture he described the procedure as "summing over histories" and offered no underlying mechanism for *why* nature should compute amplitudes by integrating over an infinite continuum of spatial paths, most of which the classical particle never traverses.

The McGucken framework supplies the missing physical content — and supplies it in a form that the author wishes to state in his own words, because the formulation is novel and the geometric reading it captures is the substantive content of the present section:

> **Author's statement of the geometric content of Feynman's "every path."** Consider a photon propagating on the spherically symmetric expanding wavefront of x₄. Feynman has always stated that a particle follows every path. This is because x₄'s expansion represents an expanding nonlocality, and thus every point on that nonlocality is the photon's path — the photon's position is always on the expanding surface of nonlocality. Thus, to us in 3D, it seems as if the photon is following every single possible path, which we see as being every single possible radius of the expanding sphere.

This is the structural reading. The remainder of the section develops it formally, situates it within the existing derivation chain of the McGucken corpus [MG-PathIntegral, MG-FeynmanDiagrams, MG-QM], and shows that it strengthens Propositions III.1 (Born rule), V.1 (apparent collapse as cross-section reading), and VIII.1 (nonlocality from null-surface identity) of the present paper.

### XII.2 The McGucken Sphere as the Geometric Locus of "Every Path"

A photon emitted at event A creates a McGucken Sphere Σ₊(A) — the spherically symmetric forward null surface centered on A and expanding at velocity ic from A in the four-dimensional manifold. By the structural geometry of dx₄/dt = ic [MG-Proof, §3], every point on Σ₊(A) is null-separated from A: the line element ds² between A and any event on Σ₊(A) vanishes, and the entire wavefront is x₄-coincident with the emission event in the geometric sense established throughout the McGucken corpus [MG-Nonloc, §I]. The McGucken Sphere is not a probability cloud, not a "many photons" superposition, and not an ensemble of trajectories. It is one geometric object — one expanding null surface — and the photon's geometric extent in 4D *is* the entire surface.

The structural identification follows immediately:

**Definition XII.1 (McGucken Sphere as path-integral locus).** *The four-dimensional locus on which the photon resides between emission at A and detection at B is the union of all points P on the expanding McGucken Sphere Σ₊(A) such that B lies on the future null surface Σ₊(P). This locus is, by construction, the set of all spatial paths from A to B that lie along null wavefronts.*

The 3D projection of this 4D fact is precisely what Feynman's path integral computes. From the 3D perspective at observer time t, the photon appears to have explored every spatial path connecting A to B — because in 4D it was geometrically present on the entire expanding wavefront, and the projection onto the 3D spatial slice Σ\_t makes the wavefront's geometric extent look like an integration over spatial trajectories.

The "every path" of Feynman is the geometric continuum of points on the McGucken Sphere's wavefront. The mystery dissolves because the foundational object is geometric: the photon really is on every point of the expanding null surface, so the "sum over paths" is a literal description of the wavefront's geometric extent in 4D, not an arbitrary calculational prescription.

### XII.3 Formal derivation: the path integral as a theorem of dx₄/dt = ic

The formal derivation has been developed in the prior corpus through four propositions [MG-PathIntegral]. We restate them here in the structure required by the present paper, with cross-references to the existing derivation.

**Proposition XII.1 (Huygens' principle from x₄-spherical expansion).** *The McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic asserts that x₄ advances spherically symmetrically from every spacetime event at rate c. The three-dimensional cross-section at observer time t from emission event p₀ is the McGucken Sphere Σ₊(p₀) of radius c(t − t₀) centered at the spatial location of p₀. This sphere is geometrically the forward light cone of p₀ and structurally the carrier of Huygens' secondary wavelet construction. Huygens' principle is therefore a theorem of dx₄/dt = ic, not an independent postulate.* [Cf. MG-PathIntegral, Proposition L1.]

**Proposition XII.2 (Iterated Huygens generates all paths).** *Divide the time interval [t\_i, t\_f] into N intervals of duration ε = (t\_f − t\_i)/N. By Proposition XII.1, at the end of each interval the wavefront from any preceding event has expanded into a McGucken Sphere of radius cε. Applying Huygens' principle at each step produces a continuous chain of intermediate positions q₁, q₂, …, q\_{N−1}, with each q\_k lying on the McGucken Sphere centered on q\_{k−1}. In the limit N → ∞, the set of all such chains is, by the standard density argument, the set of all continuous paths from q\_i to q\_f. The Feynman sum over paths is therefore geometrically the sum over chains of McGucken Spheres.* [Cf. MG-PathIntegral, Proposition L2.]

**Proposition XII.3 (Accumulated x₄-phase is the Feynman weight).** *For a particle of rest mass m moving with three-velocity v, the four-velocity norm u^μu\_μ = −c² fixes the x₄-advance rate at dx₄/dt = ic/γ where γ = (1 − v²/c²)^{−1/2}. The x₄-oscillation at the Compton frequency ω\_C = mc²/ℏ, carried by the rest-mass phase factor exp(−imc²τ/ℏ) of [MG-QM, Theorem 5] along proper time τ with dτ = dt/γ, accumulates a phase per coordinate interval ε of*

$$\Delta\phi = \exp\!\left(-\,\frac{i\, mc^2 \gamma^{-1}\, \epsilon}{\hbar}\right).$$

*In the non-relativistic limit v/c ≪ 1, the expansion γ⁻¹ ≈ 1 − v²/(2c²) gives*

$$mc^2\gamma^{-1} \approx mc^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2.$$

*The first term mc² contributes a global phase exp(−imc²ε/ℏ) absorbed by rephasing; the second term, entering with the overall minus sign, contributes exp(+i·½mv²·ε/ℏ) = exp(+iTε/ℏ) with T = ½mv² the kinetic energy. Adding a potential V(q) by minimal coupling (which enters the energy with the opposite sign to the kinetic term) yields the short-interval phase*

$$\Delta\phi = \exp\!\left(\frac{i\epsilon}{\hbar}(T - V)\right) = \exp\!\left(\frac{i\epsilon}{\hbar} L_{\mathrm{classical}}\right).$$

*Integrated over the path, the accumulated phase is*

$$\phi[\mathrm{path}] = \exp\!\left(\frac{i}{\hbar}\int L_{\mathrm{classical}}\,dt\right) = \exp\!\left(\frac{iS[\mathrm{path}]}{\hbar}\right).$$

[Cf. MG-PathIntegral, Proposition L3.] The same factor $i\hbar$ that appears in the phase $\exp(iS/\hbar)$ is, in the operator language of §XIII.9, the multiplicative factor in the quantum McGucken operator $\hat{M} = i\hbar D_M$. The path-integral phase and the canonical-quantization $i\hbar$ are therefore two readings of the same source quantity: the perpendicularity marker $i$ in $D_M = \partial_t + ic\partial_{x_4}$ together with the quantum of $x_4$-oscillation $\hbar$ [MG-Constants, MG-McGuckenOperator]. The co-generation theorem of §XIII.10 establishes that the path-integral side and the operator-algebra side are not two separate formulations of quantum mechanics but two derivative consequences of the single source-pair $(\mathcal{M}_G, D_M)$.

**Proposition XII.4 (Feynman path integral as continuum limit).** *Composing the iterated Huygens propagation of Proposition XII.2 with the accumulated phase of Proposition XII.3 and taking N → ∞ yields*

$$K(q_f, t_f; q_i, t_i) = \int \mathcal{D}x(t)\, \exp\!\left(\frac{i}{\hbar}S[x(t)]\right).$$

*The Feynman path integral is therefore a theorem of dx₄/dt = ic.* [Cf. MG-PathIntegral, Proposition L4.] **∎**

The four propositions together establish the formal derivation. What the author's statement above adds — and what the present section is centrally concerned with — is the *physical reading* of the formal result: the "every path" is the expanding null surface of the McGucken Sphere; the integration measure 𝒟x(t) is the geometric extent of that surface in 4D; the phase exp(iS/ℏ) is the accumulated x₄-advance along each path with i the perpendicularity marker of x₄ and ℏ the quantum of x₄'s oscillation.

### XII.4 The interpretation: every path is every point on x₄'s expanding nonlocality

The author's statement deserves explicit unpacking, as it captures the structural reading that distinguishes the McGucken account from all prior treatments of the path integral.

**The expanding surface of nonlocality.** In the McGucken framework, x₄'s spherically symmetric expansion at velocity ic from every event constitutes an expanding surface of nonlocality: every point on the wavefront Σ₊(A) is x₄-coincident with the emission event A, and therefore every point on the wavefront is, in the geometric sense of the First Law of Nonlocality [MG-Nonloc], part of the same locality as A. The expansion is not "the photon moving away from A"; it is "the photon's geometric extent growing in 4D, with every point on the growing null surface continuing to share the original locality of A through x₄-coincidence."

**Every point on that nonlocality is the photon's path.** Because the photon is geometrically extended along the entire wavefront, and because every point on the wavefront is part of the same nonlocality as the emission event, the photon's "position" in the standard 3D-particle sense does not exist as a single point. The photon's position *is* the entire expanding null surface. Each point on the surface is, from the photon's geometric standpoint, equally its location.

**The 3D shadow.** Observers in 3D view the photon through the spatial slice Σ\_t at their instantaneous time. The 3D cross-section of the McGucken Sphere is a 2-sphere of radius c(t − t\_A) centered on A's spatial location. From the observer's restricted viewpoint, the photon appears to have "explored" every point on this 2-sphere — every spatial route from A to that point — because in 4D the photon was indeed geometrically present on the entire wavefront as it expanded through every such point.

**Every single possible radius.** The author's phrase "every single possible radius of the expanding sphere" captures the spatial-trajectory reading precisely. A radial line from A's spatial location to any point P on the 3D sphere of radius c(t − t\_A) is a geometric path along which the wavefront passed through every intermediate radius r ∈ [0, c(t − t\_A)]. The "every path" of Feynman is, in 3D, the continuum of radial trajectories along which the wavefront expanded — and the path integral's integration measure 𝒟x(t) is the angular continuum of these radii together with the temporal continuum of intermediate wavefronts.

This is the structural content of the McGucken reading of the path integral. The question "why does nature compute amplitudes by integrating over all paths?" is answered by the geometry: the integration over paths is the 3D shadow of the expanding 4D wavefront, so the path integral describes the wavefront's geometric extent rather than implementing a computational prescription over trajectories the particle never traverses.

### XII.5 Reinforcement of Proposition III.1: the Born rule

The geometric reading of the path integral reinforces Proposition III.1 of §III in a structural respect. Proposition III.1 establishes the Born rule P = |ψ|² through three pieces — complex character of ψ from i as perpendicularity marker, quadratic exponent from C1–C4, and SO(3) Haar-measure shape from spherical symmetry. The path integral reading sharpens the third piece.

The amplitude ψ at a spatial point B at time t is, by the propagator construction, the path integral over all paths from A to B:

$$\psi(B,t) = \int \mathcal{D}x(t)\, \exp\!\left(\frac{i}{\hbar}S[x(t)]\right)\,\psi(A, t_A).$$

The probability density at B is |ψ(B,t)|². The geometric content: ψ(B,t) is the amplitude of the McGucken Sphere wavefront at the point B in 3D; |ψ(B,t)|² is the SO(3)-Haar-weighted geometric measure of the wavefront's contribution to the spherical expansion at the radius corresponding to B.

The forced character of the squared exponent now has a sharper structural source. The path integral's amplitude is a *complex* quantity because the phase exp(iS/ℏ) is complex; the i in the phase is the same i as in dx₄/dt = ic, the perpendicularity marker of x₄. The probability density must be a *real, positive* quantity formed from this complex amplitude. The unique rotation-invariant real positive density on the McGucken Sphere's wavefront cross-section is the squared modulus |ψ|² — and the path integral construction makes the geometric origin explicit: the squared modulus measures the wavefront's geometric "size" at the radius B, with the SO(3)-Haar measure providing the rotation-invariant weighting.

The path integral and the Born rule are thus two readings of the same geometric structure: the path integral computes ψ as the wavefront's amplitude at a point; the Born rule computes |ψ|² as the wavefront's geometric measure at that point. Both descend from dx₄/dt = ic; their consistency is automatic because they derive from the same structural facts.

### XII.6 Reinforcement of Proposition V.1: apparent collapse as cross-section reading

The geometric reading of the path integral also reinforces Proposition V.1, which establishes that apparent wave function collapse R is the 3D spatial cross-section reading of an x₄-extended state evolving unitarily.

In the path integral framework, the photon's "every path" is the entire wavefront of the McGucken Sphere — the expanding null surface in 4D. When the photon is detected at a specific pixel P on a screen, the standard interpretation of collapse asserts that the wavefunction has reduced from a spread state to a localized state at P. The McGucken framework rejects this interpretation: nothing has collapsed. The McGucken Sphere has simply intersected the detector's 3D spatial slice at the specific pixel P. Every other pixel on the screen was equally a point on the wavefront's geometric extent — every other pixel was a spatial location where the wavefront geometrically passed — but the observer's local cross-section at the moment of detection happened to intersect the wavefront at P rather than at another pixel.

The path integral makes this geometric reading vivid. The "every path" that contributes to the amplitude at each pixel is the same wavefront, viewed from the perspective of each pixel. The amplitude ψ(P, t) at pixel P is the path integral from A to P; the amplitude ψ(P', t) at any other pixel P' is the path integral from A to P'. Both are well-defined; both are non-zero (for non-shadowed pixels); both correspond to real geometric content of the wavefront at the corresponding radius. The observer's restricted access to the 3D cross-section at the detection moment selects one pixel — the one the wavefront's geometric centroid happens to land at, weighted by the Born-rule probability |ψ|² — but the others were equally part of the four-dimensional state.

The collapse therefore is not a separate dynamical event. It is the geometric fact that a 4D wavefront intersects a 3D spatial slice at one configuration, with the configuration determined by the SO(3)-Haar-weighted geometric extent of the wavefront. Proposition V.1 already establishes this; the path integral reading shows that the *every-path* construction of standard quantum mechanics is precisely the construction that gives the multi-radial geometric content from which the cross-section selection is made.

### XII.7 Reinforcement of Proposition VIII.1: nonlocality from the shared wavefront

The geometric reading of the path integral finally reinforces Proposition VIII.1, which establishes that quantum nonlocality is the geometric consequence of x₄-mediated correlation through the six-sense null-surface identity of the McGucken Sphere [MG-Nonloc].

Two photons emitted in an entangled state from a common source share a common McGucken Sphere — they are at different points on the expanding null surface from the same emission event. The path integral for each photon is the integral over all paths from the source to that photon's detection event; both path integrals are integrals over the same wavefront, viewed from the perspective of each detection event.

The author's phrase — "x₄'s expansion represents an expanding nonlocality, and thus every point on that nonlocality is the photon's path" — applies *jointly* to both photons of an entangled pair. Both photons' "every paths" lie on the same expanding nonlocality. The correlations between their detection outcomes are not the result of faster-than-light signaling; they are the consequence of being two cross-sectional readings of the same 4D wavefront.

The path integral reading thereby supplies a vivid geometric content for Bell-type correlations: when Alice's photon "follows every path" and Bob's photon "follows every path," the geometric content is that both photons' paths lie on the same expanding McGucken Sphere from the source, and their detection events are two cross-sections of the same 4D structure. The cos²(θ/2) angular dependence of the correlations is the SO(3)-Haar measure on the angular relationship between the two cross-sections — the same Haar measure that grounds the Born rule in Proposition III.1 and that grounds the path-integral measure in Proposition XII.4.

### XII.7.1 Theorem XII.A: The deep unification — null-distance equality, quantum nonlocality, and quantum probability as one geometric fact

Section §XII.7 establishes that Bell-type correlations are the SO(3)-Haar measure on the angular relationship between two cross-sections of the same expanding McGucken Sphere. The present subsection states the deeper structural identification: *relativistic null-distance equality* (the fact, established in special relativity, that null vectors along a light cone all have zero proper length) and *quantum nonlocality* (the fact, established in quantum mechanics, that entangled systems exhibit correlations stronger than any local hidden-variable theory permits) are **the same geometric fact** about the McGucken Sphere — and *quantum probability* (the Born rule P = |ψ|²) is the *natural child* of that geometric fact, not an independent mystery. This is the deepest structural unification of relativistic and quantum content in the present paper.

#### XII.7.1.1 The four geometric features of the McGucken Sphere surface

Recall (Convention I.5.2; Proposition VIII.1) that the McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_+(p_0)$ at proper time $\tau$ after emission event $p_0$ is the spherically symmetric wavefront expanding at velocity $c$ from $p_0$. Every point on the surface $\Sigma_+(p_0)$ has four geometric properties that are conventionally treated as distinct features of separate areas of physics, but that are structurally one and the same:

**(a) Null distance in relativity.** Every point on $\Sigma_+(p_0)$ is connected to $p_0$ by a null worldline. The relativistic line element $ds^2 = -c^2 dt^2 + d\mathbf x^2$ evaluates to zero along every radius of the Sphere because $|d\mathbf x| = c\, dt$ at every point on the wavefront. *All points on the McGucken Sphere are at null distance from the emission event* — they are all "equidistant" in the relativistic sense, with that distance being identically zero. The wavefront is the locus of null-distance equality.

**(b) Spatial nonlocality in quantum mechanics.** From the 3D perspective of any observer at proper time $\tau$, the McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_+(p_0)$ is a *spatially extended* 2-sphere of radius $c\tau$. The photon emitted at $p_0$ is "somewhere on" this 2-sphere, but the 2-sphere is spread across a spatial region that may extend over astronomical distances. *In 3D, the photon is nonlocal: it is everywhere on the 2-sphere at once.* The nonlocality is not a peculiarity of quantum mechanics but a direct geometric consequence of x₄'s spherically symmetric expansion at velocity c. The 2-sphere is the 3D shadow of the 4D wavefront.

**(c) Path equivalence in the path integral.** From the path-integral perspective (Propositions XII.1–XII.4), every radius of the McGucken Sphere from $p_0$ to a point $q$ on $\Sigma_+(p_0)$ is an admissible path that the photon "takes." The set of all such radii is geometrically a one-parameter family of trajectories parameterised by the angular direction $(\theta, \phi)$ on the 2-sphere. *Every radius is an equally weighted path in Feynman's "sum over all paths"* — they are all of the same length in relativistic terms (zero proper length, null distance), and they are all weighted by the same accumulated x₄-phase $\exp(iS/\hbar)$ (with $S$ vanishing for null worldlines, so the weight is unity for every radius).

**(d) The Born-rule angular distribution.** The probability of finding the photon at angular direction $(\theta, \phi)$ on the Sphere is $|\psi(\theta, \phi)|^2$, weighted by the SO(3)-Haar measure $\sin\theta\, d\theta\, d\phi$ (Proposition III.1, Piece 3). For a spherically symmetric emission, $|\psi|^2$ is uniform over the 2-sphere, so the photon can be detected anywhere on the Sphere with equal angular probability. *The Born-rule probability density is the angular-direction measure of which radius the photon's detection event occurs along.*

These four features — null distance (relativity), spatial nonlocality (QM), path equivalence (path integral), and Born-rule angular distribution (probability) — are conventionally treated as belonging to four different domains of physics: special relativity, the foundations of quantum mechanics, Feynman's path-integral formalism, and quantum measurement theory. They appear in separate textbooks, are presented under separate names, and are typically attributed to separate physical mechanisms. *In the McGucken framework, all four features are geometric properties of one and the same object: the surface of the McGucken Sphere.*

#### XII.7.1.2 Theorem XII.A: The geometric unification

**Theorem XII.A (Null distance, nonlocality, path equivalence, and Born probability are one geometric fact).** *Under the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic, the relativistic null-distance equality of all points on the light cone from an emission event $p_0$, the quantum nonlocality of the photon's position on the 2-sphere at any observer time, the path equivalence of all radii in the Feynman path integral over wavefronts from $p_0$, and the Born-rule angular distribution of detection events on the 2-sphere are the same geometric fact: every point on the McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_+(p_0)$ is geometrically equivalent under the SO(3) symmetry of x₄'s spherical expansion from $p_0$, with the equivalence carrying simultaneously the relativistic content (null distance), the quantum-mechanical content (nonlocality), the path-integral content (path equivalence), and the probabilistic content (Born-rule angular measure).*

**Proof.** The proof is the unification of four geometric statements about the McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_+(p_0)$.

*Step 1 (null distance).* By dx₄/dt = ic, the wavefront from $p_0$ expands at velocity $c$ in spherically symmetric fashion. At observer proper time $\tau$, the wavefront occupies the 2-sphere $\Sigma_+(p_0; \tau)$ of radius $c\tau$ centered on $p_0$ in spatial coordinates. Any point $q \in \Sigma_+(p_0; \tau)$ is connected to $p_0$ by a null worldline (light-cone radius); the relativistic line element along this worldline gives $ds^2 = -c^2(d\tau)^2 + (c\, d\tau)^2 = 0$. *All points on $\Sigma_+(p_0; \tau)$ are at relativistic null-distance from $p_0$.*

*Step 2 (spatial nonlocality).* The 2-sphere $\Sigma_+(p_0; \tau)$ is, in the 3D spatial reading at proper time $\tau$, a spatially-extended surface of radius $c\tau$. The photon's spatial position is *on* this 2-sphere but not at any single point of it. *The photon is spatially nonlocal: it is everywhere on the 2-sphere at once.* The spatial extent of the nonlocality is $4\pi (c\tau)^2$, which grows quadratically in $\tau$ and may be astronomical for $\tau \gg \text{laboratory scale}$.

*Step 3 (path equivalence).* By Propositions XII.1–XII.4, every radius from $p_0$ to a point $q \in \Sigma_+(p_0; \tau)$ is an admissible Feynman path. The set of all radii is parameterised by $(\theta, \phi)$, the angular direction on the 2-sphere; every radius has the same null length (Step 1), the same x₄-phase $\exp(iS/\hbar) = 1$ along null worldlines (with $S = 0$), and the same SO(3)-Haar measure $\sin\theta\, d\theta\, d\phi/(4\pi)$. *Every radius is an equally-weighted Feynman path.*

*Step 4 (Born-rule angular distribution).* By Proposition III.1, the probability density of detecting the photon at angular direction $(\theta, \phi)$ on the 2-sphere is $|\psi(\theta, \phi)|^2$ weighted by the SO(3)-Haar measure $\sin\theta\, d\theta\, d\phi/(4\pi)$. For a spherically-symmetric emission, $|\psi|^2$ is uniform on the 2-sphere, and the photon is found with equal angular probability at any point on the wavefront. *The Born-rule probability of detection at $(\theta, \phi)$ is the angular measure of the direction along which the photon's detection event occurs.*

*Step 5 (identification of the four steps).* The four geometric facts of Steps 1–4 are not four separate properties of the McGucken Sphere; they are four readings of one property — the SO(3) symmetry of x₄'s spherical expansion from $p_0$. Every point on the wavefront is geometrically equivalent under this symmetry: equivalent in null distance (Step 1), equivalent in spatial accessibility (Step 2 — the photon is at any of these points), equivalent in path weighting (Step 3 — every radius is equally weighted), and equivalent in angular probability (Step 4 — the Haar measure is uniform over the directions). *The four conventionally-distinct features are the same geometric equivalence read in four physical languages: relativistic, quantum-mechanical, path-integral, and probabilistic.* **∎**

#### XII.7.1.3 The structural payoff: quantum probability as the natural child of relativistic null-distance equality

Theorem XII.A has a structural reading that exalts the relationship between relativity and quantum mechanics from "two foundational theories awaiting unification" to "two readings of one geometric structure."

The fact that the relativistic null-distance equality and the quantum-mechanical nonlocality are the same geometric content of the McGucken Sphere means that *quantum probability is the natural child of relativistic null-distance equality*. The argument runs:

1. Relativity establishes that all points on the light cone from an emission event are at null distance (proper length zero) from that event.
2. Equivalence in null distance is geometric equivalence: under the SO(3) symmetry of the spherical expansion, all points on $\Sigma_+(p_0; \tau)$ are interchangeable.
3. Geometric equivalence forces a uniform probability measure over the equivalence class — by Haar's theorem [Haar1933], the unique SO(3)-invariant probability measure on the 2-sphere is the angular Haar measure $\sin\theta\, d\theta\, d\phi/(4\pi)$.
4. The uniform Haar measure is the Born rule's angular distribution (Proposition III.1, Piece 3): $P(\theta, \phi) = |\psi(\theta, \phi)|^2 \sin\theta/(4\pi)$ with $|\psi|^2$ uniform for a spherically symmetric emission.

*Therefore: relativistic null-distance equality forces a uniform probability measure on the wavefront 2-sphere, and this measure is the Born rule's angular distribution.* On this reading the Born rule's angular form is the natural SO(3)-invariant probability measure on the equivalence class of points at null distance from the emission event, rather than an independent angular postulate. (The step from this invariant geometric measure to *detection probability* is Theorem 7.4 of [MG-BornCentury], the Born density as the forward–conjugate x₄-overlap, with the conjugate factor supplied by Theorems 7.7 and 7.11 of [MG-BornCentury]; §III.4.5.) Without relativistic null-distance equality, there would be no equivalence class; without the equivalence class, no uniform measure; without the uniform measure, no Born-rule angular distribution.

Quantum probability is therefore *forced* by relativistic content. The two foundations of twentieth-century physics — special relativity and quantum mechanics — are not two independent theories; they are two readings of the McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_+(p_0)$ generated by dx₄/dt = ic at the emission event.

The deepest content of Theorem XII.A is the structural identity:

  *Relativity's null-distance equality on the light cone* = *Quantum mechanics' nonlocality of the photon's position* = *Path integral's path equivalence over the wavefront* = *Quantum probability's Born-rule angular distribution on the 2-sphere*.

#### XII.7.1.5 The formal structural development: sphere-surface x₄-locality, the Uniqueness Theorem, and the Identity Theorem

Theorem XII.A asserts that null distance, nonlocality, path equivalence, and Born probability are four readings of one geometric fact. The deeper formal development — that this single fact has a name (*sphere-surface x₄-locality*), that the McGucken Sphere is the *unique* surface configuration consistent with the five empirical features it sustains, and that Lorentz invariance and quantum nonlocality are formally *the same theorem* — is developed in [MG-LorentzNonlocality, §§3–7]. We import the formal content here, retaining the proof structure at the level needed for the present paper.

**Definition (Sphere-surface x₄-locality, [MG-LorentzNonlocality §2.3]).** Let $p_0$ be an emission event and let $q \in \Sigma_+(p_0; t)$ be a point on the McGucken-Sphere surface at observer time $t > t_0$. The *accumulated x₄-advance of q relative to $p_0$*, denoted $X_4(q; p_0)$, is the advance X₄ = ∫ic dτ accumulated along the radial null geodesic from $p_0$ to $q$ — proper time along the geodesic up to the factor ic (Appendix A (R4)). Along a null geodesic dτ = 0 pointwise: a photon's four-velocity budget is allocated entirely to spatial motion, its Sphere-tangent share — the standard time-dilation factor c·dτ/dt — is v_{x₄} = 0 (Convention I.5.2, four-fold ontology, State 2, absolute rest in x₄), and the coordinate rate dx₄/dt = ic holds at every event of the geodesic (Appendix A (R1)). The accumulated advance along the photon's null worldline is therefore identically zero:

$$X_4(q; p_0) = 0 \;\;\; \text{for every } q \in \Sigma_+(p_0; t), \text{ for every } t > t_0.$$

The McGucken Sphere surface $\Sigma_+(p_0; t)$ is the locus of points sharing accumulated x₄-advance zero relative to the emission event $p_0$, despite their 3-spatial separation $|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0| = c(t - t_0) > 0$. The surface is *spatially extended* yet *x₄-coincident*: all points carry the accumulated x₄-advance of the apex $p_0$. This structural property — that the future-null-cone surface of every event is x₄-coincident with the event — is *sphere-surface x₄-locality*.

The equivalent metric reading: the spacetime interval between $p_0$ and $q \in \Sigma_+(p_0; t)$ is

$$ds^2(p_0, q) = -c^2(t - t_0)^2 + |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0|^2 = 0$$

since $q$ lies on the future null cone of $p_0$. With $x_4 = ict$, the contribution of the timelike sector to the squared-distance, $-c^2(t-t_0)^2$, exactly cancels the spatial contribution $|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0|^2$, so the x₄-coordinate-differential and the spatial-coordinate-differential cancel along the null geodesic. *The relativistic null-distance identity is the geometric content of sphere-surface x₄-locality.*

**Theorem XII.A.1 (Uniqueness of the McGucken Sphere, after [MG-LorentzNonlocality, Theorem 1]).** *The McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_+(p)$ with x₄-local surface generated at every event p by dx₄/dt = ic is the **unique** surface configuration of the future null cone of p simultaneously consistent with: (i) saturation of the Tsirelson bound $|\text{CHSH}| \leq 2\sqrt{2}$; (ii) rotational invariance of entanglement correlations under SO(3); (iii) the absence of a fundamental entanglement-distance limit in vacuum; (iv) Lorentz invariance of the speed of light at the precision of gamma-ray-burst timing constraints; and (v) self-replication of the wavefront via Huygens' Principle.*

The uniqueness is established in [MG-LorentzNonlocality §3] through five Failure-Mode Propositions (Propositions A–E): each of five plausible alternative surface configurations breaks at least one of the five empirical features, with the McGucken Sphere being the unique configuration that satisfies all five simultaneously. We summarize the failure modes:

| Failure mode | Modification | What breaks |
|:-------------|:-------------|:------------|
| Proposition A | Random x₄-scatter on the surface | Tsirelson saturation and the Born rule fail (SO(3)-Haar measure does not produce coherent correlations) |
| Proposition B | Systematic x₄-gradient on the surface | Rotational invariance of correlations fails |
| Proposition C | Finite x₄-thickness of the surface | Entanglement-distance limit appears in vacuum |
| Proposition D | Directional rate-anisotropy $c(\hat{n})$ | Lorentz invariance of c fails (empirical bound $E_{\text{LIV}} > 7.6 M_{\text{Pl}}$ from GRB timing) |
| Proposition E | Failure of Huygens self-replication | Wavefront cannot propagate (causal propagation breaks at the first Planck tick) |

The Uniqueness Theorem is the *converse* statement of these five failure modes: the McGucken Sphere is the unique surface that violates *none* of (i)–(v). The five empirical features that quantum mechanics and relativity have established as foundational are jointly *forcing* the McGucken Sphere as their unique geometric carrier.

**Theorem XII.A.2 (Identity of Lorentz invariance and quantum nonlocality, after [MG-LorentzNonlocality, Theorem 2]).** *Under the McGucken Principle, the Lorentz invariance of the future light cone and the saturation of the Tsirelson bound by quantum entanglement are two readings of a single geometric fact — sphere-surface x₄-locality. Specifically:*

*(i) The the dx₄/dt = ic Algebraic Channel (algebraic-symmetry) reading of sphere-surface x₄-locality produces the Lorentz invariance of c through the invariance of dx₄/dt = ic under boosts.*

*(ii) The the dx₄/dt = ic Geometric Channel (geometric-propagation) reading of sphere-surface x₄-locality produces the Tsirelson saturation at $|\text{CHSH}| = 2\sqrt{2}$ through the SO(3)-Haar measure on the x₄-coherent sphere surface.*

*(iii) Breaking sphere-surface x₄-locality breaks both readings simultaneously: any failure mode (Propositions A–E above) that breaks one reading also breaks the other. The two empirical features are not independent facts that happen to coexist consistently; they are the Algebraic Channel and the Geometric Channel projections of the same underlying geometric fact.*

**Proof sketch.** Step 1: The the Algebraic Channel lemma of [MG-LorentzNonlocality §5.1] establishes that the Algebraic Channel's invariance content of $\Sigma_+(p)$ produces the Lorentz invariance of $c$. Step 2: The the Geometric Channel lemma establishes that the Geometric Channel's propagation content of $\Sigma_+(p)$ produces the Tsirelson saturation at $2\sqrt{2}$. Step 3: Both readings depend on sphere-surface x₄-locality, and the joint-forcing lemma establishes that sphere-surface x₄-locality is jointly forced by the Algebraic Channel and the Geometric Channel contents of dx₄/dt = ic. Step 4 (co-failure under perturbation): If sphere-surface x₄-locality is broken in the manner of Proposition D (directional rate-anisotropy), the rate $dx_4/dt$ becomes direction-dependent. This breaks the Algebraic Channel (Lorentz invariance of $c$ fails: the rate is not boost-invariant). It *also* breaks the Geometric Channel (the SO(3)-Haar measure is well-defined only when $\Sigma_t(p)$ is a true 2-sphere of constant radius $c(t - t_0)$; under direction-dependent $c(\hat{n})$, the surface is a deformed shape with no SO(3) symmetry, the SO(3)-Haar measure does not exist, and the Tsirelson-saturation derivation of the Geometric Channel lemma fails). The two readings therefore co-fail under any perturbation of the kind Proposition D considers. **∎**

The Identity Theorem is the strongest statement of the structural unification of relativity and quantum mechanics in the McGucken corpus. *Lorentz invariance and quantum nonlocality are the same theorem read in two physical languages.* The pre-McGucken framing — Lorentz invariance as a constraint on quantum mechanics, with Bell-violating nonlocality as the puzzle that must remain consistent with Lorentz invariance — is structurally inverted: x₄-locality is the geometric fact; the apparent nonlocality of 3D physics is its shadow under projection onto the spatial slice.

#### XII.7.1.7 The First McGucken Law of Nonlocality

The Uniqueness Theorem (Theorem XII.A.1) and the Identity Theorem (Theorem XII.A.2) together supply the structural content to elevate the long-conjectural "principle of nonlocality" of quantum mechanics to a *theorem*. In the orthodox tradition, Bell-violating correlations between spatially separated systems have been described as nonlocal in a way that resists explanation — Einstein's 1935 "spooky action at a distance," Bell's 1990 "dirty theory," Shimony's "peaceful coexistence" puzzle. **Theorem XII.A.4 (First McGucken Law of Nonlocality, after [MG-LorentzNonlocality §7]).** *Under dx₄/dt = ic and the Uniqueness Theorem, every entangled pair traces back to a common past event $p_{\text{source}}$ whose McGucken Sphere $\Sigma_+(p_{\text{source}})$ has self-replicated outward at rate $+ic$, propagating x₄-phase coherence to both systems through a chain of secondary, tertiary, and higher-order Spheres each of which is itself generated by dx₄/dt = ic at its apex. The apparent nonlocality of the entangled pair is the 3-spatial shadow of the locality (sphere-surface x₄-coincidence) of their common past Sphere.*

**Plain-language statement.** *All nonlocality begins as locality.* Two entangled systems do not communicate faster than light; they share a *common past* on the surface of a McGucken Sphere generated at their joint emission event, and the locality of that past (every point on the Sphere is x₄-coincident with the apex) propagates forward via Huygens-iterated Sphere self-replication, with the locality preserved through every secondary Sphere. The 3-spatial separation of the two detection events is large; their separation in accumulated x₄-advance is zero; their detection-event correlations reflect the latter rather than the former. Spooky action at a distance is not spooky and is not action at a distance; it is the locality of a shared past in the fourth dimension.

The First McGucken Law of Nonlocality is presented as a *theorem* of dx₄/dt = ic, with formal proof in [MG-LorentzNonlocality §7.1], rather than as a metaphysical interpretation. The structural content: Bell-violating entanglement requires shared x₄-coherence (Step 1); shared x₄-coherence requires a common past Sphere (Step 2); the propagation occurs at rate $+ic$ (Step 3); the chain of intermediate Spheres carries the coherence forward via Huygens' Principle (Step 4). Each step is forced by the Axiom dx₄/dt = ic.

#### XII.7.1.9 Historical predecessors who got close

Three historical predecessors approached the McGucken identification without arriving at it [MG-LorentzNonlocality §10]:

**Costa de Beauregard (1953, 1976, 1977).** Costa de Beauregard's "cone-carries-the-correlation" interpretation [CostaDeBeauregard1953] argued that entanglement correlations propagate along the light cone, with retarded waves carrying the correlation forward and advanced waves carrying it backward to the source. The structural content was close to the McGucken reading: the light cone is the locus of correlation. Costa de Beauregard lacked the *physical-geometric content* of dx₄/dt = ic — what propagates along the cone, in what direction, and why the cone is x₄-coincident. The McGucken framework supplies the missing content.

**Penrose (1967 onward).** Penrose's twistor programme [Penrose1967] takes null structure as foundational: every massless particle's spacetime trajectory is a null line, and the natural geometric arena is the space of null lines (twistor space $\mathbb{CP}^3$). The structural content was close to the McGucken reading: null lines are foundational, and the twistor space encodes their geometry. Penrose lacked the *dynamical* content of dx₄/dt = ic — twistor space is static; the dynamical expansion of $x_4$ at velocity $c$ is what generates the null lines. [MG-Wick §13] establishes that Penrose's twistor space $\mathbb{CP}^3$ is the geometry of $x_4$'s expansion, with twistors arising as null lines on the McGucken manifold.

**Hardy (1992).** Hardy's "quantum theory without inequalities" [Hardy1992] is the closest formal predecessor: Hardy derived Tsirelson saturation from a structural-symmetry argument that did not require Lorentz invariance as a separate input. The McGucken framework's Identity Theorem is the deepening of Hardy's result: not merely "the symmetry that produces Tsirelson saturation is consistent with Lorentz invariance," but *the symmetry that produces Tsirelson saturation IS Lorentz invariance, read in a different physical language*. Hardy lacked the source-pair categorical primitive $(\mathcal{M}_G, D_M)$ and the foundational principle dx₄/dt = ic co-generating it (Theorem IX.0.A.4 of [MG-Duality]). The McGucken framework supplies these missing pieces.

*Why the identity claim required the dynamical $x_4$.* The structural identity of Lorentz invariance and quantum nonlocality could not be made before the dynamical content of dx₄/dt = ic was identified, because the static-coordinate reading of $x_4 = ict$ (Minkowski 1908, Pauli 1921, the textbook tradition) treats $x_4$ as a notational device with no physical content. Costa de Beauregard, Penrose, and Hardy each came close in different ways, but each lacked the physical-geometric content that dx₄/dt = ic supplies. The identity is forced *only* under the McGucken Principle's recognition that $x_4$ is a *dynamically expanding* dimension, with the expansion rate $ic$ being the physical content from which both Lorentz invariance (the Algebraic Channel) and quantum nonlocality (the Geometric Channel) descend.

#### XII.7.1.11 Response to the orthodox framing: "Path integrals are math, not a literal movie of nature"

The orthodox foundational position — articulated in numerous popular science treatments and academic papers, with a typical formulation being that "path integrals are mathematical regularizations needed to make the calculational tool work; the formalism isn't a direct ontological description; path integrals are math and not a literal movie of nature" — rests on the assumption that the path-integral procedure is a *calculational* device whose ontological status is unsettled. Different quantization procedures (canonical, geometric, path-integral, deformation) yield equivalent predictions; the orthodox question is: *which math determines the ontological commitments?*

The McGucken framework answers: *neither* the canonical formalism nor the path-integral formalism nor the geometric-quantization formalism is the foundational ontology; *the McGucken Principle dx₄/dt = ic is the foundational ontology*. All three quantization procedures are *projections* of that ontology onto different mathematical apparatus. Canonical quantization (Stone's theorem on time-translation invariance) reads dx₄/dt = ic through the Algebraic Channel (Theorem XIII.J, §XIII.11.1). Path-integral quantization (Huygens-iterated McGucken-Sphere expansion) reads dx₄/dt = ic through the Geometric Channel in Lorentzian signature (Propositions XII.1–XII.4). Geometric quantization (symplectic structure on phase space) reads dx₄/dt = ic through the McGucken Sphere's intrinsic symplectic structure as a generalised cotangent bundle (cf. Kostant 1970 [Kostant1970]; Souriau 1970 [Souriau1970]). All three are mathematically equivalent because all three are descriptions of the same physical-geometric content: the spherical expansion of $x_4$ at velocity $c$ from every event.

*The "math vs. ontology" question is therefore mis-posed.* It assumes that the ontological commitments come from the math, and that selecting one math over another commits the theorist to one ontology over another. Under the McGucken framework, the ontological commitment comes from the *physical principle* dx₄/dt = ic, and the three mathematical formalisms are equivalent precisely because they are three readings of one physical-geometric content. The path integral is not a "calculational regularization" or a "computational trick"; it is a *direct geometric description* of the spherical wavefront expanding at $+ic$ from every event, projected into 3D as the integration over all paths the photon's wavefront-surface contains.

On this reading the photon's "every path" describes the photon's actual 4D geometric extent rather than a heuristic. The photon surfs the expanding McGucken Sphere; its position is everywhere on the Sphere at once (Step 2 of Theorem XII.A); each radius of the Sphere is an equally-weighted path under the SO(3)-invariant Haar measure (Step 3); and the photon is detected at whichever radius the apparatus's McGucken–Wick rotation (Theorem X.D) happens to dominate at the measurement event. Feynman's 1948 "every path" interpretation, on this reading, describes what dx₄/dt = ic forces rather than serving as metaphor. The orthodox dismissal of "every path" as a calculational figure of speech — typified by the framing that "the path integral isn't a literal movie of nature" — is the dismissal of a structural fact whose physical content has been visible since Feynman 1948 [Feynman1948] but has been suppressed by the orthodox refusal to recognise the Geometric Channel geometric-propagation content of the Schrödinger equation as physically real (§X.14, the half-equation diagnosis).

The McGucken framework's structural correction is the claim that the physical-geometric content of dx₄/dt = ic underlies the quantum predictions the orthodox tradition has confirmed empirically, carrying definite physical commitments rather than functioning as an interpretive overlay. On this reading the path integral is a direct description of nature at the 4D level, with the 3D path-sum its observer-level shadow. The orthodox treatment of Feynman's "every path" as a calculational figure of speech corresponds, in this framework, to reading only the 3D shadow of what x₄ is doing.

### XII.8 The Wick rotation: path integral, Brownian motion, and Huygens unified

The path integral derivation of §XII.3 has an immediate companion in the McGucken treatment of Wick rotation [MG-Wick]. Under the substitution t → −iτ — equivalently, x₄ = ict → x₄ = cτ, replacing the imaginary fourth axis with a real Euclidean axis — the oscillatory phase exp(iS/ℏ) becomes the real Gaussian weight exp(−S\_E/ℏ), where S\_E is the Euclidean action. The Feynman path integral in real time becomes the diffusion kernel summing over Brownian paths in imaginary time.

The structural identification is striking: the Feynman path integral (quantum, real time), Brownian motion (thermal, imaginary time), and Huygens' wavelet construction (wave, geometric optics) are *the same geometric object* — spherically symmetric propagation in four-dimensional spacetime whose fourth axis advances at c. The three regimes are related by the analytic continuation x₄ = ict that *is* the McGucken Principle.

This unification grounds the structural reading further. The "every path" of Feynman is not a peculiar feature of quantum mechanics that has no classical analog — it is the same spherically symmetric expansion of x₄ that produces classical Huygens wavefronts in optics and diffusive paths in thermodynamics. The three readings differ only in the analytic-continuation status of x₄: imaginary x₄ (i.e., x₄ = ict) gives quantum interference; real x₄ (i.e., x₄ = cτ) gives Brownian diffusion; the SO(3) symmetry shared by both gives Huygens' wavefront construction in either regime.

### XII.9 Comparison with Feynman's original interpretation

Feynman's 1948 paper introduced the path integral as a postulate derived from Dirac's 1933 hint that the quantum amplitude is "analogous to" exp(iS/ℏ). Feynman did not claim a foundational source for the procedure; he treated it as an alternative axiomatization of quantum mechanics that recovered the Schrödinger equation in the short-time limit. Later treatments (e.g., Glimm and Jaffe's *Quantum Physics*; Zinn-Justin's *Quantum Field Theory and Critical Phenomena*; Polyakov's *Gauge Fields and Strings*) take the path integral as primitive and develop quantum field theory upon it.

In the McGucken framework, the path integral is a theorem of dx₄/dt = ic rather than a postulate, with the four-proposition derivation of §XII.3 supplying the formal chain. Beyond the formal derivation, the geometric reading of "every path" supplies the physical content that Feynman's original presentation lacked: the path integral is the 3D shadow of the 4D McGucken Sphere's expanding null surface, with the integration measure recording the surface's geometric extent and the phase recording the accumulated x₄-advance along each path.

This is structurally superior to Feynman's original interpretation in three respects, parallel to the three structural improvements identified for the Born rule in §III.3:

**(a)** The path integral acquires a foundational source. Where Feynman could only claim the procedure is consistent with experiment, the McGucken framework derives it from a single geometric postulate.

**(b)** The integration measure 𝒟x(t) acquires geometric content. Where standard treatments leave the measure as a formal symbol whose mathematical rigor remains contested (the path integral's measure-theoretic status is one of the open problems of mathematical physics), the McGucken framework identifies the measure as the geometric extent of the McGucken Sphere's expanding wavefront in 4D — a concrete, geometrically well-defined object.

**(c)** The phase exp(iS/ℏ) acquires geometric content. Where Feynman could only assert that the phase is exp(iS/ℏ), the McGucken framework derives it as the accumulated x₄-advance, with i the perpendicularity marker of x₄ and ℏ the quantum of x₄'s oscillation [MG-Constants, MG-Commut]. The phase is not an arbitrary formal weighting; it records a geometric fact about the manifold.

### XII.10 The path integral as theorem: structural placement in the present paper

The path integral has been treated as a theorem of dx₄/dt = ic since [MG-QM, Theorem 15]. The present section adds three things to the prior treatment:

**(i)** The formal four-proposition derivation is restated in the structural language of the present paper, with cross-references to Propositions III.1, V.1, and VIII.1.

**(ii)** The author's novel geometric reading — "every point on the expanding nonlocality is the photon's path" — is preserved verbatim and developed as the substantive interpretive content. This reading is, to the author's knowledge, original to the McGucken framework: no prior treatment of the path integral identifies the "every path" with the wavefront of an expanding fourth-dimensional null surface, or identifies the integration measure with the SO(3)-Haar-weighted geometric extent of that surface.

**(iii)** The reading is shown to reinforce three of the central propositions of the paper — the Born rule (Proposition III.1), the apparent-collapse-as-cross-section-reading (Proposition V.1), and the nonlocality-from-null-surface-identity (Proposition VIII.1) — by supplying a single geometric mechanism that unifies them.

The structural significance is that the path integral, the Born rule, the apparent collapse, and quantum nonlocality are *not four independent features of quantum mechanics*. They are four readings of one geometric fact: x₄ expands at velocity ic from every event, producing a spherically symmetric expanding null surface — the McGucken Sphere — whose geometric extent in 4D is the integration measure of the path integral, whose squared amplitude is the Born rule's probability density, whose 3D cross-section is the apparent collapse, and whose null-surface identity is the source of quantum nonlocality.

### XII.11 Summary

The Feynman path integral's "every path" is, in the McGucken framework, the geometric extent of the expanding McGucken Sphere — the spherically symmetric null surface that x₄'s expansion at velocity ic creates from every emission event. Every point on this surface is, by the geometric structure of dx₄/dt = ic, a point of the expanding nonlocality of the emission event. The photon's geometric extent in 4D is the entire surface; the photon's "every path" in the 3D shadow is the projection of this surface onto the observer's spatial slice.

This reading addresses the eighty-year question of "why does nature compute by summing over histories?" On the McGucken reading the sum over histories describes the geometric extent of the expanding wavefront rather than implementing a computation: the histories are radii of the expanding sphere; the integration measure is the SO(3)-Haar-weighted geometric extent of the wavefront; the phase is the accumulated x₄-advance with i the perpendicularity marker. The path integral is the 3D shadow of the 4D geometric fact dx₄/dt = ic.

The reading reinforces the joint-derivation argument of §XI: the Born rule (Proposition III.1), the superposition principle (Proposition IV.1), the apparent collapse (Proposition V.1), the irreversibility (Proposition VI.1), the preferred basis (Proposition VII.1), the nonlocality (Proposition VIII.1), the absence of a separate (R) law (Proposition IX.1), and now the path integral itself — eight foundational features of quantum mechanics, all theorems of one geometric principle. The structural reduction continues: where standard quantum mechanics presents these as eight independent features requiring eight independent foundational accounts, the McGucken framework presents them as eight readings of one geometric fact.

The path integral has been the calculational backbone of quantum field theory for eighty years. It has had no foundational source. The McGucken framework supplies one — and supplies, with it, the physical content that Feynman acknowledged was missing from his own formulation: the photon really does follow every path, because every point on x₄'s expanding nonlocality is the photon's path, and the photon's position is always on the expanding surface of nonlocality.
